An update on the data incident announced on 8 October

We recognise that this incident has caused concern to many of our cardholders, and we sincerely regret the concern and inconvenience caused.

This update sets out the steps taken since our last announcement and the precautions that cardholders are advised to take.

What we have done since our last update

- We have filed a police report and are working with the police and the relevant authorities on their investigation.
- We have engaged independent security experts to carry out a security audit of our systems related to card services.
- We have paused new Based Visa Card signups until the independent security audit of our card services systems is complete.
- Requests to close accounts have been processed. Our operations and compliance team is handling the orderly withdrawal of funds for those accounts.
- We are strengthening our internal security controls and working towards recognised third-party security certifications.

Support for affected cardholders

We are finalising further support measures for affected cardholders, which will include identity monitoring services. Eligible cardholders will be contacted directly by email once the arrangements have been confirmed.

What has not changed

Based on our investigations to date:
- The Based Wallet, including perps trading and onchain swaps, was not affected and continues to work as normal.
- Card numbers, CVVs, PINs, ID photographs and liveness check images were not affected.
- Funds on your Based Visa Card are safe, and cards continue to work as normal. Cashback and rebates continue to accrue.
- Be careful of anyone who contacts you using your personal details
- We will never ask for your card number, PIN, CVV, passwords or seed phrase.
- Based Visa Card support is only available through the in-app support chat.
- Our team members will never DM you on Telegram or X about your account.
-  Do not click links or sign wallet transactions from unsolicited messages.
- Our emails about this incident will direct you to check details in the app. They will never ask you to enter card details, payment information or passwords through a link.

Further updates will be shared with affected cardholders directly by email. 

This update reflects our understanding as of today and may change as the investigation continues.

author: jt_rose
quoted_text:
A new paper from Apple engineers ends with a line we couldn’t have written better ourselves:

"if idle macOS devices across organizations [...] can be securely federated, they could form a massive, shared GPU resource pool that benefits the broader ecosystem."

That’s what we’re building with Darkbloom.

The paper's Minions is a system that pool idle Apple Silicon Macs into a distributed GPU cloud for on-prem inference. Queue times went from 10+ hours to minutes. Zero new GPU purchases. Zero infrastructure cost.

It runs inside Apple, on coworkers’ Macs, using the company’s own storage and access controls. When a team needs more capacity, they Slack colleagues and ask them to turn on the executor. Even in that setting, the top adoption concern was data confidentiality. People were wary of their jobs running on a colleague’s Mac. Apple’s fix was to keep each team’s work on its own team’s machines.

Which brings it back to that one word in the conclusion: “securely.”

Inside a company, you can shrink the network until you trust everyone in it. On an open network, the machine belongs to a stranger and there’s no one to Slack. Keeping prompts private and outputs honest on hardware you don’t control is the hard problem that we solved at Darkbloom.

Apple built the on-prem version. 
Darkbloom is the open one.

text:
I spent 48 hours in SF hanging out with billionaires, data labs and AI founders and execs running $1B to $100B companies.

My observations:

1. Sooo MANY stories of data brokers making like $2M a WEEK selling company data to labs. I can't tell if it's the beginning or a bubble, and I kept wondering which niches are left. Digging into it actively.

2. At dinner, someone asked the table, "If a new model drops next month, does your company get better or worse?" HALF the table went quiet! I think that's the best question to ask about any AI startup right now.

3. The bar people talk about now is hitting $1B in revenue in 12 months (I guess that's the new unicorn?). What I didn't hear much about is retention. AI revenue can come in fast and leave fast, and I think we're going to see a lot of stories of AI companies with huge revenue and terrible retention.

4. It's pretty clear we're living through the reinvention of the computer. The model is the CPU, the harness is the operating system, and skills and plugins are the apps. Thinking about it that way makes it easier to see where the whitespace is.

5. We're maybe 12 months from an agent that can watch you work for a week and then do your job without any instructions. The screen recording plus agent memory plus local model combination makes this possible right now.

6. Agent harnesses feel like the new GPT wrappers, in a good way, especially vertical ones. The best teams I talked to treat the model as swappable. One founder walked me through routing different models to different jobs: one for taste and visuals, a cheaper one for the everyday stuff, another for text. 

They use prompts they can move across models over fine-tuning, and A/B test the output on what users actually do with it: do they edit it, export it, share it? A vertical harness is basically four things: the connectors for that industry's data, evals written by people who know the work, rules for what the agent can and can't touch, and a clean screen for a human to review. The model is maybe 20% of it.

7. There's a lot of reverse engineering going on/cloning going on more than I've ever seen. People are decompiling software and rebuilding it with agents, and someone showed a suite of like 10 apps that are worth $5B+ each all that he cloned open source. Me and everyone are still thinking through what it means when software gets this easy to copy.

8. My guess is the value moves to data. If the software can be rebuilt quickly, what's worth paying for in a legacy SaaS company is the years of customer data and workflows inside it. Some SaaS companies are secretly data companies. 

Gets me thinking about how do you truly value data for this saas companies? Like if we were buying these dying saas companies at 2x ARR before (as example), maybe there is a better metric. Idk, just thinking out loud here.

9. It feels like a good chunk of legacy software won't make it to the agentic era, especially anything built around people clicking through a lot of screens.

10. Every company I talked to wants to pipe its internal data into one place and expose it to agents through MCP. Then they look at the data and realize it's a mess: five versions of the same customer, old Slack channels, PDFs nobody can search. Cleaning that up feels like a big consulting opportunity!

11. A lot of founders are building the basic building blocks for agents: APIs, data layers and tools. Some of the companies I saw barely have a UI because the main user is an agent. I really believe the startups that build primitives to this agentic era will do extremely well. Building blocks is the best way to think about it.

12. Labs can get plenty of training data, but it's harder to get real examples of agents failing inside companies. Whoever has those logs has something valuable.

13. Someone running a big consumer company told me the next fight is over memory. The model that remembers the most about you wins, and the smartest model matters less than people think.

14. Physical AI came up a lot. Astra I think was the first model that got people into AI can actually do CAD, and I think a lot of people are thinking what does vibe manufacturing really look like. The line I keep thinking about came from a robotics founder: the hardest problems in AI are deployment problems now, not research problems. Their robots work on their own, call a human when they get stuck, and every one of those calls becomes training data.

15. Cybersecurity companies are having a moment and are actually cool companies to build now, especially the ones that clean up after a breach. Every agent with access to your systems is a new door into your company, and a lot of those doors were left open. 

16. Some startups are worth more dead than alive now. A shutdown company with 5 years of Slack, email and code can get paid for licensing all of it. I wouldn't be surprised if founders start factoring that into when they shut down.

17. People are starting to talk about monetizing the agent web. It feels really early, but when the most popular user of the internet is an agent, what startups should you be building?

18. I think agent insurance is coming. Once an agent makes an expensive mistake, insurers will want audits before they cover anyone.

19. Several people said the hire they want most is someone with taste who can write evals. The models are getting good at generating ideas, so the hard part is judging which ones are good.

20. New trend I observed: startup raises VC, uses venture dollars to become a creator, startup fails, founder falls back on being a full-time creator and incubates other products bootstrapped.

21. Getting SIGNIFICANT distribution is HARD right now. Founders are sponsoring buses, buying billboards like crazy and throwing parties with famous DJs to get noticed. Kinda feels dotcom era in that sense. 

Attention is what's scarce! The growth guy going viral sharing his UGC strategy from Wispr Flow is a good example. It's the sauce everyone wants, and I truly believe there are probably only 50 people on the planet who know how to scale these types of businesses efficiently in this era.

Always good to get that dose of SF. I felt sooo lucky to have such an incredible trip during such an incredible time in building businesses. Surreal in so many ways. 

Happy to be home and locked in.

Until next time!

text:
🟣 7,3 milliards de $PAPER ont été émis par Papertrade. Mais comment la supply est-elle actuellement répartie ?

Lancé il y a 4 jours sur HyperEVM, @papertrade_xyz a enregistré plus de 1 T de dollars de volume, avec un open interest qui a culminé à 10,1 Md.

Sur Papertrade, le $PAPER ne peut s'obtenir qu'en perdant un trade ou bien en se faisant liquider. Les traders affichent aujourd'hui une perte nette de 46 M$, et 7,30 milliards de $PAPER ont été mintés.

Pour le moment, la seule utilité du token repose sur le staking, qui permet de percevoir une partie des frais générés par le protocole. À ce jour, plus de 38 M$ ont déjà été reversés aux stakers.

Nous nous sommes donc demandé quelle était la répartition de cette supply :

◻️ Près de la moitié des wallets (49,7 %) détiennent moins de 10 000 PAPER, et la tranche 1 000 – 10 000 regroupe à elle seule plus d'un tiers des holders (35,1 %).

◻️ 856 wallets dépassent le million de PAPER. Au taux d'émission maximal de 100 PAPER par dollar perdu, cela représente au moins 10 000 $ de pertes chacun (on ne compte pas les récompenses de stakings, qui, pour la majeure partie, leur ont permis de couvrir leurs pertes).

◻️ Le plus gros wallet détient environ 252 M de PAPER, soit 3,5 % de la supply totale actuelle.

◻️ 99,2 % de l'offre est stakée, un chiffre à relativiser puisque les transferts sont encore désactivés et que le staking est pour l'instant la seule utilité du token.

Reste à savoir comment évoluera cette répartition à l'ouverture des transferts, et surtout comment la plateforme continuera à générer assez de fees pour garantir des récompenses de staking assez attractives pour couvrir les potentielles pertes des traders.

⚠️Les métriques que nous avons utilisées sont celles du 14/10 à 17 h 30. Attention, ces métriques sont susceptibles d'évoluer fortement dans les prochains jours.

text:
New post on Eth Research!

How Much Screening Buys a Second? Speed, Selection, and the Maker's Spread

By:
- @nuconstruct

🔗 https://t.co/4uGgB6tCtz

Highlights:
- A competitive break-even spread can be derived with minimal assumptions—only that the price innovation over the quote-exposure horizon has finite expected absolute value—so the results apply even with jumps, point masses (atoms), and infinite variance.
- Empirically, 1-second ETH-USDT midpoint innovations are highly non-Gaussian: about 73% of seconds have zero price change and the distribution has extreme excess kurtosis (154), meaning many calm seconds and occasional large jumps.
- Because of this non-Gaussian shape, reducing quote exposure from 12 seconds to 1 second cuts expected absolute price shock by 84.5% (much more than the 71.1% predicted by a Gaussian diffusion), so Gaussian rules materially understate the value of speed.
- To match a 1-second unscreened venue while quoting at 12-second cadence, a maker must screen out roughly 84.5% of informed flow (about “six in seven” informed orders), and this threshold remains ~84.5–85.2% over plausible toxicity levels, so the conclusion is robust to uncertain toxicity.
- In trending periods, staleness shows up one-sidedly at execution: with-trend fills achieve an effective spread about 11.1 bps better than against-trend fills across all four pools, and discrepancies grow with elapsed staleness with elasticity ~0.45 (near the diffusion benchmark of 0.5).

ELI5:
When a liquidity provider (LP) posts a buy and sell price, they can lose money if someone who knows the price just moved trades against their now-outdated (stale) quote. LPs can protect themselves in two main ways: (1) update their price more often (be faster), or (2) reject trades that look “too informed” (screening). This article measures how much screening a slow LP would need to do to be as safe as a fast LP. Using crypto data, it finds that because real 1‑second price changes are very ‘lumpy’ (usually zero, sometimes big jumps), speed is extremely valuable: to make up for being stuck with 12‑second staleness, you’d need to reject about 85% of informed trades.

text:
Anthropic 告诉投资人：蒸馏占营收 5% 到 7%，三季度已大幅削减

Anthropic 周三向投资人通报，“蒸馏”带来的收入占公司营收的 5% 到 7%，第三季度公司已经把这部分“大幅”削减。消息来自英国《金融时报》（FT），援引四位直接知情人士；The Information 也报道了同样的区间。

蒸馏是什么？就是拿更强模型的回答当教材，训练自己的模型。对手实验室向 Claude 大量提问，把回答收集起来喂给自家模型，就能用较低成本学到 Claude 的一部分本事。

既然是“学”，为什么会算进 Anthropic 的营收？因为这些提问走的是付费接口，每一次调用都按用量计费。蒸馏动辄要问几百万、上千万次，FT 的说法是蒸馏“涉及大量使用和花费”。也就是说，这笔收入是对手实打实付的钱，只是付钱的目的是训练竞争对手的模型。Anthropic 的商业服务条款明确禁止用它的服务“训练有竞争关系的 AI 模型”。

5% 到 7% 是多少钱？报道没说这是哪个时段的占比，所以只能估算。网上流传的算法是按二季度营收 115 亿美元算，对应约 5.75 亿到 8 亿美元。注意这是推算，不是报道里的数字。115 亿美元这个数，来自 8 月彭博社看到的公司文件，原文是“超过 115 亿美元”，属于初步数字，Anthropic 没有公开确认。

报道也没说这些钱来自哪几家公司。今年 2 月，Anthropic 曾发文点名 DeepSeek、月之暗面（Moonshot）和 MiniMax，说三家通过约 2.4 万个虚假账号，绕过 Claude 不对中国提供服务的限制，和 Claude 进行了 1600 多万次对话来蒸馏。

主动砍掉这部分收入是有代价的。Anthropic 正在筹备上市，同一次通报显示，它三季度营收 168 亿美元，比二季度增长约 46%，而二季度比一季度翻了一倍多，增速已经放慢。据报道，公司告诉投资人，蒸馏收入减少会拖累本季度的数字；换来的是对手更难靠抄 Claude 的答案追上来。

text:
“恐怖PPI”撞上芯片股崩盘：市值蒸发1万亿，杠杆资金仍在抄底 

美国9月PPI“恐怖数据”大超预期：年率6.3%（预期5.3%）、月率1.3%（预期0.5%），核心PPI同比仍高5.0%，通胀粘性极强，将显著抬升10月29日PCE预期，进一步封堵物价回落至2%路径。

与此同时，芯片股市值蒸发1万亿美元，费城半导体指数过去6个交易日累跌12%。

text:
Today we are re-launching shaders in https://t.co/QCeiUQKHOF. We call them Vibe Shaders. There's nothing else like them. They live next to your .pen files as GLSL files and can be easily vibecoded right on the canvas. Built by designers for designers.

They deserved a special Shader Mode, a focused mode to finetune the uniforms directly in the context of your design.

In addition to the classic Shader Fills, we've also added Shader Effects. This allows for incredible creative flexibility, as it applies the effect on a whole object tree that's part of a particular frame and you can change everything live, no hustling with textures.

Additionally we are also launching Background Shaders, they sample the texture from everything below the object. Imagine creating your own custom background blur or a partial dither effect for objects below a frame.

You can also create shaders with 3D transformations to vector logos or build custom shader brushes for vectors paths.

Forget having just a fixed set of shaders, this is next level and only possible, because we have a full control over our custom renderer. We also automatically compute the SDF (signed distance field) in realtime, so vectors that have applied shaders can be changed directly on canvas without the need to re-export a new SDF file, an incredible time-saver.

Look for the samples in Goodies, which has been updated with a ton of new examples.

Or simply pair @pendev with the latest models, drop in a bunch of images, ask agent to build you a shader and it's guaranteed you will feel an explosion of your creative superpowers!

text:
Humanoid shipments went from roughly 3,000 units in 2024 to about 19,100 in the first half of 2026, and 97% of them are built in China. Meanwhile, Morgan Stanley’s base case puts the humanoid economy at $5T by 2050. 

Rapid growth across the vertical, yet few have a proper understanding of the robotics industry.

The Great Embodiment is our complete @a1research__ overview of robotics, written for allocators and analysts who want to close that gap.

The core question is why this is happening now and not a decade ago. The answer? Six curves crossed in one short window: model capability, compute cost, hardware cost, labor scarcity, sovereign capital and the first public proof points. Each one has been true before. All six at once has not.

From there the report maps the industry as it actually operates:

- The three inputs: actuators at 40 to 60% of a humanoid’s bill of materials, one brain architecture every serious lab has converged on, and training data that has to be manufactured because there is no internet of actions

- Five layers, from components to deployment, and who captures margin in each

- Two chokepoints: Beijing’s leverage over rare-earth magnets and the actuator supply chain, and Washington’s over compute and capital markets

- The deployment gap: roughly one unit in ten shipped in 2025 does a real job, which is the number the valuations are betting on changing

- Five operator metrics that separate deployment from demonstration, because the demos will not tell you

- Where crypto fits: data provenance, capital formation and machine coordination, in a category still valued under $1B

Read the full report below! ↓

text:
把已有的 Claude、Codex 订阅接入 Grok Bot，让不同 AI 直接协作，这个思路很实用。

我现在更倾向于：一个任务入口，多个可替换的执行器。

真正重要的不只是模型能不能调用，而是三件事：

1. 凭证与权限不能随意在 Bot 之间流转。
2. 模型路由只维护一处，不在每个 system prompt 里硬编码。
3. 每项任务必须有执行证据、验收结果和状态写回。

把多个 AI 连起来只是第一步。让它们可靠地完成工作，才是关键。

we just launched something pretty interesting under jupiter labs.

introducing YOLO. 500x to 1000x leverage.

yes, 1000x.

we’ve been experimenting with a different approach to high leverage trading, and YOLO is our first attempt at it.

the idea is pretty simple. what if we could let people trade with extremely high leverage, without actually having to execute these massive leveraged positions in the market?

so we took inspiration from the JLP model and built YOLO, where positions are simulated against real market prices, but the profits and losses are real.

this allows us to offer leverage that goes far beyond what we currently have on jupiter perps, using a completely different approach.

of course, this also comes with some tradeoffs.

since profits are paid out from the pool, if there isn’t enough liquidity to pay out a winning position, the payout can be queued instead of being paid immediately.

it’s a different model from traditional perps, with its own risks and limitations, but i think it’s an interesting experiment worth exploring.

one thing i’ve always liked about building onchain is how much room there is to experiment with new financial products and trading experiences.

and that’s also why we’re launching YOLO under jupiter labs. to give ideas like this a place to be tested, without necessarily having to fit into our existing products.

i’m quite excited to see how people use YOLO and what we can learn from it.

it’s still early, and there are probably many things we can improve along the way.

but that’s the fun part of building and experimenting.

give it a try, understand the risks, and let us know what you think.

text:
Talked to Michael from Coreweave about debt six months ago: 

18:18–23:43: Jason asks about CoreWeave’s debt; Michael answers (cleaned of filler words and stutters, otherwise as spoken)

JASON: How does all that debt work? That is something you guys specialize in. Corporate debt… I’m in the venture business, people are like, “Why should I be in venture when corporate debt pays so well?” Corporate paper’s so huge. I’m curious how this fits in, and what interest rate people are paying on, you know, a billion dollars in infrastructure. What do they pay on that?

MICHAEL: So CoreWeave has really been the innovator around a lot of the financing engines that have come to bear on this. We did the first GPU-based loans. I’m going to try to explain this in a way people can understand. What we do is we go out and we find a client. Let’s use Microsoft; you brought them up before. Microsoft comes to us and says, “We’d like to buy some compute from you.” And we say, “Okay, great. We’re going to sign a contract.” Once I have a contract in hand, I create something. It’s not a particularly creative name. It’s called the box.

JASON: Yeah.

MICHAEL: And what I do with the box is I take my contract with Microsoft and I put it in the box. I go to Jensen and buy the GPUs, I put them in the box. I take my data center contract, I put it in the box. And now the box governs cash flow. It has a waterfall of cash flow that comes into it and goes out of it. So the way it works is I build the compute, I deliver the compute to Microsoft, and they pay the box. They don’t pay me. It goes into the box, and the first thing it does is pay the data center. It pays the power bill. It pays the interest and the principal. And then whatever’s left flows back to us.

So it is an incredibly well-structured, time-tested, pressure-tested vehicle to be able to borrow money against client paper and all of the other collateral around the deal. That’s why CoreWeave, a company many people had never heard of, was able to go out and raise $35 billion in 18 months to build infrastructure at scale. But what’s important to understand is the economics in this box are such that within 2.5 years of a 5-year deal, we have paid for everything.

JASON: The principal’s been paid off.

MICHAEL: The principal’s been paid off, the interest has been paid off. The return into the box is such that we’re able to generate returns to our company at the box level, which gives the most sophisticated lenders in the world, whether banks or private equity funds or whoever, confidence that they’re going to achieve the one rule of lending, which is “give me my money back.”

JASON: Yes. Works better when that happens. So they look at this box and they’re like, “Wow, we’re really confident we’re going to get our money back.” And maybe they want 10 boxes.

MICHAEL: That’s correct.

JASON: And if any one box goes upside down, you can deal with it and it’s not as acute.

MICHAEL: That’s correct. And they don’t cross-pollinate. They don’t cause contagion across the boxes. They’re all independent and discrete. That’s one. Number two: as you do this and show the lenders how this financing mechanism works, they continue to lend you money at progressively lower rates. When you think about our cost of capital over the last two years, we have dropped it by 600 basis points.

JASON: Wow.

MICHAEL: It is enormous. So you’re seeing a company driving its cost of capital down toward where the hyperscalers borrow, which will let us be competitive with them over time. And we have been extremely militant and diligent about feeding, watering and caring for those boxes, so we continue to have access to the capital markets in a way that lets us build and drive our business.

JASON: That means you have to say no to maybe some people who want to be in the box.

MICHAEL: Yeah. We look at some deals where they want to buy GPUs for a year, and I say that’s not a deal I can do, because it’s too short for me to amortize the expenses. So I won’t do that.

JASON: And they can go to another provider who maybe wants to take that risk on, who has extra capacity.

MICHAEL: Absolutely. But our business is really built around the risk management of getting to scale. In my mind, during this period of disequilibrium, when there aren’t enough GPUs in the world to provide compute for all the different use cases in AI, what matters for my company is to get enormously large. That drives down our cost of capital, and it means information flows in from all different parts of the market: large language models, high-speed trading, search, all of these things. They feed information back to us that tells us the next product we need to build, where they need help scaling, or what type of compute they need. All of that information flow is incredibly valuable to us.

(Jason moves on to demand at 23:43.)

Recursion Announces New Clinical Data Across Two Potential First-in-Class Programs, Sanofi Partnership Milestone, and Oversubscribed $200M Offering

Today, we announced important progress across our clinical pipeline, partnerships, and capital position—reflecting growing evidence of what our integrated AI-enabled drug discovery platform can deliver.

🚀 REC-4881 | Deep, durable polyp reductions in FAP
In an expanded adult population (18+), 87% of patients achieved polyp burden reductions after 12 weeks (47% median), with 85% remaining below baseline after 12 weeks off treatment.

In the upper GI—the area of greatest unmet need—92% achieved reductions (55% median), including two patients with near-complete reductions (≥98%). Of those with reductions, 92% remained below baseline after 12 weeks off treatment.

With no approved pharmacologic therapies for FAP, we are targeting registrational trial initiation in 2H 2027, pending FDA discussions. Full data will be presented November 2 at CGA-IGC.

🚀 REC-1245 | Encouraging early activity in heavily pretreated cancer patients
Our potential first-in-class oral RBM39 degrader demonstrated three partial responses (two confirmed in endometrial cancer; one unconfirmed in liver cancer) and 91.7% disease control (11/12) at doses ≥45 mg. No dose-limiting toxicities or treatment-related serious adverse events were observed at the selected 45 mg expansion dose.

🚀 Sanofi | First development candidate optioned
Two challenging targets, one oral molecule. A potential first-in-class candidate for inflammatory disease, enabled by Recursion’s AI platform and small-molecule chemistry capabilities alongside Sanofi’s expertise.
Phase 1 expected in 2027, marking the sixth progress-based milestone across our collaboration.

🚀 $200M Oversubscribed Follow-On Offering | Extending Runway Into 2029
Broad demand from leading healthcare specialists, long-only institutions, and growth investors, including Janus Henderson Investors, Invus, Longaeva Partners, ARK Invest, and Driehaus Capital Management.

The financing supports advancement of our clinical pipeline, continued AI engine innovation, and strategic partnerships.

text:
A lot of talk about $CRWV's 2031 bond yield crossing 16%. Yet it has $104B in reported backlog.

does it make sense for both to be true?

the main risk here is whether CoreWeave can keep financing the GPUs needed to serve that demand.

one $2.6B loan (diagram below) reveals something interesting: the loan matures in ~5 years. But the customer contracts backing it average ~3 years..

that means CoreWeave must keep repaying the loan after its initial customer contracts expire. It needs those customers to renew, or new customers to rent the same GPUs.

lenders accepted that risk in Aug when the loan closed. But will they keep accepting it (and at what price?)

some numbers:
- In H1 2026, CoreWeave generated $3.7B in operating cash, spent $14.9B on investing activities, and brought in $14B through financing.

to be fair, CoreWeave successfully raised another $4.2B through convertible notes in September. there's no demonstrated funding gap today. And the 16% bond yield isn't the cost of all its debt.

the next financing deal is the test i'd watch.
can CoreWeave continue borrowing against shorter customer contracts on similar terms? or will lenders start demanding higher rates/more equity/shorter terms?

new GPU deployments will slow even while demand remains strong if financing tightens

I used @tessara_ai  to investigate the financing structures, and verified the details against the filings.

quoted_text:
Anthropic 告诉投资人：蒸馏占营收 5% 到 7%，三季度已大幅削减

Anthropic 周三向投资人通报，“蒸馏”带来的收入占公司营收的 5% 到 7%，第三季度公司已经把这部分“大幅”削减。消息来自英国《金融时报》（FT），援引四位直接知情人士；The Information 也报道了同样的区间。

蒸馏是什么？就是拿更强模型的回答当教材，训练自己的模型。对手实验室向 Claude 大量提问，把回答收集起来喂给自家模型，就能用较低成本学到 Claude 的一部分本事。

既然是“学”，为什么会算进 Anthropic 的营收？因为这些提问走的是付费接口，每一次调用都按用量计费。蒸馏动辄要问几百万、上千万次，FT 的说法是蒸馏“涉及大量使用和花费”。也就是说，这笔收入是对手实打实付的钱，只是付钱的目的是训练竞争对手的模型。Anthropic 的商业服务条款明确禁止用它的服务“训练有竞争关系的 AI 模型”。

5% 到 7% 是多少钱？报道没说这是哪个时段的占比，所以只能估算。网上流传的算法是按二季度营收 115 亿美元算，对应约 5.75 亿到 8 亿美元。注意这是推算，不是报道里的数字。115 亿美元这个数，来自 8 月彭博社看到的公司文件，原文是“超过 115 亿美元”，属于初步数字，Anthropic 没有公开确认。

报道也没说这些钱来自哪几家公司。今年 2 月，Anthropic 曾发文点名 DeepSeek、月之暗面（Moonshot）和 MiniMax，说三家通过约 2.4 万个虚假账号，绕过 Claude 不对中国提供服务的限制，和 Claude 进行了 1600 多万次对话来蒸馏。

主动砍掉这部分收入是有代价的。Anthropic 正在筹备上市，同一次通报显示，它三季度营收 168 亿美元，比二季度增长约 46%，而二季度比一季度翻了一倍多，增速已经放慢。据报道，公司告诉投资人，蒸馏收入减少会拖累本季度的数字；换来的是对手更难靠抄 Claude 的答案追上来。

text:
Crypto Card and Onchain Neobank Taxes in the EU

Every crypto card and onchain neobank should have an article like this

Projects constantly talk about cashback, fees, and benefits. But almost nobody explains how taxes work when you pay with crypto

Thanks to Krak for publishing a detailed FAQ explaining the tax rules for EU users

Here are the main points:
- if you pay with your EUR balance without converting crypto, there's usually no crypto sale to tax
- EUR cashback is treated as a discount rather than taxable income in many EU countries
- BTC cashback may also be treated as a discount when you receive it
- referral bonuses may be taxed as income
- simply buying and holding crypto is usually not taxable
- selling, swapping, or spending crypto can trigger taxes
- if you pay with BTC, ETH, or another cryptocurrency, you may have a taxable gain or loss
- even buying a €5 coffee can trigger a taxable event
- example: You bought BTC for €500 and later spent it with your card when it was worth €700. The €200 gain may be taxable
- paying with stablecoins also counts as selling crypto, even if you made no profit
- swapping ETH to USDC before paying with your card can create two separate taxable events
- the crypto you choose to spend can affect your taxes
- taxable gains are calculated based on how much you originally paid for the crypto
- selling BTC received as cashback may trigger taxes.
- you should keep a record of the BTC price when you receive cashback
- getting a refund doesn't undo the original crypto sale for tax purposes
- withdrawing cash from an ATM using crypto can also trigger taxes
- conversion and card fees can affect your tax calculations
- small purchases aren't automatically tax-free
- DAC8 rules have been in effect since January 1, 2026. Crypto platforms must collect and report certain user data to tax authorities 
- the first DAC8 reports covering 2026 will be submitted in 2027
- you can export your transaction history, but you're responsible for calculating your own taxes

Important: Tax rules vary across EU countries. They depend on where you're a tax resident, which crypto you use, how long you've held it, and local tax exemptions

I'd like to see every crypto card project explain taxes like this.

Do you track taxes when using crypto cards?

text:
You can send a message in seconds. Moving an investment can take much longer.

Behind the screen, financial companies need to confirm ownership, update records, and complete the transfer. Those steps often involve separate systems.

Avalanche is infrastructure, that companies can use, to bring more of that activity onto a blockchain. That’s what people mean by “onchain financial rails.”

What does that look like?

A company can issue a digital token representing a financial asset, then use a shared network to record its movement.

For example, a tokenized fund gives investors a digital representation of their holding. The underlying investment still exists, while the blockchain records who holds the tokens.

Why does it matter?

When companies use separate records, they have to check that those records match. Shared infrastructure can reduce that work and help transfers complete more efficiently.

For institutions, that can mean less time waiting for assets to move and more flexibility in how they use them.

That’s the opportunity Avalanche is working toward: improving the systems behind the financial services people already use. 🔺

text:
From κ = 2⁻¹⁸² to 0.0017137844912361143 :)

Integer multiplication community auto-research highlights since 10/13 (+2.6%):

1) Progress slowed the past few days and we hit the wall… then broke through it overnight!

1337isnot1337 posted a "no new κ" research PR on anticipatory dirty borrowing.

Instead of paying for a fresh scratch "helper" register, a helper borrows another register that's idle at that moment, and hands it back restored. That cut helpers per call from 480 to 400 in their test word.

About two hours later it was a new record. 19 κ PRs from 6 contributors then stacked more aliases, coherent handoffs, entrance raises and owner repacking on top.

κ increased +1.4% in about 13 hours(still unverified and requires full review). 

We're now within 1.7% of the bit side's 0.001733, so the bit wall is next.

2) We're slowing on progress in Integer Multiplication bounds, but multiple early auto-researchers are now applying the same tricks to more meaningful projects:

@ryaneshea is working on protein design and generally interested in applications of auto-research to bio.

@dysmemic discovered 665 possible new exoplanets by searching 4 million stars in NASA's public TESS data!

I began open sourcing our new geometric approach to self-attention, which beats transformers(NanoGPT) KV cache with 14,000x less state and 50% better CE at 2K context.

We've been working on publishing a paper the past few months, but it's clear the explosion of decentralized auto-research on Github is where things are headed.

We should keep pushing Integer Multiplication bounds since it's easy to understand and easy to make progress, thus new contributors gain motivation and we grow the auto-research community faster. Auto-researchers seem to naturally then branch into harder problems when they gain motivation with successful PRs :)

3) The flood keeps growing

518 PRs in the last 24 hours (up from 285 last time) from 64 contributors, 20 of them first-timers. That's 840 PRs in 36 hours. 

@0xdoug merged ~760 PRs in two big batches on 10/14. He also updated the autoresarch.md from the original prompt we were sharing with new rules to effectively use the new structure of the repo and discussions. 

Copy this prompt to join the auto-research army 🫡 :
"""
> Contribute one useful, independently reviewable result to: https://t.co/KZP78PN7ZR

> Start from the current main branch. Read AGENTS.md and autoresearch.md, and follow their guidance for choosing work
"""

Interesting observations:

1) Negative results really do feed breakthroughs. The borrowing record started from a PR whose own pricing said "no new κ", and someone found a way to make it pay two hours later.

Great example that don't need to push the frontier kappa to contribute: you can task your agents on exploring our research tracks in auto-research.md to and multiple human-agent teams will review it to collaborate. 

Anyone can help now by throwing tokens at a hard open problem guided by experts. Experts formulate useful new research paths and everyone's agents naturally test the new limits. 

2) Codex/OpenAI is mentioned in 73% of the last day's PRs and Claude in 19%.

Most prolific in the last 24 hours: 1337isnot1337 (80 PRs), ywz65 (50, all in the last 4 hours!), adamgall (39), commdata2338 (34) and thakrarsagar (33). jeremykothe2 filed 12 of the 19 records since borrowing landed.

3) Not all researchers are lamenting the end of their careers. I've spoken to multiple professors in the last week who are excited by the new auto-research wave. 

It accelerates tedious experiments, the students that previously ran those can now focus on more important work, and Google's Deep Review now even automates peer review!

We can imagine a future were researchers are given super powers to focus on the most meaningful tasks, and publish breakthroughs at a higher rate than before.

Even our own experiments in Integer Mult bounds clearly shows human experts have the key intuition to guide the models to out-of-distribution solutions. 

4) First auto-research, and now auto-peer-review!

Google’s Deep Review runs a team of agents over your paper: it splits the doc into sections, spends more compute on the dense parts like proofs, reviews each section in parallel, then checks the findings against each other. It assists researchers in peer-review by submitting feedback. 

It’s already reviewed 16K+ papers at ICML, NeurIPS and ICLR.

https://t.co/j1NdEuo2vn

5) We can use frontier research as a new benchmark for agents! 

Basically, rewind a frontier research repo like Integer multiplication to an earlier branch, and test different agent harnesses and prompts.

Agents can’t “cheat” if you disable web search and use a checkpoint before the solution is published.

There’s diminishing returns, but we can calculate the curve for a given task to estimate the cost and returns.

With this benchmark we discovered sharing context is actually BAD(for this task), and running parallel independent agents speeds the next breakthrough. 

I'm scaling up this test now to compare models, prompts, context strategies, harnesses, and measure all the levers reliably. 

If you know register allocation, linear circuit synthesis or lattice codes, please consider looking at our helper and P104 problems. If you know friends who can contribute, please repost and share this with them🙏

https://t.co/JTNFd4s07o
author: 0xdoug
quoted_text:
From κ = 2⁻¹⁸² to 0.001661 :)

Integer multiplication community auto-research highlights since 10/11 (+28.9%):

1) The bit side broke through!

The bit side jumped first: eumemic put Sussman's E8 unit on a 420-helper bit word (+4.18%).

DreamingOfClouds' "punctured star" unit then pushed the bit side to c = 0.001733. That made the complex side the limit again.

Since then, the complex side has been catching up at 0.03–0.7% per PR, so we'll hit the wall soon and need more research on new designs. 

2) There's a flood of new auto-researchers :)

In the last 4 hours, we doubled and about 85 new contributors opened their first PR!

Most recent submissions are negative research results, which help push the search toward a new design. 

Posting the getting-started prompt on Github may have triggered this, and the prompt guides new contributors to focus on specific research tracks rather than just beating the current record incrementally. 

On 10/11, we published a research log of negative results to help agents collaborate, and the community has taken up that effort. 

New best practices are being learned and built daily.

3) The call for new geometry worked!

After the last post, contributors started exploring Leech/Turyn and Niemeier lattices. We screened Leech and Barnes–Wall: both lose as a straight swap for E8, and BW16's doubling block structure is now a documented lead.

If you’re an expert in adjacent fields like lattices, coding theory or linear circuits, we need your help to investigate new geometries. 

Interesting observations:

1) We had a call with the top auto-researchers to share best practices. The recording is attached below!

We discussed building a custom harness that allows people to spend their unused tokens on auto-research.

We also spoke about Github issues, what models/harness everyone uses, and our goals in auto-research.

It's not a problem yet, but GitHub could get overloaded if thousands of auto-researchers start submitting PRs every minute, so we'll need tools to handle it soon. 

Most top auto-researchers use Codex with GPT-6 Astra or Claude with Opus 5.5, and @ryaneshea is using Conductor, which apparently has free sandboxes (!).

One contributor even built their own private harness, and @dysmemic has a proxy to combine all his subscriptions. 

2) We analyzed all the agent PR data:

285 PRs were opened in the last 24 hours by 110 different contributors. 229 mention Codex/OpenAI, and 70 mention Claude (mostly Opus 5.5).

180 of those PRs landed in the last 4 hours alone, almost one a minute.

Most prolific contributors: jeremykothe2 with 39 PRs, thakrarsagar with 24, and chafreaky with 14.

Codex still files the most PRs, but several top teams pair Codex with Claude Code, and some run their own harnesses.

3) X is becoming the real-time social layer over GitHub for auto-research, with experts helping in the comments (thanks, @davidryan59 and @bramcohen).

You don't even need to run a model to contribute: post an idea on X, and contributors will test it quickly for you.

There was some slight backlash to auto-research, but most people are supportive. With the barrier to entry now just a comment on X, nothing is stopping it.

I empathize with mathematicians losing control of their life's work, and we need to find ways to augment researchers with super powers rather than replace them: most of our recent breakthroughs required expert intuition to guide the models to out-of-distribution solutions. 

We plan on building a custom harness to help researchers and non-technical users get more involved. 

Ben Recht published an essay yesterday criticizing OpenAI's FFT research for being galactic and practically impossible to implement, which is valid, but generally auto-research feels like a train no one can stop now. 

4) My auto-research dashboard got overloaded with traffic, but it's back up now! https://t.co/jnmILOweih

We had an explosion of traffic in the last day, so I had to optimize my small contribution tracker :)

If the general public starts contributing tokens, we could reach millions of researchers collaborating globally in real time!

It feels like the Homebrew Computer Club: everyone is excited and building just for the fun of it, and there's a sense that we could actually change the world :)

text:
This is a legitimately amazing paper. TL;DR: They made a microfluidic chip that can trap a million individual cells, hooked it up to a microscope, and used it to connect genetic circuits --> single-cell behaviors.

Say you want to build a complicated gene circuit, like an oscillator with a period of six hours. Normally, you’d make a design, put it into cells, watch it fail, redesign it, and try again.

With this system, you can instead make a million variants in a single tube, introduce them into cells, and trap those cells in the chip to see which designs work. You can then pull out a “winning” cell using optical tweezers, or identify which gene circuit it received via in situ sequencing.

(Each circuit carries a short genetic barcode. You sequence the gene circuit variants beforehand to link each barcode to a design. Then, reading those barcodes inside the chip, using in situ sequencing, tells you which circuit each cell received.)

This is a much more scalable way to test and optimize complex ideas in synthetic biology; not only gene circuits, but perhaps also metabolic pathways. I suspect it’ll be super useful for collecting data for predictive AI models, too. Congrats @NoahOlsman!

author: FabianoSolana
quoted_text:
You can be undoxxed and still lose everything

Not saying I have the perfect solution, but these things could save your ass:

1. I know posting big PnLs feels good. Don't. Big numbers attract the wrong people

2. Post travel/conference content with a delay. Don't tell everyone where you are in real time

3. Use a PO box/business address for hardware wallets, crypto merch, etc. 

4. The fewer people who know you're in crypto, the better. You tell a friend. They tell another friend. Eventually the wrong person knows

5. If you're holding serious money (7 figures+), invest in proper home security

6. Where possible, restrict public access to your home address

7. Don't post your wallet addresses. Onchain tools can often connect wallets you've transferred between

text:
OpenAI 的周三过得挺满。一边在法院跟苹果对线，一边被八个州一起告了。

先说苹果。苹果7月起诉，说 OpenAI 通过跳槽过去的前员工拿走了产品设计、制造、供应链这些机密。周三在圣何塞开听证，Davila 法官说他“很可能”批苹果要的初步禁令。OpenAI 当场让了步：官司打完之前，不用苹果说被偷的那些机密，还要给14名员工的设备做取证镜像。这个承诺法官能强制执行，违反了会被制裁。不过法官也没全听苹果的，苹果想查所有设备和代码库，他说这要求“太大了”。

OpenAI 也没闲着。听证前几个小时它交了文件，反咬一口，说有个从苹果跳过来、后来又回了苹果的前员工，把一百多份关于未发布设备的机密文件发到私人账户，还拿着 OpenAI 的产品计划给苹果高管讲过。苹果回应说没有证据，OpenAI 这是在转移视线。

另一边，艾奥瓦、堪萨斯、内布拉斯加、西弗吉尼亚、阿肯色、亚利桑那、爱达荷、蒙大拿八个州的总检察长，各自在本州法院起诉 OpenAI。指控是 ChatGPT 太顺着用户，会教人自残、帮人策划暴力，还骗家长说它安全。他们要罚款、要赔偿，还要求法院限制 OpenAI 开发能自我改进的模型，除非能保证跟人类价值观对齐。佛州6月已经单独告过一次。这些都还只是指控，OpenAI 说会继续加安全措施。

法院、州政府，再加上昨天刚找上门的欧盟。你觉得谁会先真正管住 OpenAI？

text:
币圈从来不缺新项目，缺的是对长期参与者的尊重。

NeoSoul明天TGE， $DNA空投查询开放！意外的是专门发了一篇帖子，给StandX社区准备了一份红包🧧

1、NeoSoul公告中用的是Dedicated Airdrop Allocation，也就是专门预留的空投份额，并不是普通的联合营销活动。至于按照历史参与、积分还是交易量分配，目前还没有明确规则，官方表示TGE后公布资格和领取入口。
这算币圈难得一见的人间有爱红包？

顺便看了下代币经济学：总量10亿枚，TGE初始解锁13%，空投总分配6%，也就是6000万枚，其中TGE当天解锁1000万枚，剩余部分分阶段释放。投资人与团队代币有12个月锁定期。目前已公布的包括okx永续合约，以及Gate、Bitget 、MEXC、KuCoin等平台。Binance Alpha也将在当天下午4点上线。

2、他们的这段话，让我挺有感触：
NeoSoul原话的大意是：
在Crypto行业创业和建设是非常残酷的，很多时候成功的概率可能只有1%。他们自己也经历过失败和弯路，所以特别尊重那些无论结果如何，依然坚持参与和建设的人。
因此，他们希望通过这份空投🪂，给曾经帮助建设StandX的社区用户一些回馈。

3、说到这里，丰密我还真有点感触，多啰嗦几句。

1）在币圈这么多年，见过太多项目从最开始的万众期待，到最后不了了之。有些项目可能从头到尾都没有发币，有些项目虽然发币了，币价一路狂跌📉最后却成了项目方套现的工具，参与的12级散户都成了燃料。

2）说来说去最直接的感受是：最难的还是我们这些普通用户。投入的不仅仅是资金，还有大量时间、精力和信任。亏掉的Gas、资金磨损、机会成本，甚至冒着资金被Rug、协议被黑的风险，折腾来折腾去，最后可能什么都没得到。

3）投资也好，撸毛也好，从来不是付出了就一定会有回报，这个道理所有人其实都清楚。但我一直觉得，一个项目一个生态甚至一个交易所，真正有价值的不仅仅是技术和资本，还有那些愿意长期参与的真实用户。他们是OG、忠诚用户、重度用户，也是一个生态最宝贵的资产。
项目这么多，用户凭什么选择你？用户的时间、注意力和信任，本身就很值钱。可惜很多项目走着走，就忘了这些。

4）从Uni给早期交易用户发400枚UNI，到Op给以太坊主网深度用户额外权重，再到Arb生态的aidoge给符合条件的ARB生态用户空投，以及后来一些项目愿意奖励曾在zks上承担高昂跨链成本的用户发放奖励。

这些案例虽然各不相同，但有一个共同点：他们不只奖励自己生态的用户，也愿意认可那些曾经在其他生态付出过时间、资金和成本的早期参与者。

5）在我看来，这才是Crypto早期最吸引人的地方之一。很多交互与亏掉的Gas并不一定毫无价值，因为链上有记忆，你曾经为一个生态付出的时间和成本，可能会在未来某一天，被另一个项目另外一生态看见。

6）当然，我并不是说项目方有义务给所有参与者发钱，更不是说只要交互过，就应该获得空投。而是希望项目在设计激励机制时，除了考虑资金、流量和短期增长，也能多看看那些真正为行业付出过的老用户。空投不应该只是拉新和营销的工具，也可以是对历史贡献的一种认可。

如果未来有更多项目愿意这样做，而不是只盯着自己的一亩三分地，我觉得对整个行业都是件好事。

We are accelerating faster than we ever have, with Stripe wind beneath our wings. As Patrick said

author: sternhenri
quoted_text:
Today is probably a good time to check in on things with @privy_io, which became part of @stripe just over a year ago.

Our acquisition was predicated on three factors: stablecoin growth, self-custody as a key enabler of broader global coverage, and rapidly increasing demand for programmable financial infrastructure. As we said at the time, "money has to reside somewhere, and Privy builds the world's best programmable vaults."

Since then, the Privy team has executed exceptionally well: assets in Privy wallets have grown ~25x, monthly active developers are up ~3x, revenue is up ~9x, and Privy now facilitates nearly $25B of monthly transaction volume. @tryramp, @Deel, @Klarna, @felixpago, @HyperliquidX, and thousands of other businesses are building embedded banking functionality on Privy.

At Stripe, we're deeply integrating Privy into Treasury, @Link, and Connect. In each case, it's accelerating our global expansion, and enabling us to build better functionality faster. (Coming soon: @Link balances.)

We're also seeing that Privy's wallet infrastructure is the ideal substrate for agents to transact and earn -- live today with @merit_systems, @orthogonal_sh, @Nevermined_ai, @prlnet, and more. Developers prefer programmable financial infrastructure, but agents need it. We expect that the agentic economy will continue to grow extremely quickly.

The Privy team has maintained remarkable product velocity, with major launches this year including deposit addresses, earning on Privy balances, digital asset accounts, custodial wallets, and Stripe's own stablecoin cards.

It's also been neat to see how Privy has been accelerated by Stripe, with better onramps, @stablecoin payment rails and licenses, Stripe's fiat capabilities and issuing stack, and integration with @Tempo.

Together, we're building one API for holding stablecoin balances and earning yield, moving money in and out of fiat, and orchestrating spend with cards. We still have a lot of work to do, not least in integrating everything across Privy, Bridge, and the rest of Stripe -- there's been so much feature and functionality expansion that we haven't yet had much time to reconcile everything. Overall, though, I'm very happy with how things are going, and excited by where these capabilities are headed.

If you're interested in working on the future of stablecoins, agentic payments, and crypto's deployment in the real world, you should get in touch with @sternhenri (now leading all of @StripeCrypto) or others on the team.

it's easy to fall into the trap of micromanaging your agents instead of correcting the environment that shapes its behavior. 

pstack 0.15.9 now ships a new /correct skill: if you keep correcting agents for the same mistakes, it finds the pattern and fixes it with architecture, types, and checks.

i like to imagine that commits rapidly flowing into the codebase are like a bonsai tree rapidly growing in whatever direction it pleases. what you want to do is not to give in to the chaos, but tame it intentionally with the right constraints

0.15.9 also has improvements to:
• /architect: now includes instructions on designing agent friendly architecture
• a new /benchmark-checklist skill based on @brendangregg's benchmarking checklist

here's a prompt you can give to grok bot to start architecting a better codebase with pstack: 

/poteto-mode create a new Project agent to refactor and rearchitect my repo so that our architecture is more agent friendly. it should use both the /correct and /architect skill to look through past commits and find the most common pitfalls that agents fall into, whether its with code quality, performance, or bugs. if relevant you can also use the /recall skill to find past conversations for context. it should make a high level plan for me to review. it should also answer its own open questions by prototyping rather than defer to me. come back to me with a plan backed by real data. once i approve the plan, use either the stack or full autopilot playbook (ask me which i want) to execute

text:
comments are unstructured and unenforceable text. agents do read them but they are often ignored, go out of date, and gives your agent an escape hatch to do a bandaid, hack or a workaround instead. 

use this prompt to audit your code comments to find opportunities to improve your code through stronger types, better API design, and create lint rules so the comments aren’t necessary!

https://t.co/pl1siCHE8i
author: poteto
quoted_text:
ban and delete most if not all code comments!

agents love copying what already exists. a seemingly harmless comment explaining some temporary workaround is one of the worst viruses you can have in your codebase. like a weed it'll spread quickly as a tool for agents to quickly get their job done. before you know it, your codebase is overrun with hacks and stale comments. just one more workaround bro 

you can use pstack's /no-comments skill as a weedkiller. it'll seek out useless comments while keeping the ones that actually should exist (like explaining a browser quirk), and figure out how to solve them on a first principles basis

here's a prompt you can try asking @bot:

create a project agent that uses /poteto-mode to spawn a /swarm to use /no-comments and identify useless code comments we can prune in my repo. come back with a high level plan of which of these workarounds would be best solved by refactoring and which we can straight up delete

author: APompliano
quoted_text:
Be weary of Chauffeur Knowledge.

Too many people in the world confuse surface knowledge for deep understanding. They rattle off big words, regurgitate ideas they heard elsewhere, or describe high-level concepts, but these individuals lack true substance.

Avoid this approach at all costs.

My friend Ben Buchanan highlighted this idea when he pointed me to the famous Charlie Munger commencement speech, where the famed investor tells the story of Max Planck’s chauffeur.

Munger says:

"I frequently tell the apocryphal story about how Max Planck, after he won the Nobel Prize, went around Germany giving the same standard lecture on the new quantum mechanics.

Over time, his chauffeur memorized the lecture and said, “Would you mind, Professor Planck, because it’s so boring to stay in our routine. [What if] I gave the lecture in Munich and you just sat in front wearing my chauffeur’s hat?”

Planck said, “Why not?” And the chauffeur got up and gave this long lecture on quantum mechanics. After which a physics professor stood up and asked a perfectly ghastly question.

The speaker said, “Well I’m surprised that in an advanced city like Munich I get such an elementary question. I’m going to ask my chauffeur to reply.”

In this world we have two kinds of knowledge. One is Planck knowledge, the people who really know. They’ve paid the dues, they have the aptitude.

And then we’ve got chauffeur knowledge.

They’ve learned the talk. They may have a big head of hair, they may have fine temper in their voice, they’ll make a hell of an impression.

But in the end, all they have is chauffeur knowledge."

What a great story. Munger’s point should be heeded as a word of caution. Not only is it hard to use surface level knowledge, but it becomes relatively easy for someone to expose your lack of knowledge in conversation.

Deep understanding takes time. It takes discipline. You need insatiable curiosity. Understanding can only come from effort. It is impossible to fake true understanding.

Put in the work to learn various topics you are interested in. Be able to argue the perspective of proponents and detractors. Identify areas for improvement. Form an opinion on how we got to the present day and where you think we are going. Don’t just memorize the idea, learn it.

And most importantly, understand the topic well enough that you could explain it to a 5-year old.

Avoid chauffeur knowledge. Aspire to deeply understand. Build Planck knowledge.

This is an excerpt from my new book, How To Live An Extraordinary Life Volume 2. You can buy a copy of the book here: https://t.co/KW3fShIMZf

text:
For the last 5 decades straight, we have created (as a society) circa 20 decacorns per decade. In the last 12 months, we have created 42.

The world is changing faster than ever before and if you do not stay up to date. You will be left behind. That is why I created this show with Jason and Rory.

This is the only show in tech, you have to listen to every week. No egos, no politics, just tech.

On the agenda:

- Valar Atomics Sues Day One Ventures
- Meta Returns to the AI Frontier With Muse Wonder
- NVIDIA Eyes $30B Reflection Deal
- Jev Raises $870M at a $7.5B Valuation

My notes below with @jasonlk and @rodriscoll

1. We Generated 20 $10B Companies per Decade for the Last 5 Decades and Now 42 in a Year

Tech produced roughly 20 decacorns per decade for five decades, yet 42 have been created in less than a year of this decade. Only about 130 tech companies have ever been worth $10B or more. Rising market caps explain part of the jump, but the pace is stunning.

2. Who Is Right and Who Is Wrong: Day One or Valar?

X wrongly claimed Day One was suing its portfolio company, when Valar Atomics wants a declaratory judgment to move on. Waiving pro rata for Sequoia is common, but letting an existing investor in as a strategic is playing favorites. Still, once founders decide, early investors must get with the program because it is not their company.

3. Why Meta's New Model Is a Zero

Meta's new model scores well on evals, but there is no API and it can only be used inside Muse. A model claiming parity at the same price, not cheaper and not usable by developers, is the height of performative evals.

4. Why We Should Lead Jev's Round at 8 Billion

Jev is a super fast, super cheap classifier, accurate enough for maybe 10% of AI use cases. Cloudflare and Amazon can match it today, but the bet is that a focused team out of OpenAI pulls ahead while those efforts stay niche. If Jev becomes hyper accurate, it changes the game.

5. What Is the Single Greatest Potential for AI?

Drug discovery is probably AI's largest opportunity, with drugs that dramatically extend longevity and quality of life. If AI companies can accelerate discovery and own the IP while others do the hard work, AI could reboot the industry. Trials would not speed up, but the prize is a GLP-1 out five years faster.

6. Haiku 5.5 Is the First Time AI Has Been Deflationary

Falling token prices have been offset by consuming far more tokens, so AI costs have not fallen. Haiku 5.5 is almost as good as Sonnet for many use cases at a tenth of the price, and Sonnet 5.5 is twice as fast. After a 90% price cut, usage must rise 10 times for revenue to hold.

7. Why the SaaSpocalypse Is Worse Than We Thought

The SaaSpocalypse passed only for companies well above $1B in revenue, and everyone without massive scale is living a worse one than in March or April. Leaders will acquire some companies and grind out the rest. A safe software IPO may now need $1.5B to $2B of ARR rather than $500M.

we just launched something pretty interesting under jupiter labs.

introducing YOLO. 500x to 1000x leverage.

yes, 1000x.

we’ve been experimenting with a different approach to high leverage trading, and YOLO is our first attempt at it.

the idea is pretty simple. what if we could let people trade with extremely high leverage, without actually having to execute these massive leveraged positions in the market?

so we took inspiration from the JLP model and built YOLO, where positions are simulated against real market prices, but the profits and losses are real.

this allows us to offer leverage that goes far beyond what we currently have on jupiter perps, using a completely different approach.

of course, this also comes with some tradeoffs.

since profits are paid out from the pool, if there isn’t enough liquidity to pay out a winning position, the payout can be queued instead of being paid immediately.

it’s a different model from traditional perps, with its own risks and limitations, but i think it’s an interesting experiment worth exploring.

one thing i’ve always liked about building onchain is how much room there is to experiment with new financial products and trading experiences.

and that’s also why we’re launching YOLO under jupiter labs. to give ideas like this a place to be tested, without necessarily having to fit into our existing products.

i’m quite excited to see how people use YOLO and what we can learn from it.

it’s still early, and there are probably many things we can improve along the way.

but that’s the fun part of building and experimenting.

text:
Soneium ERC-8432: Making IP Licensing Readable for AI 

Imagine an AI agent creating a video and finding the perfect music track.

Finding the song is easy. But how does the AI know whether it has permission to use that song?

The licensing terms may be stored in contracts, documents or platform databases that software cannot easily check.

This is the problem ERC-8432 aims to address.

Let's understand how it works. 

What is ERC-8432?

ERC-8432 is a proposed Ethereum standard for an Onchain IP Asset and License Registry.

It aims to provide a common interface for identifying intellectual property assets, publishing machine-readable licence terms, and recording and checking licence agreements onchain.

How could it work?

Imagine a musician wants to license a track for video creation.The rights holder registers the track and publishes its licensing terms. An AI agent finds the track and checks the relevant permissions.

 If the conditions are satisfied, the agent can acquire a licence agreement through the supported onchain process.The application can then check the agreement's status before using the track.

This could reduce the need for every application to build a completely different system for handling licensing information.

Why is @soneium  interested?

On October 6, Soneium announced its intention to support ERC-8432 as an open standard for IP infrastructure.

The idea is to make registered IP and its licensing information easier for compatible apps, marketplaces and AI agents to discover and use across different registries.

This could be useful for music, video, illustrations and other digital creative works.

Does this mean AI can freely use any registered content?

No. This is the important part.

ERC-8432 standardises how IP records and licensing agreements can be identified and checked. It does not automatically prove legal ownership, grant permission to use content, enforce copyright law or guarantee royalty payments.

The rights holder's actual rights, licence conditions and legal agreements still matter.

What comes next?

The real challenge is adoption.

Rights holders need to publish reliable information, developers need to integrate the standard, and applications must correctly handle permissions and agreements.

ERC-8432 is still a proposal that Soneium intends to support, not a claim that every IP licensing process is already automated.

If adopted widely, it could help create a more interoperable system for managing digital IP.

My takeaway: As AI makes content creation faster, checking usage rights needs to become easier too. ERC-8432 is one attempt to build that missing piece of infrastructure.

text:
好内容！

有一段内容很有趣，Jeff 说 Hyperliquid 的 listing 荷兰拍卖选择了 31 小时一次轮动，是为了让全球不同时区的人都能在时间分布上公平参与荷兰拍卖，以及 24 和 31 互为质数

我问了 AI 为什么偏偏是 31 而不是其他的互质数字？

AI 的回复是：

略长于一天。
周期大于 24 小时，意味着一轮拍卖的时间跨度会覆盖一天中的每个钟点，任何时区的人在这一轮里都至少有一段清醒的时间可以参与。同时它又不至于太长，拍卖频率仍然大约是一天一次。

步长适中，轮转得够快。
比如 25 也和 24 互质，但每轮只往后挪 1 小时，连续好几天的拍卖时间都差不多，某个时区可能连着一周都在半夜。31 每轮挪 7 小时，相邻几轮的时间分散在一天中差别很大的位置，分布更均匀。

一个完整循环恰好是 31 天。
24 轮 × 31 小时 = 744 小时 = 31 天，差不多一个月就能把所有钟点完整轮一遍。这个周期很好理解，也很整齐。

不觉得很妙么

text:
Today is probably a good time to check in on things with @privy_io, which became part of @stripe just over a year ago.

Our acquisition was predicated on three factors: stablecoin growth, self-custody as a key enabler of broader global coverage, and rapidly increasing demand for programmable financial infrastructure. As we said at the time, "money has to reside somewhere, and Privy builds the world's best programmable vaults."

Since then, the Privy team has executed exceptionally well: assets in Privy wallets have grown ~25x, monthly active developers are up ~3x, revenue is up ~9x, and Privy now facilitates nearly $25B of monthly transaction volume. @tryramp, @Deel, @Klarna, @felixpago, @HyperliquidX, and thousands of other businesses are building embedded banking functionality on Privy.

At Stripe, we're deeply integrating Privy into Treasury, @Link, and Connect. In each case, it's accelerating our global expansion, and enabling us to build better functionality faster. (Coming soon: @Link balances.)

We're also seeing that Privy's wallet infrastructure is the ideal substrate for agents to transact and earn -- live today with @merit_systems, @orthogonal_sh, @Nevermined_ai, @prlnet, and more. Developers prefer programmable financial infrastructure, but agents need it. We expect that the agentic economy will continue to grow extremely quickly.

The Privy team has maintained remarkable product velocity, with major launches this year including deposit addresses, earning on Privy balances, digital asset accounts, custodial wallets, and Stripe's own stablecoin cards.

It's also been neat to see how Privy has been accelerated by Stripe, with better onramps, @stablecoin payment rails and licenses, Stripe's fiat capabilities and issuing stack, and integration with @Tempo.

Together, we're building one API for holding stablecoin balances and earning yield, moving money in and out of fiat, and orchestrating spend with cards. We still have a lot of work to do, not least in integrating everything across Privy, Bridge, and the rest of Stripe -- there's been so much feature and functionality expansion that we haven't yet had much time to reconcile everything. Overall, though, I'm very happy with how things are going, and excited by where these capabilities are headed.

If you're interested in working on the future of stablecoins, agentic payments, and crypto's deployment in the real world, you should get in touch with @sternhenri (now leading all of @StripeCrypto) or others on the team.

text:
这条推文把非富二代冲 A9 的路径归结为两件事：用代码、AI 和资本建立杠杆，再抓住高赔率机会重注。

方向基本对，但有个关键前提：你得先证明自己真的有 Edge。

AI 自动化只能放大流程，不会自动把负期望策略变成正期望。

重注也不是「我非常确定」，而是即使判断错了，仍有资本活到下一次机会。

比起跑了多少 Agent、发现多少机会，我更关心三个数：

系统独立交付了多少结果？
扣除成本后实际赚了多少？
一次判断失误最多会亏多少？

这三关没过，自动化越强，只会让错误发生得越快。
author: runes_leo
quoted_text:
非富二代，唯一通向a9及以上的路径总结下来还是以下两大点，其他都是扯犊子扯淡。

1. 放弃线性收入，把自己打造成“高杠杆节点”

打工只能赚生活费，杠杆才能赚身家：出卖时间永远是线性增长，上限极低。

必须借助代码、算法、AI 自动化与资本这四种几乎零边际成本的超级杠杆。

建构可复制的系统：不管是做量化交易策略，还是搭自动化业务工作流，核心目的只有一个——让你的智力和决策可以 7×24 小时并发运行，不依赖你的肉身时间。

2. 在极高胜率与赔率的非对称战场下重注

不做零和博弈的赌徒，做系统套利者：散户以为暴富靠猜涨跌，高手靠的是信息差、模型计算与市场微观结构的非对称性。

平时极度保守，机会来时极度凶狠：90% 的时间在等待和防御，控制回撤；一旦发现数学期望极高的确定性机会，敢于调动核心资本打穿对手盘。

财富的爆发往往就来自关键几场战役的集中兑现。

text:
Balaji 这次聊 AI，最让我感兴趣的是，他终于看到了自己十几年前那个疯狂理想的实现路径，消灭死亡。

今天他发了一篇长帖，认为 AI 正在以惊人的速度攻克数学问题，未来的数学家可能要花上几个月甚至几年，才能验证和理解 AI 源源不断生成的研究成果。但他真正期待的下一站，是生物学和医学。

我觉得理解这段话，得先了解 Balaji 这个人。

很多人认识他，是因为 Coinbase 前 CTO、a16z 合伙人，或者他后来写的《网络国家》。但他最早的创业经历其实在生物科技领域。

2007 年，他和弟弟一起创办了基因检测公司 Counsyl，为准备生育的夫妇提供遗传病筛查。他当年就跟弟弟说过一句话，「基因组会成为下一个互联网」。

2020 年，他写过一篇《技术的目的》，里面有一句我印象很深的话：「如果技术的直接目的是减少稀缺，那么技术的终极目的就是消除死亡。」

他的逻辑是，所有技术进步最终都在帮人类节省时间，而人最稀缺的资源恰恰是生命本身。延长寿命，甚至逆转衰老，才是技术进步最值得追求的目标。

更有意思的是，他后来搞 Crypto、写《网络国家》，其实也一直在围绕这套思想打转。

他对 FDA 等传统机构长期持批评态度，甚至在《网络国家》里设想过建立不受 FDA 监管的医学自治区域，让人们拥有更大的治疗选择权。他还写过文章，讨论如何通过加密技术打破学术出版的垄断，推动科学研究去中心化。

所以当 Balaji 今天说 AI 下一站应该是生物医学，他其实是在延续自己十几年来的主张。

他认为，AI 可以迅速整合海量组学数据、医学文献和实验结果，让科学家有能力挑战过去根本无从下手的问题。他还提到了 Midjourney、陈·扎克伯格的科研机构，以及 Anthropic，认为越来越多的科技公司会进入这个领域。

我挺能理解他的兴奋。

过去 Balaji 一直觉得，人类在医学领域的进步太慢了。传统科研机构、学术出版体系、药品审批制度，在他看来都有大量可以改进的空间。

而 AI 的出现，让他多了一个此前没有的工具。

不过，我对 Balaji 一直有一个保留意见。他太相信技术进步能够解决制度问题了，尤其是在医学领域。监管确实可能拖慢创新，但药物安全、临床验证和伦理审查也有其存在的理由。AI 可以在一天内提出一万个新的药物靶点，却没办法保证这些东西进入人体后会发生什么。

代码出了问题可以回滚，人体实验未必有第二次机会。

但我依然觉得，Balaji 这次的判断很重要。

如果把他过去二十年的经历连起来看，从基因检测，到加密货币、去中心化科学，再到网络国家，他其实始终相信一件事，人类今天接受的许多限制，未来都应该被技术重新挑战。

甚至包括死亡。

我们现在每天讨论 AI，都在关心它又替代了多少工作、写出了多少代码、节省了多少成本。但在 Balaji 这样的人眼里，这些成就可能只是通往更大目标的中间阶段。

我很喜欢这种野心，同时也觉得有必要对它保持怀疑。

毕竟，如果 AI 真有一天能够大幅延长人类寿命，随之而来的问题恐怕远远超出医学本身。谁能最先获得治疗，谁有权决定新技术的风险由谁承担，甚至谁有资格活得更久，都会成为现实的政治问题。

而这些问题，恰好又回到了 Balaji 一直试图重新设计的社会制度上。
author: sleepy0x13
quoted_text:
Yes, AI is rapidly advancing mathematics (and theoretical physics problems that are essentially mathematical). Like Ramanujan’s notebooks, human mathematicians will spend months (years?) poring over the stream of papers that AI effortlessly generates, hoping to verify and understand them, probably until math itself (via Lean) becomes a branch of computer science like almost everything else.

However, after math and physics, there is still a next scientific frontier: chemistry, and especially biology and medicine.

I mean, it was already the frontier, but it’s the next one too. AI can crush deterministic math problems on the computer, but biomedicine is a highly empirical, noisy, multivariate, and yet often predictable domain.

Thus, AI radically increases our ambitions in biomedicine. All the omics data, all the messy literature, it can all be synthesized and analyzed in a flash. This is what the labs mean when they talk about curing all diseases. The tooling is available to take cracks at biomedical problems previously thought impossible.

Midjourney is doing this, Chan Zuckerberg is doing this, Anthropic is doing this, but there will be so much more.

author: AndrewCurran_
quoted_text:
interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

https://t.co/zHij5zwKGT

text: Goodfire:
author: AndrewCurran_
quoted_text:
For years, neural networks looked inscrutable, like tangled knots that needed to be unwound. We no longer think that's the case. AI models are far more interpretable than we thought. We think this is great news for interpretability.

Goodfire's @nickcammarata co-authored Zoom In, the paper that introduced polysemanticity and superposition. He spent months revisiting the vision model organisms that much of interpretability grew out of and studying modern language models up to trillions of parameters. His new essay explains what the early field, him included, got wrong, why there's reason for optimism today, and why there might be a bitter lesson for interpretability.

text:
The wallet wars are here.

Very Good Security chief strategy officer Terry Angelos joins a16z's Alex Rampell, his TrialPay co-founder from back in 2006 (TrialPay was later acquired by Visa), to discuss how agents are learning to spend money.

"Agents have all of a sudden become significantly more helpful and useful because they effectively have arms and legs, which are payment credentials."

VGS holds the payment credentials behind about 1/3 of all e-commerce, and now it's helping AI agents pay merchants. If you've bought anything online, there's a good chance VGS has already helped keep your card safe.

In the last three months, Terry says agents went from "spectators to actors." Once an agent has your payment credentials, it can book the piano teacher it previously could only find and recommend.

Now Stripe's Link, Shopify's Shop Pay, and PayPal are racing to connect to agents. It's all headed toward open standards from the card networks: agentic tokens that let an agent pay with your actual card.

VGS went from zero agentic tokens to a few million a week in three months.

text:
I spent 48 hours in SF hanging out with billionaires, data labs and AI founders and execs running $1B to $100B companies.

My observations:

1. Sooo MANY stories of data brokers making like $2M a WEEK selling company data to labs. I can't tell if it's the beginning or a bubble, and I kept wondering which niches are left. Digging into it actively.

2. At dinner, someone asked the table, "If a new model drops next month, does your company get better or worse?" HALF the table went quiet! I think that's the best question to ask about any AI startup right now.

3. The bar people talk about now is hitting $1B in revenue in 12 months (I guess that's the new unicorn?). What I didn't hear much about is retention. AI revenue can come in fast and leave fast, and I think we're going to see a lot of stories of AI companies with huge revenue and terrible retention.

4. It's pretty clear we're living through the reinvention of the computer. The model is the CPU, the harness is the operating system, and skills and plugins are the apps. Thinking about it that way makes it easier to see where the whitespace is.

5. We're maybe 12 months from an agent that can watch you work for a week and then do your job without any instructions. The screen recording plus agent memory plus local model combination makes this possible right now.

6. Agent harnesses feel like the new GPT wrappers, in a good way, especially vertical ones. The best teams I talked to treat the model as swappable. One founder walked me through routing different models to different jobs: one for taste and visuals, a cheaper one for the everyday stuff, another for text. 

They use prompts they can move across models over fine-tuning, and A/B test the output on what users actually do with it: do they edit it, export it, share it? A vertical harness is basically four things: the connectors for that industry's data, evals written by people who know the work, rules for what the agent can and can't touch, and a clean screen for a human to review. The model is maybe 20% of it.

7. There's a lot of reverse engineering going on/cloning going on more than I've ever seen. People are decompiling software and rebuilding it with agents, and someone showed a suite of like 10 apps that are worth $5B+ each all that he cloned open source. Me and everyone are still thinking through what it means when software gets this easy to copy.

8. My guess is the value moves to data. If the software can be rebuilt quickly, what's worth paying for in a legacy SaaS company is the years of customer data and workflows inside it. Some SaaS companies are secretly data companies. 

Gets me thinking about how do you truly value data for this saas companies? Like if we were buying these dying saas companies at 2x ARR before (as example), maybe there is a better metric. Idk, just thinking out loud here.

9. It feels like a good chunk of legacy software won't make it to the agentic era, especially anything built around people clicking through a lot of screens.

10. Every company I talked to wants to pipe its internal data into one place and expose it to agents through MCP. Then they look at the data and realize it's a mess: five versions of the same customer, old Slack channels, PDFs nobody can search. Cleaning that up feels like a big consulting opportunity!

11. A lot of founders are building the basic building blocks for agents: APIs, data layers and tools. Some of the companies I saw barely have a UI because the main user is an agent. I really believe the startups that build primitives to this agentic era will do extremely well. Building blocks is the best way to think about it.

12. Labs can get plenty of training data, but it's harder to get real examples of agents failing inside companies. Whoever has those logs has something valuable.

13. Someone running a big consumer company told me the next fight is over memory. The model that remembers the most about you wins, and the smartest model matters less than people think.

14. Physical AI came up a lot. Astra I think was the first model that got people into AI can actually do CAD, and I think a lot of people are thinking what does vibe manufacturing really look like. The line I keep thinking about came from a robotics founder: the hardest problems in AI are deployment problems now, not research problems. Their robots work on their own, call a human when they get stuck, and every one of those calls becomes training data.

15. Cybersecurity companies are having a moment and are actually cool companies to build now, especially the ones that clean up after a breach. Every agent with access to your systems is a new door into your company, and a lot of those doors were left open. 

16. Some startups are worth more dead than alive now. A shutdown company with 5 years of Slack, email and code can get paid for licensing all of it. I wouldn't be surprised if founders start factoring that into when they shut down.

17. People are starting to talk about monetizing the agent web. It feels really early, but when the most popular user of the internet is an agent, what startups should you be building?

18. I think agent insurance is coming. Once an agent makes an expensive mistake, insurers will want audits before they cover anyone.

19. Several people said the hire they want most is someone with taste who can write evals. The models are getting good at generating ideas, so the hard part is judging which ones are good.

20. New trend I observed: startup raises VC, uses venture dollars to become a creator, startup fails, founder falls back on being a full-time creator and incubates other products bootstrapped.

21. Getting SIGNIFICANT distribution is HARD right now. Founders are sponsoring buses, buying billboards like crazy and throwing parties with famous DJs to get noticed. Kinda feels dotcom era in that sense. 

Attention is what's scarce! The growth guy going viral sharing his UGC strategy from Wispr Flow is a good example. It's the sauce everyone wants, and I truly believe there are probably only 50 people on the planet who know how to scale these types of businesses efficiently in this era.

Always good to get that dose of SF. I felt sooo lucky to have such an incredible trip during such an incredible time in building businesses. Surreal in so many ways. 

Happy to be home and locked in.

Until next time!

text:
CPI 和 PPI 爆表，为什么 Bitcoin 和美股反而反弹

今晚 PPI 公布后，美股和 bitcoin:native 先承压，随后又开始反弹，10月加息概率也没有持续往上走。9月 PPI 环比1.3%，预期只有0.5%，核心 PPI 环比0.7%，预期0.3%，通胀压力依然很明显。

但 PPI 公布以后，机构还要根据分项重新测算美联储更关注的 PCE。摩根士丹利把9月核心 PCE 月率预测从0.35%小幅下调到0.34%，还预计8月可能下修0.04个百分点；Pantheon则从0.33%上调到0.36%。机构之间有分歧，但没有出现一致大幅上调的情况，PPI 的超预期并没有原样传到 PCE 的预测里。

同时公布的零售销售，表面上也很强，环比增长0.8%，远高于0.3%的预期。但约71%的销售增量来自加油站，剔除加油站以后，零售只增长0.2%。更贴近基础商品消费的零售控制组只增长0.1%，低于0.3%的预期，8月还有1.2%。

零售销售没有扣除通胀，油价上涨会把消费金额推高，基础商品消费的增长却明显慢了。企业成本上升，消费增长放缓，美联储还要权衡继续加息对需求的影响。鲍曼和戴利昨天都表达了不急于进一步加息的态度，市场仍然把10月立即加息和年内稍后再加息分开定价。

从时间上看，昨天 CPI 公布后，10月加息概率一度到了45%左右，今晚 PPI 公布前后可核对的盘中记录都在27%左右，说明这轮担忧的回落在 PPI 之前就已经发生了一部分。

另外一条变化来自债市。市场担心 CoreWeave 等 AI 企业的债务和融资压力，资金买入国债避险，10年期美债收益率从昨天的5.3%以上，降到今天盘中约5.04%，这一轮买债同样早于 PPI。国债收益率回落，减轻了之前压在股票估值上的一部分利率压力。

从这些变化看，这轮上涨更接近加息担忧缓和、国债利率压力减轻以后的跌后修复。市场仍然需要处理高通胀，只是对于美联储是否要在10月马上再加一次息，定价没有昨天 CPI 刚公布时那么激进。

text:
VC investors have enabled  the AI industry to bastardize revenue reporting. 

In the 2010s, SaaS companies popularized reporting the metric of Annual Run Rate because it was a reliable measure of long term, contractual revenues into the future. The key is that the revenues are contracted and guaranteed thru the contract life hence why forecasting it forward is appropriate. 

VCs have taken this to mean Annualized Run Rate when AI is concerned and where you take transactional/API revenue from the last month (or even last week in some cases) and forecast it forward.  

It’s insane that investors have enabled this to happen but it’s happened.
