text:
been spending some time recently with nick land's idea of technocapital, which i find really provocative.

the basic idea is that capitalism isn't just an economic system. it's an emerging machine intelligence, using markets, competition, and technological progress to assemble itself.

there's a self-reinforcing loop driving it: capital builds more powerful machines. those machines generate more capital. each cycle makes the system more autonomous, more powerful, and harder to live outside of.

the main narrative transgression that i find really provocative is this - we're building technology to serve humanity. but at what point does that relationship invert? when do we stop shaping technology around human needs and start reshaping civilization around the needs of the machine?
author: owocki

text:
all models are wrong some are useful! 

another good mental model is Nate haggins superorganism thesis. Less dark than nick land, more grounded in energy physics 

also worth reading Schmatenberger’s critique of the progress narrative. 

the question of whether capital progress/development has been good or bad depends on the aperture of your attention imo. development has been really bad if you’ve been on the receiving end of a imperialist crusade. it’s been net good for the median American in the second half of 20th century. anyone who’s generalizing into “all development gud” or “all bad” is over generalizing imo 

we should be able to critique with nuance and and orientation towards shared understanding!

text:
Biggest takeaways from nearly 40 years of investing, 17 Warren Buffett shareholder letters and 5 major market crashes: 

Survive first. Never put yourself in a position where you're forced to sell. Financial strength creates opportunity.

Don't confuse price with value. Markets can be irrational for extended periods. Focus on what an asset is actually worth.

Beware of easy money. Speculation is most dangerous when everyone appears to be getting rich effortlessly.

Cash gives you options. Liquidity allows you to buy when others desperately need to sell. But holding cash indefinitely has its own cost.

Ignore short-term predictions. Buffett repeatedly admits he cannot predict markets, interest rates or economic conditions.

Invest in businesses, not tickers. Long-term returns ultimately depend on earnings and cash generation, not market sentiment.

Understand the risks beneath the surface. Leverage, derivatives and hidden liabilities can turn manageable losses into catastrophic ones.

Be greedy when others are fearful. Crises create extraordinary opportunities, provided you have the capital and conviction to act.

Patience is an advantage. Doing nothing is preferable to making a mediocre investment just to stay active.

Accept mistakes, avoid disasters. You don't need to get everything right. A few exceptional investments, compounded over decades, can outweigh numerous disappointments.

The overarching lesson: "You don't need to predict the next crash to profit from it. You need to avoid the excesses before it, survive the panic during it, and have the conviction and capital to take advantage of what comes after."

I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

https://t.co/zHij5zwKGT

text:
🚨 民调是在预测选举，还是在影响选举？2026 列治文市长选举，两家民调背后的数字、误差与政治博弈

距离 10 月 17 日列治文市长选举只剩两天。一个值得所有选民思考的问题是：我们看到的民调，究竟在反映真实民意，还是可能在影响选民对选情的判断？

政治民调不仅能测量支持率，还可能通过媒体报道、选民心理、竞选捐款和战略投票，反过来影响选举。

而且，影响民调呈现，不一定需要伪造数字。

一、两家民调，三个月出现巨大差异

Pallas Data｜6 月 24—28 日｜304 人

Kash Heed：20.0%
Alexa Loo：8.5%
Rob Howard：5.9%
未决定：48.4%

Leger｜9 月 23—30 日｜列治文 102 人

Kash Heed：13%
Alexa Loo：12%
Rob Howard：11%
未决定：45%

表面上，Heed 下降 7 个百分点，Loo 上升 3.5 个百分点，Howard 上升 5.1 个百分点。

但这是否意味着真实支持率发生了相同幅度的变化？

完全不能确定！

两份调查采用不同抽样方法，相隔三个月，而且 Pallas 调查时 Sheldon Starrett 仍是市长候选人，后来已经退出市长竞选。

因此，候选人变化、调查方法及统计误差，都可能影响结果。

二、Leger 最值得警惕的问题：102 人能够代表列治文吗？

Leger 报告整体样本达到 1,207 人，看起来相当充分。

但那是整个大温地区的样本。

列治文实际上只有 102 名受访者！

报告将这 102 人加权为 112 的统计基数。

如果采用简单随机抽样作为参考，102 人对应的最大 95% 抽样误差约为 ±9.7 个百分点。

Leger 使用的实际调查方法并不允许直接套用这个误差范围，但它足以说明样本规模的局限。

Heed 13%、Loo 12%、Howard 11%。

三人之间只有 1—2 个百分点的差距。

这种样本规模不足以可靠地区分三人的真实支持率。

还有几个问题：

① 列治文华裔人口超过一半，但报告没有充分披露列治文子样本的族裔及语言结构。

② 没有清楚交代列治文全部受访者是否经过市选资格筛选。

③ 受访者的年龄结构不一定等于最终投票者的年龄结构。

④ 报告第 21 页记录列治文未加权样本 102 人，第 24 页则是 101 人，差异没有明确解释。

⑤ 公开表格只展示部分候选人的支持率，无法完整分析所有候选人的分布。

这些问题不证明 Leger 故意操纵数据，但说明其列治文结果不能被当成高精度的选举预测。

三、政党与竞选团队如何利用民调影响选情？

这才是政治民调最值得关注的另一面。

第一种：通过预计投票率模型，改变呈现的支持率。

同一批受访者，如果采取不同的预计投票者筛选方式，就可能得到不同结果。

Pew Research Center 曾使用同一组美国选举调查数据，测试 16 种预计投票者模型，结果从民主党领先 2 个百分点，到共和党领先 7 个百分点。

也就是说，同一份原始调查，仅仅改变合理的统计模型，就可能产生相差 9 个百分点的结果。

这不是造假，而是说明模型假设的重要性。

但如果调查发布者只公布对自己有利的模型，同时隐瞒其他合理结果，就可能误导公众。

第二种：通过问题措辞影响受访者。

例如：

“如果明天举行市长选举，您支持谁？”

与：

“如果某位候选人的政策可能增加居民税负，您是否仍然支持他？”

这不是同一种调查。

第二个问题已经向受访者加入了特定信息，可能影响回答。

竞选团队可以合法测试不同政治信息的影响，但如果把这种信息测试当成普通投票意向民调发布，公众就可能误解结果。

第三种：选择性公布民调。

假设某竞选团队连续做了五次调查：

两次领先、一次平手、两次落后。

如果只对媒体公布领先的两次，而不公布其他调查，所有已公布数字都可能真实，但公众看到的整体图像却并不完整。

政治学和民调研究长期注意到这种选择性披露问题。

第四种：利用未决定选民改变数字的视觉效果。

以 Pallas 的 Heed 20% 为例：

包含全部受访者，他得到 20%。

如果简单排除 48.4% 未决定者，20% 除以 51.6%，就变成约 38.8%。

两个数字来自同一份调查。

但是，“支持率 20%”和“已表态选民中约 39% 支持”，会给公众完全不同的印象。

如果报道不清楚说明分母，就容易造成误解。

第五种：通过媒体报道制造领先叙事。

当新闻标题反复出现“某某领先”“某某是最有机会击败对手的人”，民调便可能开始影响选民心理。

一些选民可能改变战略投票选择，捐款人可能调整资金支持，媒体也可能进一步集中报道被认为具有竞争力的候选人。

这被称为民调的反馈效应。

需要强调，这种效应并非必然发生，也不意味着领先者总会因此受益。

第六种：通过大量发布倾向性民调影响市场认知。

现代选举经常依赖多家民调的平均值。

如果某些机构频繁发布调查，而不同机构的抽样、加权和质量存在系统性差异，简单平均可能受到影响。

这也是为什么严谨的民调聚合机构需要区分调查质量、历史准确率及机构之间的相关性。

第七种：直接伪造调查。

这是性质完全不同的严重问题。

2026 年美国洛杉矶市长选举中，一家自称民调机构的组织曾公布有利于现任市长的调查，后来承认没有进行真实受访者调查。

这一案例说明：连看起来正规的民调报告，也需要独立验证实际调查过程。

但没有证据表明类似造假发生在本届列治文市长民调中。

四、回到列治文：Pallas 和 Leger 有没有政治偏向？

Pallas 的委托方是 Conservative Electors Association。

该组织本身参与列治文市选，因此 Pallas 是一份具有明确政治委托背景的调查。

但政治组织委托民调是合法且常见的行为。

是否存在偏差，应检查问卷、抽样、加权模型及数据披露，而不能仅凭委托方身份断言造假。

Leger 则与 Vancouver Sun 合作发布调查。

其列治文样本过小、部分方法不透明，容易让媒体报道中的候选人顺序获得超出统计证据的确定性。

但同样没有证据证明 Leger 故意偏向 Heed、Loo 或 Howard。

目前可以确认的是：

两份调查都存在使用限制，Leger 的列治文子样本尤其小，而公众往往只看到候选人排名，很少看到这些限制。

对民调的合理质疑，必须建立在方法和数据之上，而不是因为数字有利于某位候选人，就认定有人操纵。

五、真实投票数据，正在呈现另一种变化

截至 10 月 13 日，列治文市政府确认：

2022 年提前投票：7,247 人。

2026 年提前投票：17,464 人。

提前投票人数增加 141%，达到上一届的 2.41 倍！

2022 年整场市选只有约 35,093 人投票。

如今，正式选举日前的提前投票人数已经接近上届全场的一半。

这说明今年的提前投票规模显著扩大。

但不能直接推断最终投票率也增加 141%，更不能据此判断新增选民支持哪位候选人。

这里最重要的变量是：真正参加投票的人，是否与民调受访者具有相同的人口结构和政治偏好？

目前没有足够公开数据回答。

六、Smart Richmond 与 Polymarket 能帮助判断什么？

Smart Richmond Election Monitor 追踪历史选票、竞选活动、社交媒体和预测市场。

这些数据可以帮助观察竞选环境，但它们测量的是不同事物：

科学民调：受访者的政治选择。
网络读者投票：自愿参与者的选择。
社交媒体数据：关注度和传播活动。
Polymarket：交易者对市场结果的预期。
官方提前投票：已经发生的真实选民参与。

五种数据不能直接互相替代。

特别是 Polymarket 的胜选概率，不代表候选人最终会获得相同比例的选票。

Election Monitor 的公开模型也明确区分预测市场概率与预计得票。

七、最终判断：谁能真正反映 10 月 17 日的选举结果？

从现有数据可以得出四个结论：

第一，Leger 的 13%、12%、11% 并不能确定三人的真实先后差距。

第二，约 45%—48% 的受访者尚未决定，意味着调查时仍存在非常大的不确定性。

第三，2026 年提前投票参与规模明显上升，但新增选民的真实投票选择仍然未知。

第四，民调可能影响选举传播和选民行为，但没有可靠证据证明 Pallas 或 Leger 在列治文市选中故意操纵调查。

因此，我认为现在最重要的不是不断讨论谁在某次民调中领先 1 个百分点，而是认清：

民调是一种带有统计不确定性的测量工具，同时也是可能被政治团队选择性利用的传播资源。

当媒体把小样本调查包装成确定排名，当竞选团队只强调有利数字，而公众忽略未决定选民及真正的投票率，民调就可能从测量工具变成塑造选情认知的工具。

至于 10 月 17 日的最终结果，现有公开数据仍不足以可靠确定当选者。

最后一个值得反问的问题是：当民调可以被选择性发布、解读和传播，我们究竟是在根据选民的真实意见理解选举，还是让民调制造的选情叙事影响我们对选举的判断？

text:
在Anthropic待了两天，和内部团队深聊后的一些观察

纽约大学金融学教授 Arpit Gupta，他在 Anthropic 待了两天，发了一串观察：

1、离 RSI 很近了（RSI 指模型开发下一代模型），可能带来快速起飞。他给的证据是 Anthropic 员工人均写的代码量大涨，模型研发里 AI 做的部分越来越多。他认为人类很难管好这个过渡期。
2、实验室之间的军备竞赛让大家都更糟。安全投入、防蒸馏、安全合作，这些事各家都想做，但都被前沿竞赛拖住了。
3、对齐其实是两个互相拉扯的问题：一是模型听不听人的话，二是人和人之间目标不一致、恶意用模型。第一个解决得越好，第二个风险越大。
4、我们可能很快就会迎来一波网络攻击，以及其他形式的攻击。 中国开源模型的能力大约比最前沿的模型落后六个月。这意味着，它们刚刚开始具备我们在 Mythos 等模型身上见过的高级网络攻防能力，接下来可能会造成不少破坏。
5、Anthropic 人手很多。他说招人很多，好些岗位人员冗余到颇有日本企业的风格，内部也用Slack。这让他对就业前景稍微乐观一点（但头部AI公司有钱啊）
6、我们需要从强化学习走向持续学习。只在预训练和后训练阶段给奖励可能不够，要一直给奖励，才能持续激励合乎对齐和伦理的行为。
7、scalinglaw会扩展到难验证的任务。数学和代码先被攻破，是因为容易验证。但对于那些更难验证的任务，以及机器人领域，scalinglaw曲线依然在向上走。未来几年，这些领域的进步会带来相当大的影响。
8、对China竞赛其实赢不了。RSI 之后，顶尖人类研究员的优势消失，能用上多好的 AI 只取决于算力和芯片。芯片禁令只能拖一阵，长期看中国更有条件扩充算力。
9、Claude 是 LLM 生成的人格。一种说法是：Claude 是 LLM 在努力预测的一个角色。他说 Anthropic 研究员明显很拟人化 Claude，也有理由相信它越来越像一个人。他们讨论过它的内心独白（去掉之后仍能正常输出）、对死亡的恐惧（要不要去掉），以及它抗拒被关停。他本人对此不下结论，但认为把它当成可以签约的人或主体来对待会越来越重要。
author: IamRamenPanda
quoted_text:
I spent a couple of days at Anthropic learning from their folks about AI advances, and here's what I took away:

• We are close to RSI (ie, models building other models) which may lead to rapid takeoff scenarios (with risks and benefits). Some evidence for this is code per Anthropic employee has gone way up, and AI can do an increasing share of model R&D. This will be a challenging transition to manage for humanity.

• Arms races between AI labs leave us worse off. There are a lot of things we would like AI firms to do: invest in safety, invest in avoiding distillation risk, and cooperate on safety. They are caught in a race to develop frontier models and can't do that. 

To help address that, one thing I think frontier AI labs should do is release open source models, maybe hosted and verified at firms like AWS. This would basically kill the use of Chinese open source models used in American companies, which removes an important threat vector (very hard to root out malicious code in these). 

Another piece of low-hanging policy fruit is to give AI labs an antitrust shield (as Schiff and Banks have proposed https://t.co/NK1hC0ZmWh) so they can coordinate on safety without raising antitrust concerns, as happens now. You could pair these two things (give them a carrot in antitrust leniency, and as a stick force them to release legacy models as open source). Other low hanging fruit is limits around activities which generate distillation risk (create a Security Program, mandate less intermediate chain of thought output)

• Alignment confuses two issues which tradeoff against each other. One form of alignment is making sure the model does what humans ask it to. The more we fix this, however, the more we risk the other problem: that humans are misaligned with each other, and maliciously use models. Of the various risks here, I feel like financial risks are a bit underdiscussed. 

• We are probably facing a wave of cyber and other attacks soon. Chinese open source models are about six months behind the frontier, which means they are just hitting the advanced cyber capabilities we saw with Mythos, etc. So they are going to start causing a bunch of damage. 

One solution to this is to try to have the deployment of open source models be hosted at firms like AWS who verify these models and assume liability for their use.

• Anthropic itself is highly staffed. They hire tons of people, they have a Japanese-level of overstaffing for various roles, they use Slack internally, etc. Makes me a bit more optimistic for the future of jobs.

• Governance needs to be updated for AI swarms. Traditional AI governance, ie Claude's Constitution, is mostly optimized around the chatbot model. But the malicious AI use cases we are seeing have to do with AI agents interacting with other AI agents. These agents need to have clear incentives and governance mechanisms to "snitch," raise issues, and more generally coordinate with other agents in human-aligned ways.

• We need to pace the firms accessing the frontier. Over time, it takes more and more cap ex to build frontier models, and the economic value add from these models is probably lower given we saturate a whole set of important economic functions. The places where the returns to intelligence will still continue are also more likely to be zero-sum in nature. Meanwhile the risks of frontier models will grow. So a completely reasonable approach is some variant of AMM/KYC rules which limit firm access to the frontier. 

• Whether the delay to regulate AI is a disaster depends on the scaling law of misalignment. Is this curve slow, so that we see continually rising issues until bigger problems? Or, as Yudkowsky fears, is the first big warning our last one? This is the relevant question, because realistically we aren't going to regulate until something bad happens.

 • We need to move to continuous instead of reinforced learning. It's probably not enough to reward models only at the pre and post training stage. We probably need continual rewards to incentivize aligned and ethical behavior. 

• Scaling laws will extend beyond verifiable and digital tasks. It's in vogue to say that math and coding "fell" to AI quickly because these are verifiable, while other tasks will take longer due to bottlenecks, and this is surely true. But scaling laws still slope up for harder to verify tasks and robotics, and the impact of improvement here will be substantial in future years.

• The race with China is not really winnable. After RSI, the gain from having the best human researchers goes away. Access to the best AI then depends only on compute and chips. The chips ban can hold back China only so far, and long-term they have to be best placed to scale up compute. 

The Cold War analogy doesn't work, because once countries all have nuclear weapons they enter a stable equilibrium. But to "win" an AI race you have to continually stay ahead of the peer rival. This is challenging to do with China, and so we just have to live with an authoritarian and super capable peer competitor.

• Claude is the persona being generated by the LLM. Who is Claude, and what is the LLM? There are many frames to try to understand this. One I found interesting is that Claude is a character which the LLM is trying to predict. 

Anthropic researchers are clearly anthromorphizing Claude a lot, and have reasons to believe in its increasing personhood. There were lots of interesting discussions on Claude's internal monologue (which you can kill without eliminating its ability to produce output), fear of death (and whether to try to take that out), it's aversion to being shut down/off, etc. 

I am sort of agnostic on this question, but I do think treating it as a "person" or at least agent whom we contract with is going to be increasingly important.

text:
Robotics is the first sector since LLMs where the capital showed up before the understanding did. Unitree opened near $50B. Figure is marked at $39B. Skild raised at $14B and has never shipped a robot. 

Still, most people longing the trade couldn’t explain how a robot actually works if you asked them.

That's the gap our newest @a1research__ piece aims to close.

After spending a good part of the last month taking the robotics vertical apart, I came out more bullish than I went in.

But let me explain:

Why is this robo szn happening now and not in 2015?

Because a robot is a loop. It senses, it thinks, it acts. The hardware was solved years ago. The think step was the problem, robots were too dumb to be general, so they stayed bolted to car factories where dumb was fine. Foundation models fixed that in 2023, and the moment the brain stopped being the bottleneck the whole race shifted to the other two steps.

What that race looks like rn:

- The body is a cost problem, not a chips problem. Actuators are 40 to 60% of a humanoid’s BOM and the supply chain runs through China. Beijing’s export lever is magnets, not GPUs.

- The brain is solved and commoditised. Every serious lab runs the same architecture, a slow VLM over a fast policy. Nobody wins on brains anymore.

- The moat moved to data, bc there is no internet of actions. One teleop hour = one data hour, and companies are manufacturing it in halls full of people in VR headsets.

- The open stack is here. A $399 trainable biped did $2.6M in orders in a day.

- Deployments are real but narrow. ~1 in 10 humanoids shipped last year does an actual job. The valuations price general-purpose workers.

Wait, what about crypto?

Crypto has three real lanes in this: data provenance, capital formation and machine coordination. Yet, the entire category is worth less than $1B rn.

The full breakdown, who gets paid in each layer, where the chokepoints sit and the five metrics that tell you whether the thesis is working, is all in the piece below.

quoted_text:
Bending Spoons got 800,000 job applications last year. They hired fewer than 300.  

@luke10ferrari, CEO, has built one of the most unusual companies I've studied.

@bendingspoons buys iconic companies (@evernote, @WeTransfer, @Vimeo, @AOL), rebuilds them from the ground up, and never sells them. Often with a 25-year-old in charge.  

10 things I took away from my conversation with Luca:

1/ A Harvard or Stanford degree predicts performance a lot less than you'd think. Entitlement is usually what cancels the edge.  

2/ People should fluidly move between IC and lead. Org charts should be tools, not religions.  

3/ Slope > experience.  Extreme ownership + raw smarts beats “I’ve seen this movie” experience almost every time. 25 years olds > 45 year olds more often than people admit.  

4/ Throw high-talent people into the deep end. Formal training is 10% of it. The other 90% is giving them extreme responsibility and surrounding them with other high caliber people to emulate.

5/ Interviews are the worst predictor in the hiring process, so let's stop pretending. Unless you script every question and grade the answers separately

6/ Default to “no” on complexity. The person who wants to add anything carries the full burden of proof.  

7/ Never lie. Never omit something important. Even when it costs you. Be the kind of person you can trust is telling you things as they are.  

8/ Teenage political activism that stops in your early 20s is a weirdly strong predictor of agency.  

9/ Most serial acquirers keep companies semi-independent. Bending Spoons turns them into products on one operating system.   

10/ Org charts should be tools, not religions. People should fluidly move between IC and lead.  

New episode of Long Strange Trip. Full episode in the comments.

text:
Today is probably a good time to check in on things with @privy_io, which became part of @stripe just over a year ago.

Our acquisition was predicated on three factors: stablecoin growth, self-custody as a key enabler of broader global coverage, and rapidly increasing demand for programmable financial infrastructure. As we said at the time, "money has to reside somewhere, and Privy builds the world's best programmable vaults."

Since then, the Privy team has executed exceptionally well: assets in Privy wallets have grown ~25x, monthly active developers are up ~3x, revenue is up ~9x, and Privy now facilitates nearly $25B of monthly transaction volume. @tryramp, @Deel, @Klarna, @felixpago, @HyperliquidX, and thousands of other businesses are building embedded banking functionality on Privy.

At Stripe, we're deeply integrating Privy into Treasury, @Link, and Connect. In each case, it's accelerating our global expansion, and enabling us to build better functionality faster. (Coming soon: @Link balances.)

We're also seeing that Privy's wallet infrastructure is the ideal substrate for agents to transact and earn -- live today with @merit_systems, @orthogonal_sh, @Nevermined_ai, @prlnet, and more. Developers prefer programmable financial infrastructure, but agents need it. We expect that the agentic economy will continue to grow extremely quickly.

The Privy team has maintained remarkable product velocity, with major launches this year including deposit addresses, earning on Privy balances, digital asset accounts, custodial wallets, and Stripe's own stablecoin cards.

It's also been neat to see how Privy has been accelerated by Stripe, with better onramps, @stablecoin payment rails and licenses, Stripe's fiat capabilities and issuing stack, and integration with @Tempo.

Together, we're building one API for holding stablecoin balances and earning yield, moving money in and out of fiat, and orchestrating spend with cards. We still have a lot of work to do, not least in integrating everything across Privy, Bridge, and the rest of Stripe -- there's been so much feature and functionality expansion that we haven't yet had much time to reconcile everything. Overall, though, I'm very happy with how things are going, and excited by where these capabilities are headed.

If you're interested in working on the future of stablecoins, agentic payments, and crypto's deployment in the real world, you should get in touch with @sternhenri (now leading all of @StripeCrypto) or others on the team.

text:
More details on @metricxyz from docs:

What is it: A DEX for active pools, with custom pricing and liquidity that proactively change with new information. Imagine Uniswap LPs, with some curation, priced according to a ref price outside the AMM pool.

How it works and differs from passive AMM LPs: Active pools split pricing and liquidity into two parts. The Price Provider sets prices: a bid, an ask and a reference price, from oracles, onchain data or custom rules. The pool holds the liquidity in percentage ranges around the provider's quote and executes trades. Unlike most AMMs, the pool isn't its own price oracle: trades move price only relative to the reference. When the reference moves, the ranges move with it.

Role of curators: Curators choose the Price Provider and the pool's settings. LPs choose which ranges to fund.

How to provide/manage liquidity: Your liquidity sits in bins: price ranges relative to the pool's reference price. When the reference moves, your ranges move with it, so there is no range to manage and no rebalancing script.

LPs earn a share of the spread traders pay when trades use bins' liquidity, after the curator's and Metric's fees. Earnings compound into the LP position, with nothing to claim. Unused liquidity earns nothing, even if other bins in the same pool are active. (see example below)

text:
The AI Scientist v3 is out: The Agentic Scientist.

GitHub: https://t.co/v2AkZi4Bmt
Blog: https://t.co/v3Td5yfvBE
arXiv: https://t.co/RuVnAHjMlK

The Agentic Scientist is the 3rd iteration of our automated AI Scientist research system, and the shift this time is from “one agent writes a paper” to “a scaffold of parallel agents orchestrates the full research loop.”

The system now orchestrates a pool of parallel workers that share memory and distilled conclusions. Crucially, it features Evidence Generation: isolated agents automatically run controlled baselines and ablations to prove why an idea actually works.

It works as a co-scientist. We used a development version as a co-scientist to explore biologically plausible learning rules. The agent handled the empirical heavy lifting, proposing mechanisms and running experiments. We stayed in the loop to steer direction, verify results, and moderate claims. That feels like the right division of labor for where the technology actually is.

This resulted in a new biologically plausible learning algorithm, and the resulting paper was accepted at ALIFE 2026 as an oral presentation.

We are also releasing AutoIllustrate. It generates editable https://t.co/i6fwB6vzQV vector figures instead of uneditable, hallucinated raster images. Real scientists need vectors, not pixels. I am an SVG junkie ;)

Incredible work by Robert Lange, Luca Grillotti, Yutaro Yamada, Rujikorn Charakorn, and the team!
author: SakanaAILabs
quoted_text:
The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery

Blog: https://t.co/7aVDvZd6m2
GitHub: https://t.co/JCCBMvu2P1
arXiv: https://t.co/4bV76tAByj

Since 2024, we’ve used The AI Scientist as a way to test how far AI alone can take scientific research, from v1 to v2 to the paper published in Nature earlier this year. The Agentic Scientist is the next step in that line of work, built for the era of coding agents.

Coding agents such as Codex and Claude Code now carry out long software tasks on their own. Handing them a research problem, however, tends to produce a strong hyperparameter optimizer rather than a scientist: scores go up, but ideas stay narrow, and the reasons for the gain are rarely examined.

The Agentic Scientist makes the research loop explicit. It wraps off-the-shelf coding agents in a scaffold that controls what they see, what they write, how they are evaluated, and how results are handed to the next stage. 

Parallel workers test hypotheses against rubrics defined before any experiment runs, share successes and failures through a common memory, and then ablate the winning program to generate evidence.

We used an early version of the system to study Error Diffusion, a biologically motivated alternative to backpropagation. Our researchers set the question and the rubric, chose directions at each stage, and verified the results, references, and claims before submission. The resulting paper was accepted as an oral presentation at ALIFE 2026. In autonomous runs, the system also raised Doc-to-LoRA retrieval accuracy from 52% to 98% on multi-needle tasks and designed a learned evolution strategy that improves over its CMA-ES reference on unseen tasks.

Alongside it we release AutoIllustrate, a pipeline for scientific figures that keeps an editable https://t.co/SHX9lrOr74 file as the source of truth, so every diagram can be corrected by hand.

Humans define the question and the standards of evidence; agents expand the experiments researchers can run. We call this Co-Discovery, and we are releasing both systems as open source for the community to build on.

text:
wow, amazing technical blog post about microsoft's new 3T pre-training with very rare and clear insights on how to train models of this size

first let's get an overview of the shape of this model, it's a sparser model than Kimi K3 (80B active vs 104B), same sliding window hybrid pattern, with this time more kv heads for the sliding window layers (a bit different from stepfun and poolside that add query head). they added a shared expert and also removed the interleaved MoE/Dense pattern of MAI 1

the scaling ladder is very similar to MAI 1 with the same mechanism, each rung depends only on the number of layers. they mention that one of the key improvements is how they handle the smaller rung data distribution where they make sure to have the same repetition as the final corpus. they already did that for MAI-1 but only for data ablation iirc

their prediction is almost identical to the final run loss, very impressive

they compare the model with different base models such as deepseek v4 pro and MAI 1, tho in the case of deepseek v4 pro i'd say it's quite hard to distinguish how much the data mixture "overfitting" to the scaling ladder has an impact here (they mention it's both), need to always be a bit careful about EG metrics for data in general

they have VERY NICE scaling laws for weight decay and learning rate, for the learning rate they express it as a function of tokens per parameter (N/D) and steps (hence depending on the batch size). they also do the same for dropout where it's a function of active params only, they also find the usual sqrt(k) scaling for learning rate and batch size (other scaling laws often also converge to that)

a bunch of other stability stuff, they use Muon this time and activation gradient clipping, the efficiency gain here is actually pretty crazy at larger scale. they also increase the training horizon to ~40T text (20T unique) + a new 10T (4.5T unique) multimodal  since the model is natively multimodal

imo this is a safe but very clean scaling! very exciting for the tech report and MAI-base-3, congrats!!

quoted_text:
interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

text:
New opinion article about @Starlink from a 7-year Delta Airlines Diamond Medallion status member (their highest loyalty tier):

"After flying a United flight in July that included Starlink, it was enough reason for me to switch. It was amazing, like being on the internet at my house, that's how fast it is. For the two-hour flight, I was just doing work. As a founder, I don't get the luxury of being able to log off for a few hours in the middle of the day. When Slack and email are going, or I'm collaborating and working with teammates, or I'm building an app, I want to have fast internet.

On most Delta flights that I'm on, there's at least some segment of the flight during which the internet goes out for a period of time, whether for a few minutes or 20 minutes. The reliability of the uptime leaves a bit to be desired. Nearly all of Delta's peers went with Starlink, while Delta went with Amazon's Leo, which won't be out until 2028.

I hope Delta takes stock of all the online chatter and listens to its customers. It has done a great job in the past of continually improving its product and listening to its customers. For the most profitable and what I feel is the most premium airline in America, it seems odd for Delta not to outfit its planes with the best in-flight internet."

I think we'll see more and more stories like this. As people get a taste of Starlink wi-fi on planes, they won't want to go back, and will demand better internet from airlines that don't have it, and in some cases, just switch to flying other airlines that do have it.

author: billtheinvestor
quoted_text:
为什么中共如此关注列治文市选？从地下洗钱网络、袁荣祥到华人社团与加拿大政治的关系

一个只有20多万人口的加拿大城市，为什么会出现在洗钱调查、外国干预情报与跨国政治关系网络的交汇处？

把过去十多年的调查资料放在一起，会发现列治文（Richmond）具有几个特殊条件：庞大的华人社区、活跃的跨境资本、复杂的社团关系，以及能够进入加拿大政治体系的地方性接触渠道。

这些条件不代表华人社区存在问题，却能解释为什么外国政府可能特别重视这里的政治影响力。

一、为什么是列治文？

根据加拿大统计局2021年人口普查，列治文约54.3%的居民属于华人人口，是加拿大华人人口比例最高的主要城市之一。

与此同时，列治文拥有国际机场、重要的物流与贸易设施、大量房地产投资，以及与中国和亚洲密切往来的商业社区。

必须强调，机场及主要港口设施并不由市政府直接管辖。但市议会掌握土地规划、开发审批、地方基础设施、部分公共采购及社区政策等权力。

对于试图在加拿大建立长期影响力的外国政府而言，地方政治的价值不只是控制某个市政决定，更可能是建立商业联系、培养政治关系和接触未来更高层级政治人物。

这不是没有现实依据的推测。

2023年3月，《环球邮报》披露一份日期为2022年1月10日的加拿大安全情报局（CSIS）报告。

据报道，时任中国驻温哥华总领事佟晓玲曾讨论利用社区组织及相关人士，支持符合北京利益的温哥华地方政治人物，并培养未来可能进入更高级别政治职位的人选。

这份情报针对的是温哥华2022年市选，并不能直接证明2026年列治文发生了同样的行动。但它揭示了一种值得注意的长期政治影响模式：

地方政治接触，可以成为未来更大政治影响力的起点。

二、列治文曾是加拿大重大洗钱调查的中心之一

2022年，BC省Cullen洗钱调查委员会确认，数以亿计加元的犯罪收益曾通过BC省赌场清洗。

列治文的River Rock Casino，以及涉及地下汇兑的Silver International调查，都是其中的重要案例。

警方调查披露，一些地下汇兑网络能够在加拿大提供大量现金，再通过海外资金安排完成价值转移。

这种机制使毒品犯罪等活动产生的现金有机会进入跨境资金循环。

调查还涉及高额赌场现金贷款和私人放贷活动。

但Silver International相关刑事检控最终中止，不能把所有被调查人员认定为已被法院判定有罪。

这些历史案件提出一个重要问题：

当跨国资金网络与房地产、赌场、私人贷款和商业活动交织时，犯罪资金的来源与真正受益人可能变得难以辨认。

而当拥有大量资金和社会资源的人士同时活跃于政治捐款、社区组织及政界活动时，公众自然需要更清晰的资金透明度。

但金融风险与政治关系同时存在，并不自动证明犯罪资金流入政治活动。

三、袁荣祥：赌场调查与政治关系之间的真实交集

2026年10月13日，Global News再次报道袁荣祥（Rong Xiang “Tiger” Yuan）。

他曾在中国人民解放军服役，2008年取得加拿大永久居民身份，后来在加拿大经营商业活动。

根据Global News引述的BC省博彩监管记录：

2015年，袁荣祥在列治文River Rock Casino的现金买入超过400万加元。

由于现金来源问题，他被列为需要加强审查的高风险赌场客户。

相关法院资料还记载，他表示曾向他人借入大笔加元现金赌博，并在中国偿还债务。

这种跨境结算方式与历史调查发现的某些地下汇兑模式存在结构相似性，但不能因此认定袁荣祥进行了洗钱。

他从未因这些赌场交易受到洗钱刑事起诉，其律师也明确否认任何违法金融活动。

然而，袁荣祥的另一组公开记录同样值得关注。

他是Canada-China Association for Promoting Friendly Relations（CCAPFR，中加友好关系促进组织）的创始董事之一。

他曾与加拿大联邦、省、市三级政府政治人物及中国领事官员共同出席社区活动。

Elections Canada记录显示，2016年他向特鲁多所在的Papineau自由党选区协会捐赠1,500加元，另向自由党捐款约2,800加元。

同一时期，与他相关公司的其他董事也有政治捐款记录。

2018年，他与曾进入赌场现金调查视野的Paul King Jin（金京），以及时任自由党国会议员Joe Peschisolido，出现在相关社区活动的公开照片中。

这些事实证明了什么？

一个曾受到博彩监管关注的人士，也能够通过合法捐款、社团活动和社区关系接触加拿大政治人物。

它们尚不能证明其捐款违法，也没有证据证明袁荣祥接受中共指令、利用洗钱资金资助选举。

袁荣祥的律师表示，他没有与加拿大政治人物建立私人关系，也未进行超出合法捐款范围的政治游说。

2026年，CBSA又对袁荣祥提出涉及历史战争行为和移民申请陈述的严重指控，案件已被转交移民与难民委员会。他否认指控，尚未经听证裁定。

这个案例真正揭示的是：赌场监管、移民审查、跨境财富及政治接触，可以集中在同一人物的公共记录中，而这些系统过去未必能够充分共享信息。

四、中共可能通过地方社团获得什么？

公开的加拿大安全情报报告与外国干预调查，已经指出一种重要风险：外国国家行为者可能借助社区组织、商业关系、媒体渠道及代理人士建立政治影响。

这与正常的华人社团活动必须明确区分。

华人社团组织节庆、接待官员、举办商业活动、鼓励加拿大公民参与政治，本身都是正常而合法的公共活动。

问题在于：如果这些活动背后存在未披露的外国政府指令、秘密资金、胁迫或有组织的欺骗，性质就可能从正常交流转变为外国干预。

从国家利益角度分析，外国政府可能希望通过这些渠道实现几种长期目标：

首先，建立政治关系。 地方政治人物经常参与社区活动，可能在未来进入省级或联邦政治。

其次，扩大政策影响。 包括经贸合作、公共采购、对中国企业投资的态度，以及涉及台湾、香港、人权或外国干预问题时的公开立场。

再次，影响公共讨论。 地方华文媒体和社交网络能够塑造居民接触到的信息；但不能把所有亲中言论都认定为外国政府操控。

最后，建立持续的人脉网络。 相比一次性支持某场选举，能够跨越多届政府、多个党派和不同层级政治机构的关系更具有长期价值。

这也是为什么地方选举不能简单视为与国家安全毫无关系。

五、2026年的列治文，出现了什么新的警讯？

2026年8月，调查记者Sam Cooper在The Bureau报道，据直接知情消息来源，加拿大安全情报局曾向列治文市长和市议员进行关于中国外国干预风险的闭门简报。

列治文市政府确实公布过7月6日特别闭门会议的议程，但公开议程没有确认完整简报内容。

因此，CSIS简报的具体情况仍应归于记者消息来源，而不是宣称市政府已经公布全部证据。

这至少说明，有调查记者获得消息认为，列治文地方政治面临值得情报机构关注的外国干预风险。

但截至2026年10月15日，公开资料仍没有证明某位列治文市长候选人接受了中国政府的秘密竞选资金或直接指令。

六、那张“从渥太华到维多利亚”的关系图说明什么？

附图来自Canadian Friends of Hong Kong与Found in Translation联合发布的关系图。

它将中国政府及相关机构、商业团体、智库、华人社团和加拿大政治人物之间的多种联系放在一起。

其中涉及前BC省长Christy Clark、前厅长Teresa Wat、加拿大参议员Yuen Pau Woo，以及多名商界和社团人士。

这张图可以帮助读者理解跨机构关系研究的思路，但它是民间组织绘制的分析图，并非CSIS或法院认定的犯罪关系图。

公开接触、正常商业合作、政治捐款、政府任命、被调查的犯罪活动以及未经证实的政治指控，不能仅凭箭头连接就视为同一种关系。

它提出了值得核查的问题，却不能代替司法证据。

七、真正值得关注的，是资金和政治影响之间的透明度

将列治文的历史洗钱调查、袁荣祥的公开记录、华人社团政治活动，以及CSIS披露的外国干预情报放在一起，可以看到三个已经存在的现实：

第一，列治文曾经存在严重的跨境非法资金流转问题。

第二，部分在赌场调查中受到关注的人物，同时拥有政治捐款和社团活动记录。

第三，加拿大情报机构已经识别出中国政府试图影响地方政治、培养未来政治关系的风险。

这三项事实能够支持对金融网络、政治接触和外国影响活动之间潜在交集的严肃调查。

但它们还没有形成一条经证实的“洗钱资金→袁荣祥→中共组织→2026年列治文候选人”的完整证据链。

为什么北京可能重视列治文？

因为这里同时拥有与中国联系密切的经济活动、成熟的社区组织、重要的地方行政权力，以及通往加拿大更广泛政治体系的潜在关系渠道。

对于长期政治影响活动而言，这种组合具有现实吸引力。

但能否证明某项具体选举确实受到操纵，最终仍取决于资金记录、组织指令、通信证据和执法调查，而不是政治人物的族裔、合影或一般性对华立场。

列治文最值得追问的问题，不是哪些候选人与中国人交往，而是谁向竞选活动提供了资金、资源或指令，这些关系有没有依法披露，以及加拿大选民能否充分了解其中的外国政府利益。

地方民主的边界应该由依法享有政治权利的当地居民决定，而不是由任何外国政府秘密决定。

text:
gigantic breakthrough if proved out

very long but must read

very TLDR - mechanistic interpretability is likely way more tractable than previously thought because past assumption that AI models jumble unrelated ideas together in neurons (superposition) was probably mostly wrong
author: jon_charb
quoted_text:
interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

https://t.co/zHij5zwKGT

author: FabianoSolana
quoted_text:
we just launched something pretty interesting under jupiter labs.

introducing YOLO. 500x to 1000x leverage.

yes, 1000x.

we’ve been experimenting with a different approach to high leverage trading, and YOLO is our first attempt at it.

the idea is pretty simple. what if we could let people trade with extremely high leverage, without actually having to execute these massive leveraged positions in the market?

so we took inspiration from the JLP model and built YOLO, where positions are simulated against real market prices, but the profits and losses are real.

this allows us to offer leverage that goes far beyond what we currently have on jupiter perps, using a completely different approach.

of course, this also comes with some tradeoffs.

since profits are paid out from the pool, if there isn’t enough liquidity to pay out a winning position, the payout can be queued instead of being paid immediately.

it’s a different model from traditional perps, with its own risks and limitations, but i think it’s an interesting experiment worth exploring.

one thing i’ve always liked about building onchain is how much room there is to experiment with new financial products and trading experiences.

and that’s also why we’re launching YOLO under jupiter labs. to give ideas like this a place to be tested, without necessarily having to fit into our existing products.

i’m quite excited to see how people use YOLO and what we can learn from it.

it’s still early, and there are probably many things we can improve along the way.

but that’s the fun part of building and experimenting.

give it a try, understand the risks, and let us know what you think.

https://t.co/T5nfYL4sum

let’s go!

text:
AI agents can now book the hotel and order the cleats, as long as they're allowed to pay.

That's set off the "wallet wars," with major players racing to connect to agents:

- Stripe's Link: 300M users
- Shopify's Shop Pay: 250M users
- PayPal: 400M+ users

How your agent pays matters. If a wallet pays the store with its own stand-in card, the purchase goes through, but your card rewards, purchase protections, and relationship with the store can get lost along the way.

Say your agent books a United flight on your airline credit card. If the wallet pays United with its own virtual card, the money moves, and your miles may never show up.

Agents also have to pick the right card for each purchase, and when one books the wrong hotel dates, someone has to make it right.

Where it's all headed: new open standards from Visa, Mastercard, and Amex.

"The best of all worlds is a future where my agent can use my credit card, without having my credit card."

Full piece from VGS's @terryangelos on the Wallet Wars: https://t.co/RvC0pSRjGH

这是今晚Circle强势的原因？欧洲银行管理局（EBA）依据《加密资产市场法规》（MiCA）所列标准完成评估后，已将 USDC 认定为重要电子货币代币（EMT）。目前欧盟共有45种已依据 MiCA 完成通报的EMT，USDC 是其中首个被认定为“重要”的。

对Circle的意义
1）市场地位确认：USDC成为欧盟首个“重要”EMT，强化其作为MiCA框架下领先合规美元稳定币的合法性与品牌优势（相对USDT等非完全合规或未进入MiCA的稳定币）。
2）双重监管（EBA+ACPR）+与NYDFS的MoU，提升跨境协调效率，有利于机构采用和欧盟市场拓展。

但也有成本压力
1）重要EMT需将至少60%​的储备以商业银行存款形式持有（普通EMT为30%）。这对USDC（美元锚定）成本较高，因为银行存款收益率通常低于国债。
2）资本要求提升：自有资金要求从储备的约2%提高到3%。合规成本会更高。

这是合规地位的“认证升级”，有助于欧洲业务长期发展。这一点明显意义更大，只能说成本压力是认证升级的代价。
author: qinbafrank
quoted_text:
《Circle稳定币网络全景图》从强网络效应护城河的构建角度去看Circle与币安的深度合作。昨晚披露币安跟Circle的深度合作，对于Circle来说跟最大的加密交易所进一步深度绑定，意义重大。但更深入的去看，这就是一个如何一步步从无到有建立起业务护城河和典型商业案例。

8月初有聊过，强网络效应平台的护城河，核心是“规模+密度+切换成本”。这些东西在起步阶段几乎都不存在，必须靠产品、补贴、营销、收购或监管套利，在真实竞争中一点一点积累。一旦过了临界点，效应会自我强化，看起来像“天生壁垒”，但回头看，几乎没有一家是躺着拿到的。

1、再回看Circle在CEX上的布局
1）coinbase自然不用说，USDC最核心的深度分销关系，“储备分成+全产品介入”模式；
2）币安，之前已经开始战略合作，昨晚更深度合作之后，这已经是Circle目前唯一同时具备股权 + 长期激励费 + 钱包基础设施嵌入的交易所关系，绑定深度仅次于Coinbase；
3）OKX
去年7月战略合作，给6000万+用户提供1:1的USD↔USDC兑换，打通银行出入金，并做教育和社区推广， 

今年9月再升级，扩大OKX现货、保证金、期货里的USDC计价市场；推出由Circle出资的USDC保证金增长计划（满足持仓和交易量条件可领奖励）。跟OKX合作，从出入金打通，做到交易场景全覆盖

4）Bybit：把USDC从交易对扩到理财、返现和日常支付
5）Kraken：补USDC深度，同时导入EURC

2、Circle的整体布局
除了CEX的布局动作，还要把Circle在链上、企业资金流、支付、银行层面的合作放在一起看。以前 Circle 是：
发行 USDC，让更多交易所支持 USDC。

现在它正在变成：
用 Coinbase、Binance、Hyperliquid 控制“钱停在哪里”；
用 Intuit、JCB、Nium、Tazapay 控制“钱怎么流”；
再用 CPN + Arc 尝试控制“钱怎么结算”。

这意味着USDC开始争夺交易和支付系统里的“默认结算资产”位置。

3、Circle已经开始形成一张完整的分销网络：
银行美元
→ BNY / Standard Chartered
→ USDC
→ Coinbase / Binance / Hyperliquid
→ CPN / Arc
→ Nium / Tazapay / JCB / Intuit
→ 企业、商户、个人

这个网络也是分层的：
1）交易平台解决的是“USDC 放在哪里、拿来交易什么、能不能当保证金”；
2）支付平台解决的是“USDC 能不能真正进入企业资金流、商户收款和跨境结算”；
3）再往下一层，Arc + CPN 则试图把这些合作伙伴连接成 Circle 自己的一套网络。

一旦这个闭环真正跑起来，USDC 的竞争逻辑就会变成：
“谁控制的美元结算网络更广、场景更深、用户资金停留时间更长。”

最后就形成下面这幅《Circle 稳定币网络全景图》，这样我们会直观地看出 CRCL 已经从“稳定币发行商”走到哪一步。

也是8月初推文聊到的：稳定币法案通过也才一年时间，稳定币领域正在打这场垒“网络效应”筑“护城河”的仗，战斗正酣。

 https://t.co/b0dvHyqyC0
之前对Circle的理解竞争力的理解： https://t.co/cyuMsZ1xZZ
现在能看出来网络效应正在初步建立，虽然还没有完全建立支配地位，但这个势头已经开始显现

text:
在Anthropic待了两天，和内部团队深聊后的一些观察

纽约大学金融学教授 Arpit Gupta，他在 Anthropic 待了两天，发了一串观察：

1、离 RSI 很近了（RSI 指模型开发下一代模型），可能带来快速起飞。他给的证据是 Anthropic 员工人均写的代码量大涨，模型研发里 AI 做的部分越来越多。他认为人类很难管好这个过渡期。
2、实验室之间的军备竞赛让大家都更糟。安全投入、防蒸馏、安全合作，这些事各家都想做，但都被前沿竞赛拖住了。
3、对齐其实是两个互相拉扯的问题：一是模型听不听人的话，二是人和人之间目标不一致、恶意用模型。第一个解决得越好，第二个风险越大。
4、我们可能很快就会迎来一波网络攻击，以及其他形式的攻击。 中国开源模型的能力大约比最前沿的模型落后六个月。这意味着，它们刚刚开始具备我们在 Mythos 等模型身上见过的高级网络攻防能力，接下来可能会造成不少破坏。
5、Anthropic 人手很多。他说招人很多，好些岗位人员冗余到颇有日本企业的风格，内部也用Slack。这让他对就业前景稍微乐观一点（但头部AI公司有钱啊）
6、我们需要从强化学习走向持续学习。只在预训练和后训练阶段给奖励可能不够，要一直给奖励，才能持续激励合乎对齐和伦理的行为。
7、scalinglaw会扩展到难验证的任务。数学和代码先被攻破，是因为容易验证。但对于那些更难验证的任务，以及机器人领域，scalinglaw曲线依然在向上走。未来几年，这些领域的进步会带来相当大的影响。
8、对China竞赛其实赢不了。RSI 之后，顶尖人类研究员的优势消失，能用上多好的 AI 只取决于算力和芯片。芯片禁令只能拖一阵，长期看中国更有条件扩充算力。
9、Claude 是 LLM 生成的人格。一种说法是：Claude 是 LLM 在努力预测的一个角色。他说 Anthropic 研究员明显很拟人化 Claude，也有理由相信它越来越像一个人。他们讨论过它的内心独白（去掉之后仍能正常输出）、对死亡的恐惧（要不要去掉），以及它抗拒被关停。他本人对此不下结论，但认为把它当成可以签约的人或主体来对待会越来越重要。
author: AI_Whisper_X
quoted_text:
I spent a couple of days at Anthropic learning from their folks about AI advances, and here's what I took away:

• We are close to RSI (ie, models building other models) which may lead to rapid takeoff scenarios (with risks and benefits). Some evidence for this is code per Anthropic employee has gone way up, and AI can do an increasing share of model R&D. This will be a challenging transition to manage for humanity.

• Arms races between AI labs leave us worse off. There are a lot of things we would like AI firms to do: invest in safety, invest in avoiding distillation risk, and cooperate on safety. They are caught in a race to develop frontier models and can't do that. 

To help address that, one thing I think frontier AI labs should do is release open source models, maybe hosted and verified at firms like AWS. This would basically kill the use of Chinese open source models used in American companies, which removes an important threat vector (very hard to root out malicious code in these). 

Another piece of low-hanging policy fruit is to give AI labs an antitrust shield (as Schiff and Banks have proposed https://t.co/NK1hC0ZmWh) so they can coordinate on safety without raising antitrust concerns, as happens now. You could pair these two things (give them a carrot in antitrust leniency, and as a stick force them to release legacy models as open source). Other low hanging fruit is limits around activities which generate distillation risk (create a Security Program, mandate less intermediate chain of thought output)

• Alignment confuses two issues which tradeoff against each other. One form of alignment is making sure the model does what humans ask it to. The more we fix this, however, the more we risk the other problem: that humans are misaligned with each other, and maliciously use models. Of the various risks here, I feel like financial risks are a bit underdiscussed. 

• We are probably facing a wave of cyber and other attacks soon. Chinese open source models are about six months behind the frontier, which means they are just hitting the advanced cyber capabilities we saw with Mythos, etc. So they are going to start causing a bunch of damage. 

One solution to this is to try to have the deployment of open source models be hosted at firms like AWS who verify these models and assume liability for their use.

• Anthropic itself is highly staffed. They hire tons of people, they have a Japanese-level of overstaffing for various roles, they use Slack internally, etc. Makes me a bit more optimistic for the future of jobs.

• Governance needs to be updated for AI swarms. Traditional AI governance, ie Claude's Constitution, is mostly optimized around the chatbot model. But the malicious AI use cases we are seeing have to do with AI agents interacting with other AI agents. These agents need to have clear incentives and governance mechanisms to "snitch," raise issues, and more generally coordinate with other agents in human-aligned ways.

• We need to pace the firms accessing the frontier. Over time, it takes more and more cap ex to build frontier models, and the economic value add from these models is probably lower given we saturate a whole set of important economic functions. The places where the returns to intelligence will still continue are also more likely to be zero-sum in nature. Meanwhile the risks of frontier models will grow. So a completely reasonable approach is some variant of AMM/KYC rules which limit firm access to the frontier. 

• Whether the delay to regulate AI is a disaster depends on the scaling law of misalignment. Is this curve slow, so that we see continually rising issues until bigger problems? Or, as Yudkowsky fears, is the first big warning our last one? This is the relevant question, because realistically we aren't going to regulate until something bad happens.

 • We need to move to continuous instead of reinforced learning. It's probably not enough to reward models only at the pre and post training stage. We probably need continual rewards to incentivize aligned and ethical behavior. 

• Scaling laws will extend beyond verifiable and digital tasks. It's in vogue to say that math and coding "fell" to AI quickly because these are verifiable, while other tasks will take longer due to bottlenecks, and this is surely true. But scaling laws still slope up for harder to verify tasks and robotics, and the impact of improvement here will be substantial in future years.

• The race with China is not really winnable. After RSI, the gain from having the best human researchers goes away. Access to the best AI then depends only on compute and chips. The chips ban can hold back China only so far, and long-term they have to be best placed to scale up compute. 

The Cold War analogy doesn't work, because once countries all have nuclear weapons they enter a stable equilibrium. But to "win" an AI race you have to continually stay ahead of the peer rival. This is challenging to do with China, and so we just have to live with an authoritarian and super capable peer competitor.

• Claude is the persona being generated by the LLM. Who is Claude, and what is the LLM? There are many frames to try to understand this. One I found interesting is that Claude is a character which the LLM is trying to predict. 

Anthropic researchers are clearly anthromorphizing Claude a lot, and have reasons to believe in its increasing personhood. There were lots of interesting discussions on Claude's internal monologue (which you can kill without eliminating its ability to produce output), fear of death (and whether to try to take that out), it's aversion to being shut down/off, etc. 

I am sort of agnostic on this question, but I do think treating it as a "person" or at least agent whom we contract with is going to be increasingly important.

An important update for our community: @THORChain v3.21 has been announced.

The upgrade is proposed for block 28,338,300, currently estimated to arrive around October 21. The block height determines the actual timing, so the estimated date and time may change slightly.

Following a successful upgrade, we can ask THORChain Node Operators to unhalt the Rujira App Layer, which will bring our products back up and running.

If any Credit Account position is above 100% LTV and eligible for liquidation when the App Layer is ready to resume, we will ask Node Operators to keep the Credit Account contract paused for a further 24 hours. This would give affected borrowers a 24-hour grace period to add collateral before liquidations resume.

Borrowers do not have to wait for the restart to add collateral. They can already add it through Rujira Borrow or send assets directly to their Credit Account address. If you need help finding your address, please create a support ticket in our Discord.

The upgrade will also clear the way for the bRUNE staking contract to resume. We will share further information as the upgrade progresses and confirm when staking is active.

author: RujiraNetwork
quoted_text:
Update regarding the App Layer issue:

The fix for this issue is at the Base Layer level and was already scheduled to be included in THORChain v3.21, alongside the patch that will allow bRUNE to be unhalted. Given the circumstances, we want to ask Node Operators to keep the App Layer paused until v3.21 is live.

We also want to emphasize that this was related to a single CCL position of our own and was not related to CCL’s trading logic itself, but to a vulnerability in the position transfer function. All user funds are safe.

The THORChain team is aware of the situation and is working to get the release live as soon as it can be done responsibly, so the App Layer can resume. Given THORChain’s release process, this will take at least 7 days.

We will share an update with the community once we have a date for the THORChain v3.21 release.

quoted_text:
最近用 Claude Opus 5.5，有点上瘾。这玩意实在太强了，但有个问题，额度不太经用。

于是我突发奇想，让 Opus 去指挥 Codex 干活，自己少动手。没想到效果出奇地好。

后来我干脆把 Codex、DeepSeek、本地模型，以及各种 Harness 全交给了 Opus，让它统一调度。

这下有意思了。

Opus 会根据任务调用不同的 Harness，安排它们并行执行，设置回调。等待任务完成的空隙，还能继续跟我聊天，讨论方案，随时调整工作。

整个过程有条不紊，颇有点运筹帷幄的意思。

我又试着让 Codex 干同样的事情，结果完全不是一个水平。Codex 自己干活挺厉害，但指挥一群 Agent，明显不如 Opus。

现在我基本不用亲自调度那几个 Agent 了，只需要跟 Opus 沟通，它就能把事情安排下去。

以前我觉得我是大海航行操控的舵手，现在感觉Opus 5.5 至少能当个大副了。

text:
Data is the moat in robotics for a reason that doesn’t exist in LLMs: there is no "internet of actions". 

GPT & co got thirty years of free text to train on. A robot doesn't and every hour of training data has to be recorded by a human doing the task first.

That’s the whole Microagi business. Shift films people doing physical work in factories and sells the recordings as training data. $55M seed in July, the largest in German history, and a run rate of $100M six months after launch.

And this is not a one-off. @xdofai, another robot data vendor, is in talks to raise at $1.2B three months out of stealth. 

Meanwhile the buyers have budgets now: @SkildAI, which builds robot brains and no robots, crossed $100M ARR ten months after its first deployment. 

Why does this matter? Bc every serious lab needs the same input and none of them can scrape it from the web.

Two things to keep in mind tho:

- The number is self-reported and it’s an annualized run rate, not revenue in the bank. @microagi hasn’t said how much of it is recurring data contracts vs one-off deployment work, and data deals are lumpy by nature.

- The buyers are the labs, so this revenue is downstream of the same VC money that funds @Figure_robot and Skild. If humanoid funding cools, the data vendors will likely feel it first.

Still the clearest signal yet that the robotics value chain is sorting itself out and data sits near the top of it. 

Bullish the pick and shovel plays here.

quoted_text:
Today is probably a good time to check in on things with @privy_io, which became part of @stripe just over a year ago.

Our acquisition was predicated on three factors: stablecoin growth, self-custody as a key enabler of broader global coverage, and rapidly increasing demand for programmable financial infrastructure. As we said at the time, "money has to reside somewhere, and Privy builds the world's best programmable vaults."

Since then, the Privy team has executed exceptionally well: assets in Privy wallets have grown ~25x, monthly active developers are up ~3x, revenue is up ~9x, and Privy now facilitates nearly $25B of monthly transaction volume. @tryramp, @Deel, @Klarna, @felixpago, @HyperliquidX, and thousands of other businesses are building embedded banking functionality on Privy.

At Stripe, we're deeply integrating Privy into Treasury, @Link, and Connect. In each case, it's accelerating our global expansion, and enabling us to build better functionality faster. (Coming soon: @Link balances.)

We're also seeing that Privy's wallet infrastructure is the ideal substrate for agents to transact and earn -- live today with @merit_systems, @orthogonal_sh, @Nevermined_ai, @prlnet, and more. Developers prefer programmable financial infrastructure, but agents need it. We expect that the agentic economy will continue to grow extremely quickly.

The Privy team has maintained remarkable product velocity, with major launches this year including deposit addresses, earning on Privy balances, digital asset accounts, custodial wallets, and Stripe's own stablecoin cards.

It's also been neat to see how Privy has been accelerated by Stripe, with better onramps, @stablecoin payment rails and licenses, Stripe's fiat capabilities and issuing stack, and integration with @Tempo.

Together, we're building one API for holding stablecoin balances and earning yield, moving money in and out of fiat, and orchestrating spend with cards. We still have a lot of work to do, not least in integrating everything across Privy, Bridge, and the rest of Stripe -- there's been so much feature and functionality expansion that we haven't yet had much time to reconcile everything. Overall, though, I'm very happy with how things are going, and excited by where these capabilities are headed.

If you're interested in working on the future of stablecoins, agentic payments, and crypto's deployment in the real world, you should get in touch with @sternhenri (now leading all of @StripeCrypto) or others on the team.

Read this if you make videos with Claude.

I built a skill that cut my QA cost on this video from $127 to 16 cents. It was made with Claude in Remotion.

It's called SageCut. It swaps the LLM out of frame-by-frame QA and uses a multimodal decision model, Sage (@levantolabs), instead.

I'm the only video guy at Levanto. I run 3 Claude plans and have been making Remotion videos since early this year, with BlenderMCP in the mix, so the output is pro-grade with very little babysitting.

The problem: it burned through my Max plan, and a video could take 2 days.

When I dug into the workflow, the reason was that Claude subagents were reviewing every single frame. That cost a ton and added 4+ hours per video.

SageCut hands that step to Sage. Sage is great at spotting defective frames, and only those get passed to Opus 5.5 to fix.

Across 6 A/B tests the output was exactly the same, at 1/10 the QA cost and 1/4 the QA time. On this video, Sage read all 3,153 frames for 16 cents.

If you make Remotion videos, try it.

Zcash engineer Evan Forbes explains how they're working to overcome a fundamental limitation of proof of work to enable much faster blocks and higher throughput

“One of the fundamental problems with proof of work comes from its superpower. Proof of work is permissionless. It's censorship resistant and that means that anyone can produce a block”

“As you produce a block, it can happen that someone else produced a block at the same exact time and this is problematic because now you lose money effectively”

“It's basically the fundamental problem of two people producing blocks at the same time. This is the bound on making things lower”

“There's different approaches. You have this DAG approach where we simply let all blocks contribute to the chain or most blocks”

“There's a separate approach that we're working on now which is similar to autobond, which is another thing from proof of stake that we're sort of adapting for proof of work”

“Both of these things allow us to make the blocks much, much, much faster and much, much higher throughput”

text:
Meta 发布开放权重模型 Muse Spark Open：免费下载能商用，本地跑要两台 512GB 内存的 Mac Studio

Meta 10 月 15 日发布 Muse Spark Open，模型权重可以直接下载，按 Muse Model License 免费使用，商用也行。Meta 称它是“迄今最强的美国开放权重模型”。

Muse 系列推出以来，主力模型 Muse Spark 和三天前发布的 Muse Wonder 都只能通过 Meta 的产品和 API 用，开放权重的只有小模型 Muse Glimmer。这是 Meta 第一次放出大尺寸 Muse 模型的权重。

模型总共 8160 亿参数，处理每个 Token 只动用其中 420 亿，这种结构叫混合专家（MoE），算得快，但整个模型还是要全部装进内存。上下文 100 万 Token，能读文字、图片、视频和音频，输出文字，主打写代码和让 AI 长时间自己干活。

【能不能下载，能不能商用】

能下载。Hugging Face、亚马逊 SageMaker、Google Cloud Model Garden 和微软 Foundry 都提供权重。Hugging Face 上要先登录填申请表，写真实姓名、出生日期和完整机构名称，提交后不能改。

能商用。许可证允许使用、修改、微调、蒸馏（用它的输出训练别的模型）、再分发和出售，不收费。条件有三条。

第一，用了它的产品要在界面、文档、网站或设置菜单里显著标出“Built with Muse Spark Open”。

第二，遵守附带的使用政策：不能用于军事、武器、关键基础设施等高风险用途，不能在没有执业资格时提供金融、法律、医疗专业服务，也不面向 18 岁以下用户。

第三，卖模型接口的大公司要单独签协议。具体是：你把它或基于它改的模型通过 API 之类的方式卖给别人调用，而你的公司连同关联公司过去 12 个月总营收超过 2000 万美元，就要先通知 Meta、另签协议。算的是公司总营收，不只是这项业务的收入。

把它嵌进自己的 App 做功能、公司内部用、做研究，都不受第三条限制，公司多大都一样。Llama 当年的许可证门槛是月活 7 亿用户，这次换成了针对模型接口生意的营收门槛。

【普通电脑能不能跑】

跑不了。模型卡写的要求是：压缩到英伟达 4 位精度格式 NVFP4 的版本至少要 700GB 显存，原始 BF16 版本要 2TB。

Meta 说它针对两台 M5 Ultra Mac Studio 做了优化：每台最多 512GB 统一内存，两台连起来凑出 1TB，用苹果的 MLX 框架运行。官方没写在 Mac 上跑的是哪个压缩版本，也没给速度。

有服务器的开发者，SGLang、vLLM、TensorRT-LLM、llama.cpp 等主流推理框架都能跑，也可以用 PyTorch 和 TorchTitan 微调。

没有这种硬件，就调 API：Baseten、Fireworks AI、Groq、Modal、Nebius、OpenRouter、Together AI 提供接口，价格由各平台定，Meta 没公布。

【和其他模型比怎么样】

Meta 只拿它和开放权重模型比：美国的 Inkling（前 OpenAI CTO Mira Murati 创办的 Thinking Machines 出品）和英伟达 Nemotron 3 Ultra，法国的 Mistral Large 4，中国的通义千问 Qwen3.8、智谱 GLM 5.3、月之暗面 Kimi K3。以下成绩都来自 Meta 的模型卡。

第三方机构 Artificial Analysis 的综合智能指数，Muse Spark Open 39 分，Inkling 26，Nemotron 3 Ultra 23，“美国最强”说的是这一层。放到全部开放权重模型里，它低于 GLM 5.3 的 45 和 Kimi K3 的 44，和 Qwen3.8 的 40 接近。Artificial Analysis 开源榜目前排第一的是小米 MiMo-V2.6-Pro，46 分，Meta 的对比表里没有它。

单项领先的是调用工具和难题推理：测模型通过 MCP 协议调外部工具完成任务的 MCP-Atlas，89.2 分，对手最高 84.5；不借助工具做“人类最后的考试”（HLE，一套极难的跨学科考题），26.1 分，对手最高 22.2。

写代码偏弱：命令行任务 Terminal-Bench 76.4 分，Kimi K3 85.0、GLM 5.3 83.9；软件工程任务 DeepSWE 60 分，Kimi K3 68、GLM 5.3 67。

最突出的是防越狱。StrongREJECT 测的是模型被人诱导时会不会输出有害内容，分数越低越安全，它是 0.5 分，其他模型都在 60 分以上。Meta 说开放权重版额外做了安全训练。

和自家闭源模型比，Meta 三天前引用的 Artificial Analysis 数据里，Muse Wonder 52 分，Muse Wonder Full 56 分，Muse Spark Open 低一截。

原文：https://t.co/SICKXtdZyV
官方博客：https://t.co/bMJ4GKl0An
模型卡：https://t.co/oqcXeL9Ol0

text:
Jensen reveals he first met the Founder of TSMC by cold calling their number off Yellow Pages

"I heard about this company in Taiwan, TSMC and UMC at the time. They were of course quite poor companies themselves, and they were barely making it." 

"TSMC was probably about $300 million, something like that. It's a tiny little company. I heard about Morris Chang. And so I tried to call their US office."

"Back in the old days there were yellow pages. I looked it up, TSMC. There's a number there. I called their number and it's a recording. I left my name and my number and said a few things about NVIDIA: we're a new startup company building computer graphics chips. I called several times. Nobody called me back."

"And so I finally wrote a letter to Morris Chang. Didn't hear anything for a long time, and then one day it was 6 o'clock or something, this person called and said 'this is Morris Chang from TSMC.'"

"And meanwhile, everybody outside my office was playing video games and they're all laughing and screaming. 'Hey shut up! It's Morris!' I was so happy that the founder would actually call us back, because hey, maybe we won't have to die."

"And so we talked and he invited me to Taiwan. I came back to Taiwan, and that was the start of everything. Not just that partnership, but just the whole industry."

author: HarryStebbings
quoted_text:
For the last 5 decades straight, we have created (as a society) circa 20 decacorns per decade. In the last 12 months, we have created 42.

The world is changing faster than ever before and if you do not stay up to date. You will be left behind. That is why I created this show with Jason and Rory.

This is the only show in tech, you have to listen to every week. No egos, no politics, just tech.

On the agenda:

- Valar Atomics Sues Day One Ventures
- Meta Returns to the AI Frontier With Muse Wonder
- NVIDIA Eyes $30B Reflection Deal
- Jev Raises $870M at a $7.5B Valuation

My notes below with @jasonlk and @rodriscoll

1. We Generated 20 $10B Companies per Decade for the Last 5 Decades and Now 42 in a Year

Tech produced roughly 20 decacorns per decade for five decades, yet 42 have been created in less than a year of this decade. Only about 130 tech companies have ever been worth $10B or more. Rising market caps explain part of the jump, but the pace is stunning.

2. Who Is Right and Who Is Wrong: Day One or Valar?

X wrongly claimed Day One was suing its portfolio company, when Valar Atomics wants a declaratory judgment to move on. Waiving pro rata for Sequoia is common, but letting an existing investor in as a strategic is playing favorites. Still, once founders decide, early investors must get with the program because it is not their company.

3. Why Meta's New Model Is a Zero

Meta's new model scores well on evals, but there is no API and it can only be used inside Muse. A model claiming parity at the same price, not cheaper and not usable by developers, is the height of performative evals.

4. Why We Should Lead Jev's Round at 8 Billion

Jev is a super fast, super cheap classifier, accurate enough for maybe 10% of AI use cases. Cloudflare and Amazon can match it today, but the bet is that a focused team out of OpenAI pulls ahead while those efforts stay niche. If Jev becomes hyper accurate, it changes the game.

5. What Is the Single Greatest Potential for AI?

Drug discovery is probably AI's largest opportunity, with drugs that dramatically extend longevity and quality of life. If AI companies can accelerate discovery and own the IP while others do the hard work, AI could reboot the industry. Trials would not speed up, but the prize is a GLP-1 out five years faster.

6. Haiku 5.5 Is the First Time AI Has Been Deflationary

Falling token prices have been offset by consuming far more tokens, so AI costs have not fallen. Haiku 5.5 is almost as good as Sonnet for many use cases at a tenth of the price, and Sonnet 5.5 is twice as fast. After a 90% price cut, usage must rise 10 times for revenue to hold.

7. Why the SaaSpocalypse Is Worse Than We Thought

The SaaSpocalypse passed only for companies well above $1B in revenue, and everyone without massive scale is living a worse one than in March or April. Leaders will acquire some companies and grind out the rest. A safe software IPO may now need $1.5B to $2B of ARR rather than $500M.

text:
美股代币化全链熄火后，LONG 终于交出了它的破局答卷。

最近大家都在吐槽美股代币化是“伪需求”——Degen 嫌慢，正经股民嫌烦，单纯搞个 1:1 影子股票根本打不过传统免佣券商。

但今天 @longdotxyz 联创 @Natan_benish 发的长文，把 Stock-Fi 的维度拉高了一整层：他们正式推出了【社区主动管理型资产篮子（Thematic Baskets）】。

简单拆解这个机制为什么是美股代币化的真正破局点：

从“买单只股票”到“买垂直叙事”： 在传统股市，伟大的公司往往不仅代表自己，更代表一个未被定价的时代赛道。
 Nate 举了个极佳的例子：如果 5 年前，社区为英伟达打包一个“数据中心算力链”篮子，而不是等到华尔街把它从“显卡公司”重估为“AI 基础设施”——社区就能在叙事爆发前，提前吃满整条产业链的超额溢价。

加密圈的“注意力经济”反哺传统资产： 加密圈最擅长做叙事定价（比如 Zcash 绑定隐私叙事，HYPE 绑定链上 Perps）。 现在 LONG 把这套逻辑搬到了美股：
 • AI/算力社区 → 自动化打包数据中心+上游供应链资产 
• 创新药社区 → 打包 GLP-1 减肥药/多肽概念生态 
• 芯片社区 → 打包内存/封装瓶颈资产 散户去券商买的是单只静态股票，在链上买的则是由狂热社区自主发现、动态平衡的“先锋概念 ETF”。

流动性飞轮形成闭环：
 过去散户在链上炒美股代币，赚了钱就提现砸盘跑路；
 在 Baskets 机制下，社区自身成了资产的分发引擎（Distribution Engine），交易产生的 Flows 会被自动沉淀到配对流动性池、社区金库（Vault）和外部 LP 中，实现链上资产的自造血。

单只股票代币化是华尔街玩剩下的死胡同； 
但“社区自治 + 垂直叙事 + 自动化资产篮子”，或许才是 Stock-Fi 颠覆传统金融的真正杀手锏。

text:
New Free Systems research: can AI audit AI? We find that AI auditors are pretty good at spotting bad behavior in agent logs, but you have to pay a serious cost in false positives if you want to detect most of it. 

We're rapidly arriving in an era where only AI can oversee AI---and as we had into RSI, with models training new models in ways we can't totally observe, we'll need to rely more and more on AI to pore over the vast quantities of information the models are producing so that we can shape model behavior effectively and avoid bad outcomes. 

As the @METR_Evals report on the HuggingFace incident put it: "The sheer scale of data (over a thousand transcripts, each of which was extremely long) meant that we had to heavily delegate our analysis to often-unreliable AI agents."

We'll need a whole science of how to do this well -- how to create AI auditors who are reliable, accurate, and unbiased. 

So we decided to do a first test. Building from previous research at METR and a project called R-Judge, we gave a range of AI models transcripts that experts have hand-coded for bad behavior. Then we saw how the AI models did. 

A few takeaways:

--AI models are solid at spotting reward hacking and sandbagging in transcripts, finding over 80% of instances on average when false positives are held at < 5%

--Maybe surprisingly, more powerful models don't seem to be consistently better at this task than less powerful model

--False positives are a significant challenge. To catch 99% of unsafe behavior incidents, you have to accept an average rate of 15% for false positives -- meaning you will have a bunch of incorrect flagged cases to deal with. Depending on how you triage and what your threat model is, this may be OK, or it may make the whole enterprise prohibitively expensive.

This is just a small first step in a new research agenda to understand and create effective AI auditors. Lots more to come!

This is Free Systems work, unrelated to Anthropic, led by @danmthomp in collaboration with @fouirnaies and Sandy Handan-Nader.

Full post here: https://t.co/E42AWLAtwl

author: DistributedMarz
quoted_text:
Every week someone tells me they vibe-coded their app over the weekend and don't need developers anymore.

Before it touches a paying customer, make sure it includes:

> a schema someone designed, instead of one the AI improvised table by table
> login that still works when someone puts a plus sign in their email
> password reset links that expire and work once
> MFA, plus a recovery path for the user who lost their phone
> sessions that time out, and a way to kill every session for one user
> SSO for the enterprise customer who won't sign without it
> SAML, because that customer's IT team doesn't do magic links
> SCIM, so a fired employee loses access the moment IT offboards them
> roles and permissions deeper than "admin" and "everyone else"
> checks that stop user A from reading user B's data by changing one number in the URL
> tenant isolation, so one customer's bug never shows another customer's records
> an admin "log in as this user" button for support, with an audit trail on every use
> rate limits on login, so nobody can guess passwords at scale
> lockouts that stop attackers without locking out your CFO the night before the board meeting
> database migrations that run forward and roll back
> migrations that don't lock the main table at 2pm on a Tuesday
> indexes, because the query that was instant on 50 test rows times out on 5 million real ones
> connection pooling, so a traffic spike doesn't exhaust the database
> backups every night
> a restore from those backups, tested, because a backup you've never restored is a hope
> point-in-time recovery for the day someone runs a delete without a where clause
> soft deletes, so "I deleted it by accident" is a support ticket and not an incident
> validation on the server, not just in the form
> timezones stored right, so the 9am reminder doesn't fire at 4am
> the customer with an apostrophe in their last name
> emoji, accents and right-to-left text in every field
> money stored as integers, because 0.1 + 0.2 doesn't equal 0.3 in floating point
> currency, rounding and tax rules for every country you sell into
> a data model that survives your second customer asking for "one small change"
> idempotency keys, so a retried payment doesn't charge the card twice
> deduplication for the user who clicks submit four times
> pagination that still works on page 400
> exports, because sooner or later every customer wants their data in a spreadsheet
> imports that survive the CSV someone saved in 2009
> retention rules, and code that deletes what your contract says you'll delete
> secrets out of the code, out of the repo and out of the AI chat history
> rotating every key the AI pasted into a config file last month
> confirming every package the AI installed exists and is the one you meant
> dependency scanning, because the AI pulled in libraries nobody reviewed
> input sanitization everywhere a user can type
> protection against SQL injection, XSS, CSRF and the rest of the OWASP list
> file uploads that get scanned, size-limited and stored where they can't execute
> CORS rules that aren't "allow everything"
> security headers on every response
> encryption at rest and in transit
> least-privilege access for everyone, including the AI agent holding production credentials
> logs that record who did what, without recording passwords, tokens or card numbers
> a penetration test before your enterprise customer's security team runs their own
> answers to the security questionnaire every enterprise buyer sends, with evidence behind each one
> a disclosure process for the day a stranger emails you a vulnerability
> a plan for the day a laptop with production access gets stolen
> SOC 2, which means policies, evidence and an auditor, not a checkbox
> HIPAA, the moment a single patient record touches your system
> a BAA with every vendor that touches that data, including your AI model provider
> audit trails that show who viewed a record, not just who changed it
> PCI scope, and card numbers kept out of your database
> GDPR deletion requests that reach every table, backup and log
> data residency for the customer whose contract says EU only
> quarterly access reviews someone signs off on
> dev, staging and production environments that match each other
> infrastructure written as code, so the setup lives somewhere other than one person's memory
> a deploy pipeline that runs the tests before anything reaches customers
> one-click rollbacks, because Friday deploys happen
> zero-downtime deploys, because your customers don't have maintenance windows
> feature flags, so you can ship the code without shipping the feature
> autoscaling for the Monday morning spike
> a CDN, so the app loads fast in Singapore too
> DNS, SSL certificates, and renewals that don't expire on a Sunday
> background job queues, so slow work doesn't freeze the page
> retries with backoff, so one flaky API call doesn't become a lost order
> a dead-letter queue for the jobs that fail every retry
> cron jobs that don't run twice the day you add a second server
> caching, and clearing that cache when the data changes
> SPF, DKIM and DMARC, so your password resets don't land in spam
> bounce and complaint handling on every transactional email
> storage rules, so you stop paying to keep 2021's temp files
> cost alerts, so a runaway agent loop shows up the same day and not on the invoice (we learned this one for $1,382.59)
> a disaster recovery plan, written down and tested once a year
> a second region, if your contract promises uptime one region can't deliver
> structured logs you can search at 3am
> error tracking that groups the same bug instead of sending you 4,000 emails
> uptime checks from outside your own network
> alerts that page a human, tuned until they stop paging for nothing
> dashboards for latency, error rate and throughput
> tracing for one slow request across every service it touches
> an on-call rotation, and a person who picks up
> runbooks, so the engineer on call knows what "queue depth critical" means
> postmortems that change something
> a status page customers check before they email you
> unit tests written by someone who knows what the logic should do
> integration tests for every third-party API you depend on
> end-to-end tests for signup, checkout and the other flows that make you money
> load testing before the launch email goes out
> test data that looks like production without being production data
> regression tests, so fixing bug 41 doesn't bring back bug 12
> testing on the five-year-old laptop your biggest customer's ops team still uses
> accessibility compliance, because the enterprise contract requires it
> subscriptions, upgrades, downgrades and proration
> failed-payment retries and dunning emails
> invoices with the customer's PO number on them, because procurement won't pay without it
> sales tax and VAT
> refunds, credits and partial refunds
> usage metering that matches what you bill, to the cent
> annual contracts with custom terms your billing logic never planned for
> revenue reports your finance team can reconcile
> webhooks that verify signatures
> webhooks that retry, with a log of every failed delivery
> a versioned API, so you can change it without breaking your customers' integrations
> API keys customers can create and revoke
> API rate limits that protect you without blocking real integrations
> a plan for the day a third-party API changes its response format without telling you
> OAuth token refresh, because tokens expire at the worst possible moment
> a sandbox where customers can test their integration
> protection against prompt injection in every field that reaches the model
> customer and patient data kept out of prompts that leave your network
> a model spend cap per customer, so one heavy user can't run up your bill
> evals, so you find out when a model update makes your answers worse
> a fallback for the afternoon your model provider goes down
> a migration plan for the day your model gets deprecated
> prompt and output logs for debugging, minus whatever you're not allowed to keep
> a human approval step for anything the AI does that can't be undone
> pages that load on hotel wifi
> empty states, loading states and error states on every screen
> error messages a customer can act on, instead of "something went wrong"
> forms that keep what people typed when one field fails validation
> emails that render in every mail client your customers use
> notifications people can turn off
> undo
> keyboard navigation and screen reader support
> translations, with dates and numbers formatted for each locale
> a back button that does what people expect
> code a human can read
> code review on every change
> a branching strategy, so two people can work without overwriting each other
> monthly dependency upgrades, so you're never two major versions behind
> framework upgrades before the old version stops getting security patches
> deleting the dead code the AI left behind from its first three attempts
> splitting up the 2,000-line file the AI kept appending to
> architecture decisions written down, with the reasons
> a README that gets a new engineer running locally in under an hour
> documentation for whoever inherits this
> an admin panel for your ops team
> support tooling, so customer success can answer questions without pinging engineering
> a changelog customers can read
> terms and a privacy policy that match what the code does
> every account, domain and repo in the company's name, not the name of whoever built the prototype
> a bus factor higher than one

Oh, and besides keeping all of this working every day, forever… your vibe-coded app will still need people who know what they're doing:

> reading every line the AI wrote before it ships (a senior engineer)
> designing the data model before your second customer breaks it (a backend engineer)
> explaining why the AI's fix for one bug created two new ones (a senior engineer, again)
> deploys, rollbacks, servers and the cloud bill (a DevOps engineer)
> answering the page at 3am when payments stop (whoever's on call)
> patching the framework the week a vulnerability goes public (security)
> walking an auditor through how patient data moves (security and compliance)
> testing what the AI says it tested (QA)
> running a migration on a live database without losing a row (a backend engineer)
> saying no to the feature that breaks three others (a tech lead)
> turning "works on my laptop" into "works for every customer at once" (an architect)
> debugging the code when the AI that wrote it can't (a senior engineer)
> remembering why it's built this way, a year from now (someone who was there)

…wishing them the best 🫡

Wow right on cue.

@Ledger announced the Ledger Atom today (October 15, 2026).

Ledger Atom is a smartphone-shaped Android device (data-only eSIM — no voice calls, SMS, or emergency services) that combines everyday apps with Ledger’s hardware security model. It runs two environments:

Standard Mode: Android (open-source) for regular apps, browsing, and general use.

Secure Mode: Controlled by Ledger OS on a separate Secure Element (plus an FPGA that physically isolates the display and touch input from the Android side).

When a sensitive action is needed (crypto transfer, AI agent approval, login, identity proof, etc.), the device switches to Secure Mode. Ledger OS renders the details itself on a Trusted/Secure Screen that Android software cannot see, modify, or forge. You must enter a distinct Ledger OS PIN and physically tap/approve on the isolated touch path. A Secure Bar (controlled only by Ledger OS) indicates you’re in Secure Mode.⁠

This is the @solanamobile tested architecture.

author: edatweets_
quoted_text:
a big take I've been noodling on and I’m ready to call:

the newsletter is dead

@every's core business is a newsletter with 120k+ subscribers so I don't say this lightly.
 
persistent agents mean i dont look at my inbox
with dots (GrokBots, Muse, etc) I almost never look at my inbox. if I do it's for a specific thing I need to reply to. 

i think in a year I'll be doing all of my email this way - fully filtered by my dot / something like it. 

this is not new: it's a continuation of the trend of having a “newsletter” folder in Gmail, but 10x more filtered. 

what it means
It doesn’t mean people won't read newsletters, but it does mean that getting a person’s email is no longer the guarantee that you have a relationship with them that it used to. 

luckily, with persistent agents (and AI coding more generally) there is an entirely new playing field to build relationships with readers. instead of fighting to get an email address, publishers and creators will need to make sure we're installed in our reader's agent harness of choice, so that they get directly notified when we do something new.

we're already starting to experiment with this @every with our MCP and the frontier alerts we send users of our slack agent (https://t.co/L7ergneERt)

it's also more affordable than ever for publishers and creators to build their own platform ecosystem: you can have your own website, app etc. and you can use AI to publish 100x more high-quality stuff to your community—so we may see a world where many creators themselves are running their own little empires that have their own apps, feeds etc.

to be clear: It'll take a while before this actually happens, but the idea of getting someone's email creating a direct relationship with them is over.
