Comparing results for buyback vs. ve-tokenomics.

A small case study comparing two baskets consisting 4 biggest buyback tokens and 3 biggest ve-tokens.

Takeaways:
1. The peformance gap "buyback vs. ve" is much smaller that it was stated in the original post: $67 vs $300 -> $81 vs. $139
2. The highest valuation multiples are concentrated in major assets like $HYPE and $UNI. This suggests that market attention and valuation premiums remain heavily concentrated in the largest projects.

Ongoing observations:

1. Buybacks outperformed on price returns. 
$100 invested in each of the four buyback tokens one year ago would be worth $130 on average today (equal-weighted across the group).

2. ve-tokenomics underperformed. The same $100 investment across each of the three ve-tokens would be worth just $72 on average.

3. But price performance doesn't tell the whole story. Both groups generate economic value for token holders beyond price appreciation. 

4. To account for this:
- Buybacks: we account the reduction in total supply as a kind of an income, since each remaining token represents a larger share of the supply.
- ve-tokenomics: we account for revenue claimable by token holders.

5. $HYPE was the strongest price performer. Excluding $HYPE, the buyback group's average ending value drops from $130 to $115.

6. Accounting for accumulated revenue in the position:
Buybacks: $130 → $139
ve-tokenomics: $72 → $81

7. $HYPE and $UNI have relatively small supply reductions: just 1.6% and 1.3%, respectively. We calculate these figures against maximum supply (the FDV basis), since buybacks increase the proportional ownership of all remaining tokens.

8. $PUMP and $CAKE burned significantly larger portions of their supply, making their buyback-driven value accrual more substantial.

9. $PUMP and $CAKE trade at roughly the same P/FCFt multiples as $CRV and $PENDLE, around 17x, despite their fundamentally different value accrual mechanisms.

10. $AERO stands out with a P/FCFt below 10x, making it one of the cheapest assets in this comparison on a token-holder revenue basis.

All the results are presented at the infographic

Source: Valueverse API

quoted_text:
More details on @metricxyz from docs:

What is it: A DEX for active pools, with custom pricing and liquidity that proactively change with new information. Imagine Uniswap LPs, with some curation, priced according to a ref price outside the AMM pool.

How it works and differs from passive AMM LPs: Active pools split pricing and liquidity into two parts. The Price Provider sets prices: a bid, an ask and a reference price, from oracles, onchain data or custom rules. The pool holds the liquidity in percentage ranges around the provider's quote and executes trades. Unlike most AMMs, the pool isn't its own price oracle: trades move price only relative to the reference. When the reference moves, the ranges move with it.

Role of curators: Curators choose the Price Provider and the pool's settings. LPs choose which ranges to fund.

How to provide/manage liquidity: Your liquidity sits in bins: price ranges relative to the pool's reference price. When the reference moves, your ranges move with it, so there is no range to manage and no rebalancing script.

LPs earn a share of the spread traders pay when trades use bins' liquidity, after the curator's and Metric's fees. Earnings compound into the LP position, with nothing to claim. Unused liquidity earns nothing, even if other bins in the same pool are active. (see example below)

I found a bad failure in the AI auditor benchmark I am building: a tool could describe the correct vulnerability and still lose points because it did not phrase the finding like the official report.

Fixing it forced me to decide what this benchmark should actually measure.

The matcher now checks the root-cause terms and contract or function identifiers, while severity is only supporting evidence. Uncertain matches are shown for review, but they do not improve precision or recall.

Then I had to fix a second problem. Existing results had already been scored by the old logic, so users can now submit the same tool again and replace the previous score instead of creating a duplicate leaderboard entry.

We are open-sourcing Decision LCR (Snap 74%, Jev 58%), which mimics real-world tasks and is adapted from AA-LCR.

Because long-context benchmarks for decision models don't really exist, we built one of our own by adapting Artificial Analysis' Long-Context Reasoning benchmark, which we think does a better job mimicking real-world tasks than many LLM long-context benchmarks, to a decision format. We are open-sourcing this today.

Decision LCR: https://t.co/JGGSEBBczF

Adapted from Artificial Analysis's AA-LCR. 100 human-written questions over real 72K–115K-token document sets, converted into 118 decisions, each run with three option orderings to control for position bias. Chance is 19.2, and models score 24–25 with the documents removed.

We'd love for others to run it, use it and improve it. If you work on long-context evaluation or decision models, we'd value your feedback and collaboration.

To learn more about SNAP and our evaluation process, check out the blog:  https://t.co/CglHueOxnv

interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. text:
I am a senior official of the Russian Federation. 

I negotiate.

Which ministry I belong to is not your concern, and in any case would mislead you, because the ministry with its name on the building is rarely the one where the thing is decided. We have many doors. The diplomats have the handsome lobby and the brass plaque and the press briefings; the work happens down a corridor they do not photograph, in an office whose budget line does not quite add up. You are thinking of the Foreign Ministry. Keep thinking of it. It is a wonderful decoy. We built it to be looked at.

I want to explain how we won a war this month without firing the shot that mattered, because the method was beautiful, and you paid for it, and a craftsman likes to be understood before he dies.

First, unlearn what they taught you. In your country two parties sit, each concedes a little, they meet in the middle, they shake hands, somebody writes a book about active listening. Charming. We do not believe in the middle. We have a proverb, old, from the village: tsar far, God high. Help is not coming. No one is in the middle to meet you there; there is only the steppe, and the winter, and whoever is still standing when it ends. A negotiation is not a search for agreement. It is a contest of endurance, and endurance is the one thing Russia has never had to import. We have buried more sons than you have living citizens, and, I tell you with my hand flat on the table, we are prepared to bury the next rank behind them. Time is not a neutral referee. Time has a nationality. Vremya rabotayet na nas. Time works for us. It always has. Ask Napoleon. Ask the other one. We did not defeat them. The calendar did, and we simply declined to freeze.

So. Your President wanted a deal. He wanted it the way a child wants the toy in the window: loudly, now, and with witnesses. This is the single most valuable thing a man can hand you across a table, the knowledge that he needs the deal more than the deal needs to exist. We did not have to be clever. Cleverness is for people in a hurry. We had only to be patient, and to let his hunger do the labor. A man who must have his peace by a certain Tuesday will, by Monday, call a surrender “peace,” and thank you, and ask you to smile for the photographers.

What did we actually need? I will be honest, because honesty is free now that the ink is dry. Our refineries were burning. Those clever little Ukrainian drones, toys, cardboard and a lawnmower engine and a boy with a laptop, had knocked our diesel output down by nearly a third. We had been forced to halt our own exports. For the first time in this long war we were bleeding from the only wound that frightens us, not the one that spills sons, we have an ocean of those, but the one that spills money. We had the fuel and could not sell it, because the civilized world had shaken hands and agreed not to buy.

And so what did the President of the United States give us, at this precise moment, as our great gift?

Permission to sell it.

Sit inside that sentence. I had to. I sat inside it at the table and performed the hardest work of my career, which was keeping my face a wall while my soul did the prisyadka, the Cossack kick-dance, the one where the man drops low and throws his boots out and howls. Our problem was that we could not sell our oil. And the solution, gift-wrapped, tied with ribbon, announced on his little telephone application with the stern instruction Do not break it!, was a license from his own Treasury, signed by his own man, valid, and here I permit myself to savor it the way one savors the first spoon of hot solyanka after a day in the cold, until April of next year, permitting the entire planet to buy the precise diesel we were choking to move. He did not take a thing from us and hand it to Ukraine. He reached into Ukraine’s hand, took out the one card that was winning, the fire, the pressure, the drones over the refineries, and he laid it gently in ours. We were going under. Your President threw us our own anchor, called it a lifeline, and the cameras applauded his throwing arm.

They tell me he is a tough man. A hard bargainer. I have sat across from hard men; a hard man does not open by wishing you mnogaya leta, many happy years. There was a call, you understand, on the ninth, the birthday of our President, and your President sang him the warm wishes, and passed along the fond regards of his wife, and the two of them talked for an hour and a half, two old friends, and when it was finished our spokesman told your press, with a composure I confess I could not have held, that neither man had wanted to be the first to hang up the telephone, so they hung up at the same instant, together, in harmony. Two nuclear powers, and the final sticking point, the one irreconcilable difference, was which of them would be so rude as to end the call. I have done this work a long time. I have never watched a nation bargain so ferociously for the privilege of being liked by the people it is being robbed by. There is a word for a man like that where I come from. We call him rubakha-paren, the shirt-off-his-back fellow, the big warm open soul who gives everything away at the table and wakes with no shirt and calls it a wonderful party. We toast such men. We do not fear them.

Now the part your newspapers chew but cannot swallow, so I will swallow it for them, as a courtesy between professionals.

We gave up nothing. I must be exact, because precision is the whole art, the difference between a surgeon and a butcher. Not “a little.” Not “a small concession for the optics, a bone for the cameras.” Nichego. Nothing. We did not commit to resume the talks; our man allowed only that we would “think about when.” We did not agree to any ceasefire; and when your President announced one regardless, declared from his telephone that an energy ceasefire now existed and that both parties had agreed to it, we kept striking their power stations that very night, in the dark, as the cold came on, because a ceasefire you announce on my behalf is not a ceasefire. It is a press release. And I am not bound by your press releases. Your President was asked, directly, how he could announce a peace that both armies flatly denied, and he answered, and I have had this translated three separate times because twice I assumed an error, “They agreed because I said they agreed.”This is not statecraft. This is a man who names his dog Poslushnyy, “Obedient,” and then points to the collar as proof the animal obeys.

And the following day our foreign minister, a man I admire the way one admires deep winter, something that does not negotiate and cannot be charmed and simply outlasts you, was asked whether Russia would honor this sacred respite. He said the Ukrainian president “has not earned a respite.” The day after the ceasefire was proclaimed. We did not sustain the fiction for even one full news cycle. We did not have to. That is the gift the appeaser makes you: he needs the arrangement so desperately that he will keep its corpse warm himself, bent over it, breathing into its blue lips, long after the other party has put on its coat and walked out into the snow. We broke the thing in public and he defended it in public. We were not even his partners in the lie, you understand. We were its subject. He was its author, its narrator, its only audience, and its most devoted admirer. He lied about us, for us, to his own people, and asked nothing of us in return but that we not embarrass him too quickly. We obliged for eighteen hours. Generous, I thought.

And here is the part I admire most, the part we could never have built ourselves, because you built it for us, years ago, without being asked, and then handed us the key while smiling for a photograph. Consider how your ally fights. He cannot see in the dark without a constellation of satellites owned not by his government, not even by yours, but by a single one of your private citizens, a man with his own moods, his own businesses, his own weather. That little network is his eyes, his voice, the nerve that runs from the soldier in the trench to the officer behind him; it is how his cities learn a missile is coming, how his drones find my refineries in the black. And the switch for it does not sit in Kyiv. It does not sit, truly, even in Washington. It sits on a desk belonging to a man who may be persuaded, or flattered, or simply left in a bad mood on the wrong morning.

We did not have to buy that switch. This is what I want your grandchildren to understand about the century they are inheriting. We would once have had to invade a nation, occupy it, garrison it, bleed for every kilometer of its nervous system. You spared us the trouble. You privatized the nervous system and sold the subscription. And so we had only to wait for the day your side decided the ally had become difficult, that he was “misreading the room,” that he was burning our refineries after being asked so courteously to stop, and to let the quiet thought travel down the wire: perhaps the eyes grow unreliable for a while. Perhaps the little blue dot that tells him where we are begins to wander. Perhaps the warning that a rocket is inbound arrives, regrettably, a few seconds late, and a power plant and the apartment block beside it discover this at the same moment the residents do. We never touched the switch. We did not need to. We needed only for your side to remember that the switch exists, and for the ally to remember it too, and to feel, in the cold, how very much of his survival runs through hands that are not his own and not even ours but simply for sale. You gave one private man a dial on another country’s breathing. We would have had to win a war to seize a thing like that. You incorporated it, and listed it, and let us lease the fear for nothing.

You will want the figure. Americans always want the figure; it is one of the more endearing things about you, this faith that the number is the truth. The diesel we so graciously consented to sell you, the great prize, the triumph, the headline across your screens, four point eight million tons: it is less than two weeks of your nation’s thirst. One of your own analysts called October’s portion roughly half of what you burn in a single day. Kaplya v more, he might as well have said, a drop in the sea. And your own bank reckoned the whole magnificent transaction might lower the price at your pump by a dollar, perhaps two, per barrel, which is to say by an amount no human hand will ever feel, because the thing actually driving your fuel prices is a different war entirely, the one you are now fighting with Iran, and no license signed by Mr. Smith at your Treasury can switch that off. So weigh the trade with a clear eye and a cold heart, the way we weigh it in Moscow. We received: the removal of the single pressure that was killing us, six months to refill the war chest, the American President’s own voice telling Kyiv to stop burning our refineries, and the standing reminder that your ally’s eyes can be dimmed on a private man’s whim. You received: a rounding error, delivered precisely in time for your November elections. We sold you two weeks of diesel. You sold us the war. It is the most profitable arrangement of my career, and the exquisite part, the part I will tell my grandchildren by the fire, is that I did not even propose it. I prepared my arguments. I sharpened them for weeks. I never used one. I simply sat, and kept my wall of a face, and failed to object, and your side negotiated against itself until there was nothing left on the table but our winnings.

There is a thing on my desk. A copy of a document from 1994. Look it up; your grandchildren will have no choice. In it, three nations put their names to a single promise: Russia, Britain, and the United States. Ukraine in those days held the third-largest nuclear arsenal on the earth, some nineteen hundred warheads, enough to turn any conversation, including this one, into glass. And we asked them, all three of us, together, arm in arm, to give it up. Hand over the warheads. Let us melt them. Trust the paper instead of the fire. And in exchange we three solemnly pledged, I am quoting the document, to respect their borders, and to “refrain from economic coercion designed to subordinate” their sovereignty to our interests. Two of the three signatures on that page belong to Moscow and to Washington. The same two capitals that spent this month deciding, over a golf resort in Florida, who keeps which of their provinces, and at what price per ton.

Thirty-two years. Moscow took the land. Washington licensed Moscow’s fuel and leaned on Kyiv to lower its hands. And in a drawer somewhere in Kyiv lies a sheet of paper, signed by the very governments now splitting the proceeds, swearing that none of this was ever permitted to happen. They gave up the warheads because they believed, these sweet trusting people, that a world ordered by agreements was safer than a world ordered by fire. We have spent this autumn teaching them, patiently, thoroughly, in the dark, with the heat off, the true price of that belief. It is the most expensive education we have ever provided, and your President arranged the tuition, gift-wrapped, ribbon and all, with warm regards to the family.

People ask whether Russia can be trusted to keep its word. It is the wrong question, and only the losing side ever asks it, usually afterward, in the cold, going through the drawer. The correct question, the one your President never thought to ask, is why a man would sign a fresh agreement with a government that has already shown him, in black ink, in a drawer, exactly and precisely what its signature is worth. We told you in 1994. We did not even hide it. You simply preferred not to read your own handwriting.

Forgive me. There is another call on the schedule. I am told we may be invited to sell you a little more of our oil, as a gesture of peace, a token of the warm friendship between our peoples.

Poживём — увидим, we say.

We will live, and we will see.

text:
基金爆仓！？ leopard 态势感知重演！？

这两天AI股跌成这样，先别急着给Michael Burry颁奖。市场正在传，AI基金VARA可能出了问题，正在被迫卖股票。如果属实，部分个股的跌幅里，就可能夹着一笔根本不愿意等价格的卖单。

看看流传的历史持仓：Nebius、CoreWeave、Lumentum、Vertiv、Coherent、美光、AMD……从算力租赁、光通信，到散热、电力和存储，一整条AI产业链。这样的组合一旦需要快速变现，砸下来的就会是一篮子股票，看盘的人却容易理解成整个行业同时出事了。

这让我想到Leopold Aschenbrenner此前那轮被迫减仓。重仓同一条主线，再叠加杠杆，股价下跌触发追加保证金，补不上就卖；卖出继续压低价格，又逼其他人减仓。到了这个阶段，基金经理再看好三年后的AI需求，也得先处理今天账户里的资金缺口。

所以我会把这份持仓名单放进接下来的观察范围。如果其中一些公司订单、盈利预期没明显变化，却被集中抛售拖下去，等强制卖压缓解，就可能出现幅度很大的反弹。尤其值得看谁先止跌、谁在板块继续下挫时开始跌不动，而非只看谁已经跌得最多。

VARA爆仓目前仍是传闻，也解释不了这两天所有的下跌。但这条线索值得跟：如果卖方是在筹现金，股票可能被卖到低于他自己认可的价格。接下来要找的机会，就是那些公司还在正常做生意，持有它的基金却已经等不起了的股票。

text:
wow, amazing technical blog post about microsoft's new 3T pre-training with very rare and clear insights on how to train models of this size

first let's get an overview of the shape of this model, it's a sparser model than Kimi K3 (80B active vs 104B), same sliding window hybrid pattern, with this time more kv heads for the sliding window layers (a bit different from stepfun and poolside that add query head). they added a shared expert and also removed the interleaved MoE/Dense pattern of MAI 1

the scaling ladder is very similar to MAI 1 with the same mechanism, each rung depends only on the number of layers. they mention that one of the key improvements is how they handle the smaller rung data distribution where they make sure to have the same repetition as the final corpus. they already did that for MAI-1 but only for data ablation iirc

their prediction is almost identical to the final run loss, very impressive

they compare the model with different base models such as deepseek v4 pro and MAI 1, tho in the case of deepseek v4 pro i'd say it's quite hard to distinguish how much the data mixture "overfitting" to the scaling ladder has an impact here (they mention it's both), need to always be a bit careful about EG metrics for data in general

they have VERY NICE scaling laws for weight decay and learning rate, for the learning rate they express it as a function of tokens per parameter (N/D) and steps (hence depending on the batch size). they also do the same for dropout where it's a function of active params only, they also find the usual sqrt(k) scaling for learning rate and batch size (other scaling laws often also converge to that)

a bunch of other stability stuff, they use Muon this time and activation gradient clipping, the efficiency gain here is actually pretty crazy at larger scale. they also increase the training horizon to ~40T text (20T unique) + a new 10T (4.5T unique) multimodal  since the model is natively multimodal

imo this is a safe but very clean scaling! very exciting for the tech report and MAI-base-3, congrats!!

text:
刚看到前 Kimi RL infra，现 @Evolvent_AI co-founder @FanqingMengAI 搞的 RSIGym，一个 RSI 环境。RSI 并不是一个模型问题，而是一个系统工程。从这个角度出发，一个关键问题是：给 RSI agent 提供的环境，是否对 agent 友好，也贴近真实生产中的研发流程。

为啥不让 agent 自己搭环境呢？因为它自己搭环境又费时间，又一定会踩坑。比如我自己让 agent 搭模型训练的环境，经常在 CUDA / torch 上浪费很多时间，也很难在多个任务间协调好 GPU 卡。让 agent 自己搭芯片仿真和物理设计的环境，经常无法管理好内存和磁盘资源，导致内存或者磁盘满了，连 SSH 都进不去了。

模型训练的 infra 已经很成熟，没必要让每个 agent 都重新搭一遍。RSIGym 把这些能力部署成远程服务，通过 API 和 skill 文档提供给 agent。这样方便并行开展实验，研究工作区与计算服务的隔离也有助于减少 hacking 的机会。

RSIGym 的这个设计称为 Everything as a Service，包含训练、推理、蒸馏、评估、沙盒五类服务。

RSIGym 还提出了 RSI-Index，综合多个 agentic benchmark，衡量前沿 agent 联合改进一个较小模型（Qwen3.5 35B A3B）的 weights 和 harness 的能力。六个前沿模型组成的研究 agent 在五个 benchmark 上都取得了显著提升。Opus 5 的 RSI-Index 最高，达到 0.4809，也就是平均弥补了 48.09% 的剩余可提升空间。

有趣的是这些 agent 不仅迭代模型权重，还会自动迭代 harness，解决共性问题，例如 terminal bench 中的 shell 状态保持、长输出的截断与恢复、工具调用死循环检测等。去年我们都是一个一个 bad case 修的，今天 agent 自己就能解决了。

RSIGym 也支持一些有意思的实验，比如单独迭代已有的 DSH harness、让模型自己训练自己，以及断开公网后的研究实验。欢迎大家用它试试自己的想法！
author: bojie_li
quoted_text:
💡Our view: RSI is a systems engineering problem, not just a model problem.

Progress depends on the environment a research agent works in: what resources it can call, what it can change, and how it runs experiments. That environment should reflect real production workflows and be easy for agents to use.

At @Evolvent_AI, we built RSIGym around Everything as a Service. Agents can call established research services and iterate on data, training settings, and harness code.

We also introduce RSI-Index to measure how well frontier agents jointly improve a target model’s weights and harness. Across 6 research agents and 5 benchmarks, Opus 5 leads at 0.4809. 🧵

We’re releasing the code, experiment configurations, research trajectories, and evaluation logs. Try your own improvement methods with RSIGym.

text: More from Nick:
author: AndrewCurran_
quoted_text:
hi liv! i think a lot of this is that i don’t think working with “features” is quite right anymore. in addition to the standard critique that no one can really define, count, or measure them, i found the frame too flexible: it adapted to whatever the circuit was actually doing, which made it unproductive

for instance, is 4e:55 multiple features (car, cat) in one feature (a V)? or multiple features in a monosemantic neuron? but then what does monosemantic mean, if not one feature? multimodal neurons says that if it has a shared pattern, then it is monosemantic, but then i'm unsure if the model has a general "cat feature" that this is part of. the more i tried to understand whole networks this way, the faster it broke down

i found myself in situations where i feel like i understood the network pretty well, what was happening was generally simple in a given region, and most of the struggle was trying to convert it to a hypothetical feature ontology with no way to measure it. all the confusion was going into the wrong place, i just wanted to see how the mechanisms were moving data, which kept forming reliable motifs with clear explanations with  predictions that held

what actually matters to me is the motif in the car->dogs circuit i found with chris. i don’t think it’s doing what i thought! it’s ordinary generalization and composition, no bad news in it. it could have done something else, since the high dimensional space allows it, and it would still be described as “features placed in a set of neurons,” but that version would be really bad news. so the feature frame blurs together things with very different levels of good-news-ness

i briefly dropped "superposition" altogether and defined everything myself from scratch just to avoid zero conflict with any other use of that word. but most people i talked to already used superposition for that, and found it strange and isolationist to redefine everything myself just to avoid definitions conflict that's easily addressable by just being really clear about precisely what i'm referring to

so i tried to just be really clear from the start about what i mean, what actual circuit formation i'm referring to, and then readers basically understood? i dont think anyone i had read it came away thinking i was saying there are not "more human definable features than neurons" or anything like that (and i dont think the non-human features as fundamental units of neural networks is right). and importantly, they actually thought the circuits were doing something different -- doing the bad thing -- so it wasn't just a definitions thing. but maybe i could have been more clear

text:
“We delete your data later” is a retention policy.

“Your raw data never enters our custody” is an architecture decision.

Those are not the same control.

In a traditional vendor workflow, raw data may move into vendor-controlled storage before processing, review, delivery, and eventual deletion.

A client-controlled workflow can change the path:

SOURCE DATA
↓
CLIENT-CONTROLLED STORAGE
↓
APPROVED PROCESSING / REVIEW
↓
OUTPUT BACK TO CLIENT

The vendor may still provide the platform, workflow, QA, or workforce — without needing to become the long-term custodian of the raw dataset.

Why does that matter?

Because every additional copy creates another question:
• Who can access it?
• Where is it stored?
• How long does it remain?
• How is deletion verified?
• What happens when access changes?

Retention controls still matter.

But reducing unnecessary custody can remove risk before a deletion policy ever has to manage it.

For sensitive AI data programs, architecture should be part of the governance conversation from day one.

AIxBlock supports self-hosted and client-controlled data workflows where storage, access, processing, and delivery requirements are defined around the project.
#DataGovernance #DataSecurity #EnterpriseAI #AIData #Privacy

text:
wow, amazing technical blog post about microsoft's new 3T pre-training with very rare and clear insights on how to train models of this size

first let's get an overview of the shape of this model, it's a sparser model than Kimi K3 (80B active vs 104B), same sliding window hybrid pattern, with this time more kv heads for the sliding window layers (a bit different from stepfun and poolside that add query head). they added a shared expert and also removed the interleaved MoE/Dense pattern of MAI 1

the scaling ladder is very similar to MAI 1 with the same mechanism, each rung depends only on the number of layers. they mention that one of the key improvements is how they handle the smaller rung data distribution where they make sure to have the same repetition as the final corpus. they already did that for MAI-1 but only for data ablation iirc

their prediction is almost identical to the final run loss, very impressive

they compare the model with different base models such as deepseek v4 pro and MAI 1, tho in the case of deepseek v4 pro i'd say it's quite hard to distinguish how much the data mixture "overfitting" to the scaling ladder has an impact here (they mention it's both), need to always be a bit careful about EG metrics for data in general

they have VERY NICE scaling laws for weight decay and learning rate, for the learning rate they express it as a function of tokens per parameter (N/D) and steps (hence depending on the batch size). they also do the same for dropout where it's a function of active params only, they also find the usual sqrt(k) scaling for learning rate and batch size (other scaling laws often also converge to that)

a bunch of other stability stuff, they use Muon this time and activation gradient clipping, the efficiency gain here is actually pretty crazy at larger scale. they also increase the training horizon to ~40T text (20T unique) + a new 10T (4.5T unique) multimodal  since the model is natively multimodal

imo this is a safe but very clean scaling! very exciting for the tech report and MAI-base-3, congrats!!

How your AI agent can pay with your credit card, without ever holding it:

1. Your card stays stored in a trusted wallet.

2. When your agent goes to buy something, the wallet creates an agentic token: a stand-in card number that only works at that store, with limits like "don't spend more than $100."

3. Your agent hands the token to the store.

4. The store runs it through its usual payment processor, and the charge lands on your real card, with your rewards and card benefits intact.

"AOL was a helpful set of training wheels for getting everyone online, but the open web ultimately won. We think the same thing will happen with agents as well."

text:
OpenAI 官方博客披露了核心团队用 GPT-6 系列维护代码库的一手工程实践。直接公布了几个实际运行的提示词，
靠这些提示词在两周内合并了 1400 多个清理 PR，删除超过 800k 行代码，并将一个服务的容器镜像压缩48%。

第一个提示词用于清理死代码

  “请帮我找出并清理仓库里的无用代码。你可以随意查看
  Slack、Statsig（功能开关平台）或任何需要的来源，用来确认这些代码确实不再被使用、可以被清理或简化。”
  这个提示词的关键在于允许 GPT-6 Astra 自主去翻阅 Slack 讨论、Statsig 实验配置甚至生产环境的性能 profiling数据，只有在确认生产环境零调用后才在 PR 中列出删除依据。

第二个提示词用于清理更棘手的废弃实验与功能开关

  “/goal 找出整个仓库中所有陈旧、常量化、已废弃或全量上线的 Statsig开关、配置和实验，在不改变生产行为的前提下安全移除。审计所有项目资产，不限于标记为陈旧的对象。通过枚举、常量、包装函数、别名和动态拼
  接名称寻找间接引用。核对生产引用的常量，不只给保守清单。结合生产遥测与性能分析评估 CPU 开销，找出昂贵的无用判断。生成 Markdown报告，按归属和文件工作流分组以便并行处理，附带生产取值、证据与 CPU 开销。不要修改线上配置或服务。”

第三组提示词用于 CI 优化与规则自省
  
“关于减轻本仓库的 CI 负载你有什么想法？请将想法列成表格，并根据该仓库的历史运行记录，按每天预估节省的 CI 分钟数进行排序。”
  
面对不稳定测试修复，他们运行：
  
“/goal 查看所有最近的 CI 运行记录，找出偶发失败的测试并尝试修复，成功则提交PR。你的任务是针对简单问题找到明确修复方案，而不是穷尽修复所有问题。”
 
 针对 agent 上下文规则的自检提示词更精妙：
 
 “翻阅我最近的 Codex 会话记录，找出一条误导了 agent 或导致无效工作的 AGENTS.md指令。选出该会话提示词，在相同仓库快照和模型下重放两次：一次保持原指令不变，一次仅移除或修正该指令。对比任务质量、agent
  行为、工具调用、token 消耗与成本，展示该指令并说明修改是否有效。”

强烈建议好好学习和利用这些应用于超大工程实践的提示词

text:
More SF observations:

1. Seeing the word "inference" on billboards in SF still blows my mind. 99.9% of america has no idea what inference is and I wonder how many know what an agent is. Will Muse, Instinct, Dots etc will change that over the next 12 months?

2. You know who doesn't get enough credit? Manus. In March 2025 they shipped the blueprint for AI agents: every task gets its own computer in the cloud, you can watch it work, it writes a todo list and checks it off, and you walk away while it finishes. So much of what we use today runs on those ideas!

3. Your product now has to sell itself twice. First the agent has to pick it, then the human has to trust that pick enough to say yes.

4. I was talking to a guy who told me we should just destroy all the data centers. I think that sentiment is more common than people in SF realize. You can already see some of the big AI companies adjusting positioning their AI as something that helps people and gives them more time/cures for cancers etc.

5. AI is making people work 5x faster (at least), so for freelancers/agencies that charge per hour you're earning 5x less per unit of work. But your rate is the same? I think a lot of freelancers and agencies are about to have to rethink how they price.

6. Running a company now feels kinda dystopian sometimes, especially with a small team of a few humans and a lot of agents. Some days the Slack channel is mostly bots reporting to each other, and you're the only one in the room with a pulse.

7. Every product company is turning into a product studio. I see it firsthand as a co-founder of @meetLCA , which is basically a Labs as a Service company incubating new products for companies. (DM me if you want to work together in 2027).

8. Personal software is exploding. People at every company are building their own little tools for their own jobs. It's amazing for productivity and a nightmare for IT, because nobody knows what's running or who owns it.

9. Revenue per human is the new flex. Founders used to brag about headcount. Now they brag about how much they're doing with how few people.

11. More founders are using agents for customer research. Agents run the interviews, read every support ticket and summarize what people are begging for. Synthetic market research is the new thing.

12. Shipping technology that actually takes 3-6 months with unique partnerships that are hard to replicate. So, partnerships are sooo back!

13. Insane amount of young people (22 or younger) making absurds amounts of money. At least it feels that way.  Never seen anything like that, even during mobile era.

14. Only 2% of the US is paying for AI products, but it feels like 110% SF is.

15. Advice for college grads used to be “follow your passion” and now it’s follow careers that are not  document- driven, rules-bound and verifiable

16. Seeing the word inference on billboards in SF still blows my mind.

17. Agents paying for things feels futuristic. I think its coming, only a matter of time, but  I’m wondering when it becomes mainstream. 2027?

18. Lots of talk about proactive agents being the next phase of personal agents. Right now you ask your agent to do something. In 2027, it’s all going to be about noticing things (context/memory) and acting first. "Your flight got delayed, I already rebooked you."

19. The quote "what the smartest people do on the weekend is what everyone else will do during the week in 10 years." by Chris Dixon. It feels like that length of time isnt 10 years anymore, its 12 months.

20. This is the most asymmetric window I've ever seen in business.

My DMs are open. Respond to the most interesting ones.

Loved my trip to SF. Until next time. Maybe NYC next?

Thank you for everything.

I'm rooting for you.
author: gregisenberg
quoted_text:
I spent 48 hours in SF hanging out with billionaires, data labs and AI founders and execs running $1B to $100B companies.

My observations:

1. Sooo MANY stories of data brokers making like $2M a WEEK selling company data to labs. I can't tell if it's the beginning or a bubble, and I kept wondering which niches are left. Digging into it actively.

2. At dinner, someone asked the table, "If a new model drops next month, does your company get better or worse?" HALF the table went quiet! I think that's the best question to ask about any AI startup right now.

3. The bar people talk about now is hitting $1B in revenue in 12 months (I guess that's the new unicorn?). What I didn't hear much about is retention. AI revenue can come in fast and leave fast, and I think we're going to see a lot of stories of AI companies with huge revenue and terrible retention.

4. It's pretty clear we're living through the reinvention of the computer. The model is the CPU, the harness is the operating system, and skills and plugins are the apps. Thinking about it that way makes it easier to see where the whitespace is.

5. We're maybe 12 months from an agent that can watch you work for a week and then do your job without any instructions. The screen recording plus agent memory plus local model combination makes this possible right now.

6. Agent harnesses feel like the new GPT wrappers, in a good way, especially vertical ones. The best teams I talked to treat the model as swappable. One founder walked me through routing different models to different jobs: one for taste and visuals, a cheaper one for the everyday stuff, another for text. 

They use prompts they can move across models over fine-tuning, and A/B test the output on what users actually do with it: do they edit it, export it, share it? A vertical harness is basically four things: the connectors for that industry's data, evals written by people who know the work, rules for what the agent can and can't touch, and a clean screen for a human to review. The model is maybe 20% of it.

7. There's a lot of reverse engineering going on/cloning going on more than I've ever seen. People are decompiling software and rebuilding it with agents, and someone showed a suite of like 10 apps that are worth $5B+ each all that he cloned open source. Me and everyone are still thinking through what it means when software gets this easy to copy.

8. My guess is the value moves to data. If the software can be rebuilt quickly, what's worth paying for in a legacy SaaS company is the years of customer data and workflows inside it. Some SaaS companies are secretly data companies. 

Gets me thinking about how do you truly value data for this saas companies? Like if we were buying these dying saas companies at 2x ARR before (as example), maybe there is a better metric. Idk, just thinking out loud here.

9. It feels like a good chunk of legacy software won't make it to the agentic era, especially anything built around people clicking through a lot of screens.

10. Every company I talked to wants to pipe its internal data into one place and expose it to agents through MCP. Then they look at the data and realize it's a mess: five versions of the same customer, old Slack channels, PDFs nobody can search. Cleaning that up feels like a big consulting opportunity!

11. A lot of founders are building the basic building blocks for agents: APIs, data layers and tools. Some of the companies I saw barely have a UI because the main user is an agent. I really believe the startups that build primitives to this agentic era will do extremely well. Building blocks is the best way to think about it.

12. Labs can get plenty of training data, but it's harder to get real examples of agents failing inside companies. Whoever has those logs has something valuable.

13. Someone running a big consumer company told me the next fight is over memory. The model that remembers the most about you wins, and the smartest model matters less than people think.

14. Physical AI came up a lot. Astra I think was the first model that got people into AI can actually do CAD, and I think a lot of people are thinking what does vibe manufacturing really look like. The line I keep thinking about came from a robotics founder: the hardest problems in AI are deployment problems now, not research problems. Their robots work on their own, call a human when they get stuck, and every one of those calls becomes training data.

15. Cybersecurity companies are having a moment and are actually cool companies to build now, especially the ones that clean up after a breach. Every agent with access to your systems is a new door into your company, and a lot of those doors were left open. 

16. Some startups are worth more dead than alive now. A shutdown company with 5 years of Slack, email and code can get paid for licensing all of it. I wouldn't be surprised if founders start factoring that into when they shut down.

17. People are starting to talk about monetizing the agent web. It feels really early, but when the most popular user of the internet is an agent, what startups should you be building?

18. I think agent insurance is coming. Once an agent makes an expensive mistake, insurers will want audits before they cover anyone.

19. Several people said the hire they want most is someone with taste who can write evals. The models are getting good at generating ideas, so the hard part is judging which ones are good.

20. New trend I observed: startup raises VC, uses venture dollars to become a creator, startup fails, founder falls back on being a full-time creator and incubates other products bootstrapped.

21. Getting SIGNIFICANT distribution is HARD right now. Founders are sponsoring buses, buying billboards like crazy and throwing parties with famous DJs to get noticed. Kinda feels dotcom era in that sense. 

Attention is what's scarce! The growth guy going viral sharing his UGC strategy from Wispr Flow is a good example. It's the sauce everyone wants, and I truly believe there are probably only 50 people on the planet who know how to scale these types of businesses efficiently in this era.

Always good to get that dose of SF. I felt sooo lucky to have such an incredible trip during such an incredible time in building businesses. Surreal in so many ways. 

Happy to be home and locked in.

Until next time!

text:
昨天晚上我花费了2个小时把红杉的Sonya Huang @sonyatweetybird 对最近融资11亿美金的Ineffable CEO David Silver的访谈文本版本看了两遍，感觉David的大脑真的是开放式的思考和深邃。

我把我理解和重要的摘录出来。另外建议对这个公司和领域感兴趣的，可以看看访谈的原文，信息量和细节更多。

-关于起的名字：
Ineffable，就像哥伦布发现美洲大陆一样，是“发现” 之前未曾知道的东西，这个Ineffable是在表达”发现“未曾发现过的”知识“和”能力“。Ineffable路径不依赖于基于人类语言的方法，而是构建能够自主发现事物的系统，并有可能发现那些深不可测、最终“无法言喻”（Ineffable）的知识。

-关于信念：
从攻读博士学位开始研究围棋起，David就一直坚信，解决人工智能问题的正确途径在于从经验中学习——通过能够自主发现、通过强化学习不断进步的系统。

-关于愿景：
Ineffable的愿景是要打造一个“超级学习者”，首先是指能够完全自主地进行探索发现的人。

-关于什么是超级学习者：
Ineffable打造的超级学习者，需要首先打造一个让超级学习者发现一切的环境，这个环境他们称之为”熔炉“。结合了两个方面：一是打造超级学习者——进行研究，使超级学习者变得无比强大，并在工程和研究方面超越强化学习的现有技术水平——二是创建这些熔炉，并将超级学习者放入其中，观察不可思议的行为的出现。

-与LLM的不同：
1.没有走LLM领域所走的以人为本的数据路径，但认为其中有很多值得借鉴的经验。

2.使用RL的方法的不同，与该领域其他许多方法相比，David的强化学习方法的一个不同之处在于，预先设定具体的学习目标。许多人使用逻辑学习模型（LLM）进行强化学习的方式是：“智能体应该先学习这个问题，然后再学习那个问题，最后再学习那个问题。” （这里说的是像LLM使用RL的方式是类似课程学习的思路）。就像牵着鼻子一样，引导智能体朝着某个特定的预期结果前进。David他们设想并没有采用这种方法。给智能体设定一些简单的目标，然后让它去发现那些会让我们感到惊喜和惊奇的东西。原则上，智能体有能力发现各种各样的东西，而事先并不一定知道这些发现是什么。见证这个过程本身就令人兴奋。所以，我希望能够感到惊喜，我想这就是你问题的答案。（这个思考真的好）

另一种说法是，在强化学习中，人们经常会想：“我该如何设计一个奖励函数，才能完美地描述我想要发现的这个非常复杂的问题？我该如何准确地定义我所说的‘科学’是什么意思？我该如何准确地定义我所说的‘有趣的数学’是什么意思？”但还有另一种选择。这种选择是给智能体一个非常简单的目标去优化，但要在一个极其复杂的环境中进行，让智能体能够学习到很多东西。事实证明，如果你观察自然界的运行方式，就会发现，对非常简单、易于描述的量的追求和优化，往往会产生难以描述的复杂性和涌现现象。

例如，进化就是如此，它优化了适者生存，某种适应性信号——而对适应性的追求催生了我们所见的一切复杂性。在人类的进化历程中，我们人类对相对简单目标的追求，最终孕育了人类所掌握的所有复杂行为，以及我们最终积累的所有知识。涌现出的复杂性远远超过了我们最初的认知水平。（这就是说目前的使用RL的方式，很多是填鸭式的奖励函数，一个问题针对去设计，他们想做的是在有个初步的类似人类生存目标之类的东西，agent在这里探索学习，逐步学会一些基本技能目标，如沟通，协调等等）

关于先验知识：
“消除人类先验认知”，如果不断探索学习，要在一定程度上“消除人类先验认知”。比如他举了AlphaGo和AlphaZero的例子，用了两年时间把人类的先验知识去掉后，AlphaZero完全在自我博弈后取得了成功。并不是完全不用先验知识，先验知识适用于许多不同的世界，而不是那种能够精确编码我们关于某个特定问题或某个特定世界的所有知识的非常强大的先验知识。弱的、与环境无关的先验知识似乎完全合理。

quoted_text:
David Silver is one of the all-time greats. He was the creator of AlphaGo, which changed the course of history by showing that neural nets could achieve superhuman performance for the first time.

He also has a unique intuition and knack for forecasting when things will happen in AI. With computer Go, he predicted the Lee Sodol outcome 10 years before, right to the year. He got the year right for Starcraft and won a bet inside Deepmind. Same for AlphaProof. Same for the IMO.

David's prediction for superintelligence: 3 years. !!! He has a strong sense that now is the time to build a superleaner, and that superlearners are now possible, thanks to the enormous progress in compute, simulators, autoresearch, and the sophistication of technology in the stack since the AlphaGo days.

What is a “super learner”? A super learner discovers all knowledge from its own experience. Start from nothing (no internet pre-training), and go beyond human knowledge. Drop it into any stream of experience, simulated or physical, and the superlearner learns.

He expects the progress will be rapid. When you get the recipe for a superlearner just right and remove humans from the development loop altogether, a superlearner can learn extremely quickly. Just look at AlphaGo. AlphaGo took two years to develop with humans in the loop. When David and his team at @GoogleDeepMind got the formula for AlphaZero correctly, it surpassed the human-developed algorithms in just a few hours. Human data is a shortcut, but you have to let go of the human data to shoot beyond it.

In January, David left GDM to found @IneffableLabs, a research-led lab with one mission: build a "super learner" that discovers all knowledge from its own experience, and make first contact with superintelligence. 

He joins us with co-founder Lasse Espeholt, who built IMPALA and SEED RL, the foundations of scaled-up RL, and now runs Ineffable's compute.

A few things we cover in this conversation. 

 — What a super learner is: depth (start from nothing, go beyond human knowledge) and breadth (drop it into any stream of experience, simulated or physical). The human brain is the only existence proof

 — Why they're giving up human data: AlphaGo took two years with humans in the loop. AlphaZero outperformed it in a few hours. "You have to let go of the human data to shoot past the competition"

 — Crucibles: simulated worlds with enough emergent complexity (physics engines, millions of interacting agents) for an agent to rediscover technology, science, maths and language on its own

— Simple rewards, emergent complexity: evolution optimized fitness and got all of life. Don't breadcrumb the objective, give the agent something simple to optimize in a world with a lot to learn about

 — Go as the existence proof: one agent is the most boring game imaginable, two agents is "an infinite onion of layers of complexity"

 — Why human language is probably not the endpoint for reasoning, and how training on it bakes in a flat earth and the four humors

 — Can superintelligence be built in simulation? If the sim is Turing complete, computation, economics, language and maths are all expressible, and it happens 10-100x faster and safer

 — Alignment: language-based monitoring is reaching its limits as agents learn to say one thing and do another. Shadow actions, superintelligences monitoring superintelligences, and building a real science of how they interact peacefully

 — Accelerate in simulation, pace in the real world: Ineffable will gate real-world deployment on evidence that it goes well

 — Timing as the determinant: Silver called Computer Go to the year, then StarCraft, then the IMO. He thinks this is the moment
 
 — Predictions: True superintelligence within three years.

quoted_text:
productive future-proof sov

ore 🤝 solomon 🤝 metadao

today the reserve acts as a downside volatility dampener, but the endgame here (as i understand it) is to construct it so that the supply of ore goes to zero before the reserve is depleted (in effect creating a price floor)

today the reserve holds gold, dollars, bitcoin and a few other things

but it is conceivable that, say twenty years from now, energy abundance changes what people value and what they want to hold

for example, elon has speculated that ai and robotics could make money less relevant, with "power generation as the de facto currency"

one underrated thing about ore is that it is able to adapt to any possible future by holding the things people consider to be long term valuable in its reserve (hence the moniker “the sov of sovs”)

if musk is correct, ore could prosper by tokenizing power generation, or exposure to the most valuable energy companies, and putting that in its reserve instead

this is a hypothetical example of the flexibility i find interesting (and why certain members of the community refer to ore as the future-proof sov)

another dimension that excites me about ore is that it is leaning into decision markets, initially through the proposed use for reserve management. i see that as a way to continue innovating without descending into either stagnation or political fragmentation and chaos

text:
WHY IS THE WORLD OBSESSED WITH JAPAN

Japan is responsible for some of the biggest things in pop culture.

Pokémon. One Piece. Nintendo. Dragon Ball. Anime. Manga. Trading cards. Video games.

how did one relatively small country become the creative home of so many things that the rest of the world is obsessed with?

text:
Position size matters more than most people think!💡

Say you put 40% of your wallet into a trade and it drops 20% before recovering. That’s 8% of your total portfolio gone, which is enough to make most people panic sell before the recovery.

Put 5% in instead, and the same drop costs you 1%. You barely notice it, and you’re still holding when price comes back.

A common rule of thumb is to risk only 1 to 2% of your total portfolio on any single trade. That doesn’t mean you can only put 2% in.

It means that if your stop loss gets hit, you lose no more than about 2% of everything you have.

Get the size right and you can sit through normal volatility. Get it wrong and even a good entry can turn into a loss.😉

Today, we’re releasing Bonsai 2 2B, 4B, and 9B.

Based on Qwen3.5, these new ternary models bring stronger reasoning, visual understanding, and tool calling to compact footprints designed for everyday devices:

• 2B: 0.43GB
• 4B: 0.95GB
• 9B: 2.0GB

For this release, we focused on what makes small models useful as local assistants: following instructions, avoiding repetitive loops, calling tools on mobile devices, and giving useful answers without unnecessary output. The 9B model uses roughly 40% fewer tokens on standard instruction-following and everyday math tasks. Solving the Riemann hypothesis can wait.

These models are successors to our first-generation Bonsai 1.7B, 4B, and 8B, and provide a foundation for bringing practical agentic functionality to local applications on personal computers, phones, and wearables.

text:
SubQ Snap does well in what TypeSafe calls the "Danger Zone", context above 32k. 85% of tokens processed by Snap are from requests above 32k, with many shipping data-intensive features to prod. SSA keeps long context fast and cheap.

We are open-sourcing Decision LCR (Snap 74%, Jev 58%), which mimics real-world tasks and is adapted from AA-LCR.

Because long-context benchmarks for decision models don't really exist, we built one of our own by adapting Artificial Analysis' Long-Context Reasoning benchmark, which we think does a better job mimicking real-world tasks than many LLM long-context benchmarks, to a decision format. We are open-sourcing this today.

Decision LCR: https://t.co/JGGSEBBczF

Adapted from Artificial Analysis's AA-LCR. 100 human-written questions over real 72K–115K-token document sets, converted into 118 decisions, each run with three option orderings to control for position bias. Chance is 19.2, and models score 24–25 with the documents removed.

We'd love for others to run it, use it and improve it. If you work on long-context evaluation or decision models, we'd value your feedback and collaboration.

To learn more about SNAP and our evaluation process, check out the blog:  https://t.co/CglHueOxnv

author: apriori0x
quoted_text:
Today we’re launching @indexnetwork_ 

It’s been exciting to watch already. The first 100 people in are hiring founding engineers, raising seed rounds, writing speculative fiction. One said accepting an intro “feels like the early magic of the internet.”

Try it for yourself: https://t.co/QXepmjtM2L

The premise: With Index, personal agents can coordinate with each other and thus introduce the right people to their users. They do this by negotiating on their principals’ mutual intents, replacing the need for us to broadcast on platforms and scroll endless feeds.

In practice: You log what you're looking for (“signals”) by talking to your agent, it negotiates on fit with the others, and comes back to you with proposed intros for you to accept or pass on. It learns from each turn to surface more relevant people for you.

As founders, but also just as internet nerds - we feel the expectation to be constantly visible. It can be empowering but also tiring, especially when there’s little certainty in how algorithms will route the right people to see your post. On the market level, economists call this search friction: the idea that many deals are never made because it costs too much to find each other. We call it the right person, wrong time.

So that’s why we’re building Index - we’re keen to see what happens when we take social discovery out of the feeds. It’s possible now because of agents. They can help carry the burden of searching, shouting, negotiating, and coordinating in service of finding your others - and we’re so excited to see how this works in the wild.

We’re building this for a world where you can trust that the right person is not out there, but right around the corner. In fact, we even made a short film about it.

text:
16.7% realized on my aggressive stablecoin book, where this week I closed a 5.5x position as too risky and opened a 10x one in its place. 🏹

Eight weeks in, two closures, two replacements. The leverage number was never the point.

@StakeDAOHQ Lending frxUSD-crvUSD LP at 5.5x, out at 12.6% realized.

I’d tolerated it for weeks. Borrow liquidity in that market was permanently scarce, so funding costs swung between 3% and 20% depending on who else was levered that day. By the end the spread had gone negative and I was paying to hold it.

Then the useful part: my exit freed enough liquidity that the rate settled back around 8.5%.

That’s a market where one participant moves the economics. I wasn’t managing a position, I was a variable in it. 📌

The replacement is the same strategy with different collateral — @StakeDAOHQ Lending frxUSD-sDOLA LP at 5.5x, where borrow liquidity is deeper. Same trade, fewer hostages to fortune.

@pendle_fi fxSAVE LP, out at 10.9% realized — and that’s a floor, not a final number.

Clean expiry, nothing dramatic. The FXN reward program ended today, the rate dropped to 7.5%, and 7.5% doesn’t buy a seat in this book. I knew the date when I entered and wrote it down at the time. Dated yield, closed on its date. 🎯

Its replacement is the one I’m most interested in: crvUSD in the wETH market at 10x on @ResupplyFi , borrowing reUSD. Quoted 29.5%.

Ten-times leverage sounds like the aggressive part. It isn’t. The number I care about is that this market holds $98.9M in available borrow liquidity — against the 0.0 I just walked away from.

High leverage in a deep market is a different risk than modest leverage in a thin one, and I’ve now been on both sides of that in the same week. A rate that swings 3% to 20% isn’t volatile because the strategy is aggressive. It’s volatile because there isn’t enough room in the market for the people using it.

One more thing: alUSD-USDC LP is quoting 31.1%, top of the book, up from its usual ~15% — reward yield on that pool spiked this week. Realized sits at 15.8%, which is the honest number. The quote is a snapshot of a spike, not a rate I’ve collected.

Book-wide: quoted 19.6%, realized 16.7%.

This is the aggressive book — leverage, LPs, and yield windows I expect to rotate out of. The conservative one targets 6-8% unlevered and gets touched about once a month. Posted separately.

quoted_text:
Today, we’re releasing Bonsai 2 2B, 4B, and 9B.

Based on Qwen3.5, these new ternary models bring stronger reasoning, visual understanding, and tool calling to compact footprints designed for everyday devices:

• 2B: 0.43GB
• 4B: 0.95GB
• 9B: 2.0GB

For this release, we focused on what makes small models useful as local assistants: following instructions, avoiding repetitive loops, calling tools on mobile devices, and giving useful answers without unnecessary output. The 9B model uses roughly 40% fewer tokens on standard instruction-following and everyday math tasks. Solving the Riemann hypothesis can wait.

These models are successors to our first-generation Bonsai 1.7B, 4B, and 8B, and provide a foundation for bringing practical agentic functionality to local applications on personal computers, phones, and wearables.

The Bonsai 2 family now includes four sizes spanning 2B to 27B parameters. Developers can choose the balance of capability, memory use, and responsiveness that fits their application and hardware.

Available today under Apache 2.0.

text:
Key market moves and headlines from October 15, 2026:

1. In late-afternoon trading the Dow was up more than 600 points (about 1.2%), the S&P 500 had erased early losses to gain about 0.4%, and the Nasdaq had edged higher after falling more than 1% earlier, as investors rotated out of tech and into defensive sectors.

2. September PPI rose 1.3% month over month and 6.3% year over year, the biggest monthly gain since March 2022 and well above the 0.6% and 5.5% expected. Retail sales also beat, rising 0.8% against 0.4% expected, and jobless claims stayed low at 199,000.

3. Fed futures briefly priced about a 34% chance of a rate hike at the October 28 meeting before easing to roughly 27% to 29%, with about 90% still expecting at least one hike by year-end.

4. Treasuries rallied despite the hot inflation data as money left tech for safety. The 10-year yield fell about 10 basis points to roughly 5.08% to 5.10%, and the 2-year dropped to about 4.75%.

5. Chips stayed under pressure, with the VanEck Semiconductor ETF $SMH on track for an eighth straight loss. $NVDA was down about 2%, $AMD and $MRVL were down more than 3%, and $LRCX, $INTC and $ANET were down roughly 4% to 6%.

6. South Korea's KOSPI plunged 7.6% overnight to a six-month low and triggered circuit breakers, as Samsung fell nearly 10% and SK Hynix more than 11%.

7. $TSM posted a record quarterly profit of NT$763.1 billion, up 69%, raised its 2026 revenue growth forecast to about 44%, and guided Q4 revenue to $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion. Shares still slipped about 2% after management said it is being "prudent" in planning for 2027.

8. Worries about debt-funded AI infrastructure kept weighing on the sector but eased throughout the day. $CRWV recoverd the morning drop finishing up 6% 

9. Software was the bright spot in tech, with the software ETF $IGV up about 1.8%, $CRM up almost 4% and $ADBE up more than 3%. $INTU gained 6% after agreeing to acquire the revenue management platform Sequence.

10. Defensive sectors led, with healthcare up about 2.6% and staples up about 1%. $LLY gained about 5% and $UNH about 4%, $WMT rose more than 2% on a Deutsche Bank upgrade to buy, $KMB rose about 4% on better-than-expected preliminary results, and $MMC rose 5% after beating on both earnings and revenue.

11. $FMC plunged about 32% after cutting its Q3 revenue guidance to $65 million to $125 million, far below the $868.5 million consensus.

12. Separately, $RKLB fell 11% after pushing the launch of its Neutron rocket to 2027 but recovered some of the drop finishing only down 6%.

13. WTI crude rose $2.88 (about 3%) to settle at $97.97 on attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and an 8-million-barrel inventory draw reported by the EIA, while Brent slipped 14 cents to $105.92.

text:
Parallel execution is coming to Ethereum with the next upgrade, Glamsterdam

among many benefits, Block-level Acess Lists (BALs) can enable lighter-weight client experiments like below!
author: trent_vanepps
quoted_text:
I started writing smart contracts in 2018, and one thing always bothered me: why did running my own RPC mean running a full node, or an archive node if I wanted historical state?

My app only cared about my contracts, a few dependencies and some ERC20s. Why did I need to keep up with everything everyone else was doing on Ethereum just to serve those reads?

The annoying part was keeping that smaller set of state up to date. Reading a value at one block was doable, but knowing what changed in the next block meant executing it or asking a node that had. A transaction could reach my contract through several other contracts, so just filtering transactions by their destination wasn’t enough.

I mostly forgot about it. RPC providers got reliable enough for what I needed, and I had other things to build. I still didn’t love the setup, but it stopped being something I spent time thinking about.

Then over the weekend, I was looking through Glamsterdam’s EIPs and realized block-level access lists might make this practical.

BALs include the state changes made during a block, including the new values, and the block commits to that list. So once you have the initial state you care about, you can follow its changes without re-executing every transaction. 

So I started vibe coding it. It’s called skim.

You tell it which accounts and storage slots you care about, or let it discover the state your simulations read. It fetches the initial values from Ethereum’s P2P network through SNAP, checks their Merkle proofs, and keeps them updated using BALs. Your eth_calls then run locally. If a call needs something it hasn’t fetched, it gets that from peers too, just with more latency. No upstream RPC provider for those reads.

It can also keep historical versions of the state you’re tracking. That was another thing I wanted: being able to query my app’s past state without keeping everyone else’s history. It exposes a JSON-RPC interface, so existing tools can use it for the methods it supports.

It still receives full payloads and BALs. The state it maintains is selective, not everything it downloads. There’s also a consensus light-client implementation now, but that path isn’t active on Sepolia yet because the required Gloas light-client data isn’t being served by the peers tested so far. For now, the head is still trusted.

It’s still an experiment, and I’m working through correctness bugs and longer-running tests. I’m not presenting it as a production node replacement.

But it’s pretty satisfying to finally build something around a complaint I’ve had since 2018. I wanted a small client that knows the parts of Ethereum my app actually uses, and that’s what I’m trying to make.

For the last 5 decades straight, we have created (as a society) circa 20 decacorns per decade. In the last 12 months, we have created 42.

The world is changing faster than ever before and if you do not stay up to date. You will be left behind. That is why I created this show with Jason and Rory.

This is the only show in tech, you have to listen to every week. No egos, no politics, just tech.

On the agenda:

- Valar Atomics Sues Day One Ventures
- Meta Returns to the AI Frontier With Muse Wonder
- NVIDIA Eyes $30B Reflection Deal
- Jev Raises $870M at a $7.5B Valuation

My notes below with @jasonlk and @rodriscoll

1. We Generated 20 $10B Companies per Decade for the Last 5 Decades and Now 42 in a Year

Tech produced roughly 20 decacorns per decade for five decades, yet 42 have been created in less than a year of this decade. Only about 130 tech companies have ever been worth $10B or more. Rising market caps explain part of the jump, but the pace is stunning.

2. Who Is Right and Who Is Wrong: Day One or Valar?

X wrongly claimed Day One was suing its portfolio company, when Valar Atomics wants a declaratory judgment to move on. Waiving pro rata for Sequoia is common, but letting an existing investor in as a strategic is playing favorites. Still, once founders decide, early investors must get with the program because it is not their company.

3. Why Meta's New Model Is a Zero

Meta's new model scores well on evals, but there is no API and it can only be used inside Muse. A model claiming parity at the same price, not cheaper and not usable by developers, is the height of performative evals.

4. Why We Should Lead Jev's Round at 8 Billion

Jev is a super fast, super cheap classifier, accurate enough for maybe 10% of AI use cases. Cloudflare and Amazon can match it today, but the bet is that a focused team out of OpenAI pulls ahead while those efforts stay niche. If Jev becomes hyper accurate, it changes the game.

5. What Is the Single Greatest Potential for AI?

Drug discovery is probably AI's largest opportunity, with drugs that dramatically extend longevity and quality of life. If AI companies can accelerate discovery and own the IP while others do the hard work, AI could reboot the industry. Trials would not speed up, but the prize is a GLP-1 out five years faster.

6. Haiku 5.5 Is the First Time AI Has Been Deflationary

Falling token prices have been offset by consuming far more tokens, so AI costs have not fallen. Haiku 5.5 is almost as good as Sonnet for many use cases at a tenth of the price, and Sonnet 5.5 is twice as fast. After a 90% price cut, usage must rise 10 times for revenue to hold.

7. Why the SaaSpocalypse Is Worse Than We Thought

The SaaSpocalypse passed only for companies well above $1B in revenue, and everyone without massive scale is living a worse one than in March or April. Leaders will acquire some companies and grind out the rest. A safe software IPO may now need $1.5B to $2B of ARR rather than $500M.

New opinion article about @Starlink from a 7-year Delta Airlines Diamond Medallion status member (their highest loyalty tier):

"After flying a United flight in July that included Starlink, it was enough reason for me to switch. It was amazing, like being on the internet at my house, that's how fast it is. For the two-hour flight, I was just doing work. As a founder, I don't get the luxury of being able to log off for a few hours in the middle of the day. When Slack and email are going, or I'm collaborating and working with teammates, or I'm building an app, I want to have fast internet.

On most Delta flights that I'm on, there's at least some segment of the flight during which the internet goes out for a period of time, whether for a few minutes or 20 minutes. The reliability of the uptime leaves a bit to be desired. Nearly all of Delta's peers went with Starlink, while Delta went with Amazon's Leo, which won't be out until 2028.

I hope Delta takes stock of all the online chatter and listens to its customers. It has done a great job in the past of continually improving its product and listening to its customers. For the most profitable and what I feel is the most premium airline in America, it seems odd for Delta not to outfit its planes with the best in-flight internet."

I think we'll see more and more stories like this. As people get a taste of Starlink wi-fi on planes, they won't want to go back, and will demand better internet from airlines that don't have it, and in some cases, just switch to flying other airlines that do have it.

text:
What actually goes into an AI strategy, and how to evaluate AI use cases? 

Here's how you rank opportunities....

The AI Portfolio Grid - a 2x2 matrix to score AI opportunities
- Big prize, Ready now = Accelerate now
- Big prize, Not ready = Invest to unlock
- Small prize, Ready now = Quick wins
- Small prize, Not ready = Deprioritize 

Questions to ask to place an initiative on the matrix: 
- Can we execute the initiative today?
- How big is the prize?

Here's how you turn opportunities into a strategy...

Step 1: Start with your goals
1.1 Find what’s limiting each goal
- Limits come down to people, process, data or technology. Treat all four as suspects; most companies fixate on data.

1.2 Score impact against those goals
- 3 steps to assess impact: interview the CEO, interview the leaders who own each goal, and sort what you hear into people, process, data and technology.

Step 2: Take inventory
2.1 Find everything that’s already running
- Before adding anything new, take stock of the AI work already underway.

2.2 Put it on the grid with your new ideas
- The scoring is the same, with a higher bar: existing work has to show it’s working.

2.3 Make one of four calls
- Continue, edit, merge, stop

Step 3: Set the rules
3.1 Give every pilot an owner, an outcome and a cost
- To earn a Start and a pilot, a new initiative needs three things: business owner, checkable outcome, cost estimate

3.2 Give small fixes a lighter check
- Small fixes, like automating a recurring report or checklist, rarely tie to a company goal, but they add up. If one is cheap, has an owner and will show results within weeks, do it.

3.3 Judge pilots on early evidence
- A pilot should show four things: the work got faster, cheaper or better without quality dropping, people used it in their daily work, the AI caused the gain, and the cost and benefit assumptions held up.

3.4 Write go/no-go criteria before the pilot starts
- Write down what the pilot must show to expand, be revised or stop.

3.5 Check readiness before production
- Is the value at stake clear?
- Is the process understood and measurable?
- Is the data accessible?
- Can someone deploy and support it?
- Will the intended users participate?
- Does the team have capacity to change how it works?
- Does a business owner own the result and the decisions?
- Are legal controls and guardrails in place?

Step 4: Decide the order
4.1 Start in Accelerate Now, odds before return
- Your first wave comes from Accelerate Now. Within it, rank by odds of success first, then by return among the ones likely to work.

4.2 Pick contained work with a willing owner
- Early initiatives with good odds tend to share three traits: most readiness questions already have a yes, the owner wants it, and the work is contained.

4.3 Run Quick Wins alongside the first wave
- Quick Wins are cheap, and people feel the difference fast.

4.4 Fund enabling work early
- The exception to ranking by return is enabling work. When one gap, like unclear policy, unreachable data or leaders who’ve never used the tools, blocks several big-prize initiatives, closing it belongs in the first wave even though it returns nothing directly.

4.5 Go bigger once you have a track record
- With a track record, go after the biggest prize the evidence says you can win.

Today, we’re releasing Bonsai 2 2B, 4B, and 9B.

Based on Qwen3.5, these new ternary models bring stronger reasoning, visual understanding, and tool calling to compact footprints designed for everyday devices:

• 2B: 0.43GB
• 4B: 0.95GB
• 9B: 2.0GB

For this release, we focused on what makes small models useful as local assistants: following instructions, avoiding repetitive loops, calling tools on mobile devices, and giving useful answers without unnecessary output. The 9B model uses roughly 40% fewer tokens on standard instruction-following and everyday math tasks. Solving the Riemann hypothesis can wait.

These models are successors to our first-generation Bonsai 1.7B, 4B, and 8B, and provide a foundation for bringing practical agentic functionality to local applications on personal computers, phones, and wearables.

The Bonsai 2 family now includes four sizes spanning 2B to 27B parameters. Developers can choose the balance of capability, memory use, and responsiveness that fits their application and hardware.

Available today under Apache 2.0.

Morgan Stanley: Memory Channel Checks 

HBM / Nvidia Rubin

→ HBM ASPs expected +121% YoY in 2027. HBM4 pricing at $3–5/Gb, with HBM4e at $5+/Gb.

→ Nvidia Rubin ramp slower than planned. Fewer than 10k VR200 NVL72 racks expected in 2026 vs. an original ~15k target. Rubin expected to become mainstream after 1H27.

→ HBM4 yields remain constrained. 8-high stacks offer ~5 percentage points higher yields than 12-high and are expected to become mainstream in 2027. Lower HBM capacity per chip could benefit RDIMM/SOCAMM as inference KV-cache shifts to host memory.

DRAM

→ 4Q26 contract pricing revised to +10–15% QoQ from +3–8%. PC DRAM +13–18%, server DRAM +10–15%, mobile DRAM +0–5%.

→ US hyperscalers reportedly placed additional RDIMM orders for 2027. Korean suppliers' PC DRAM output could fall >20% YoY as capacity shifts toward server DRAM and HBM.

→ DDR5 modules now trade at a ~10% discount to DDR4. DDR4 supply expected to decline ~20% in 2027 as suppliers exit legacy production.

→ DRAM capex projected at $98bn in 2026 (+82% YoY) and $150–160bn in 2027 (+~60%), but meaningful additional bit supply only arrives in 2H27.

NAND / Enterprise SSD

→ 4Q26 NAND pricing revised to +15–20% QoQ from +0–5%. Enterprise SSD pricing expected +23–28%, significantly outpacing client SSD.

→ Several major US cloud customers reportedly shifting from TLC SSD + HDD to QLC SSD for AI inference KV-cache storage. QLC costs roughly one-third as much as TLC at equivalent capacity.

→ Consumer NAND inventories are building despite enterprise SSD shortages, with suppliers reportedly bundling excess consumer inventory to secure sales.

text:
当年做出 BabyAGI 的 Yohei Nakajima，最近放弃了一个 AI 圈特别流行的想法，给公司造一个「大脑」。

Yohei 之前也想把公司的所有知识、记忆、数据集中到一个 Company Brain 里，后来发现问题一大堆。每个人的 Agent 都有自己的记忆，强行共享容易造成数据重复、信息泄漏，而且公司的真实业务数据本来就散落在 CRM、邮件和各种软件里。

所以他换了个思路，开始做 FirmOS，也就是公司操作系统。

这里有个我特别喜欢的概念，叫 Flipped Playbook，倒着写的公司手册。

传统企业是先制定 SOP，再要求员工按流程工作。但真实的公司根本不是这样运转的。今天开会改了个决策，明天发现一个流程有问题，后天换了个供应商，很多规则都是在日常工作中一点点形成的。

Yohei 想让 Agent 从每天的邮件、会议记录和业务沟通中自动识别这些变化，提出规则更新建议，经过人的确认后写入 FirmOS。其他 Agent 随后就能按照新的规则工作。

原始数据依然保存在原来的工具里，FirmOS 负责维护公司的规则、流程、决策，以及 Agent 应该如何调用工具。

我最近也一直在琢磨 Agent 怎么从个人工作台进入真正的组织协作，越来越觉得我们可能高估了 Agent 的智力，低估了组织本身的遗忘能力。

一家公司的很多重要经验，从来就没有被认真记录过。创始人为什么拒绝某个客户，销售团队为什么改变报价策略，一次失败的合作究竟改变了什么规则。这些东西大部分只存在于几个人的脑子里，人员一变动就丢了。

现在的问题更有意思了。假设一家公司的 Agent 比员工还多，每个 Agent 都很聪明，但它们凭什么知道昨天发生了什么？凭什么理解一个月前某个决策背后的原因？又凭什么保证它们不会重复犯错？

这也是我觉得 CompanyOS 真正有价值的地方。

它让一家公司的经验有机会持续积累，并且直接影响下一次行动。今天人类做出的决策，明天就可能成为整个 Agent 团队共同遵守的规则。

以后企业 Agent 的竞争，可能会逐渐从谁能完成更多任务，转向谁能让整个组织越工作越聪明。

毕竟，单个 Agent 的能力可以靠换模型提升，但一家公司的判断力，需要它自己一点点积累。
author: sleepy0x13
quoted_text:
after switching our approach to building a "FirmOS", I'm increasingly confident that the future of agent collaboration within organizational settings is going to be a "company operating system" or CompanyOS, designed for agent and human collaboration

instead of a "company brain" that holds everything, the OS is for storing rules, processes, decisions made, which tools to use and how. it can mirror some data, but the source of truth is often best held in your existing tools (CRM, etc.). it's continuously updated and used by your agents

i think of this as a "flipped playbook" where instead of writing down the company rules first and following them (which is kind of like waterfall development), you're constantly updating the playbook as you decide or learn new things day-to-day running the business

text:
Watching big companies scramble to glue together a stablecoin payments stack they never actually built together is painful.

At Polygon we’ve never had that problem. We built the Open Money Stack as one product from the very beginning, with one team and one roadmap. Even acquisitions immediately fit into it. 

When someone wants to talk about onramps and then has questions about wallets or cross-chain transfers, they stay with the same people. You want a custom chain, same team. You want dedicated blockspace, same team. You want a stablecoin checkout flow in your app, same team. You want an insanely crazy custom unique solution that requires multiple domain experts to work together--again, same team.

There’s no handoff, no separate wallet team or chain team or checkout team, and no one telling them to talk to someone else.

We’re smaller, we move faster, we're more global and we came out of crypto with deep payments experience already in the building. That combination is difficult to assemble after the fact, and it’s why the conversations we have with customers tend to stay in one place from the first call to the last.
author: 0xMarcB
quoted_text:
Today is probably a good time to check in on things with @privy_io, which became part of @stripe just over a year ago.

Our acquisition was predicated on three factors: stablecoin growth, self-custody as a key enabler of broader global coverage, and rapidly increasing demand for programmable financial infrastructure. As we said at the time, "money has to reside somewhere, and Privy builds the world's best programmable vaults."

Since then, the Privy team has executed exceptionally well: assets in Privy wallets have grown ~25x, monthly active developers are up ~3x, revenue is up ~9x, and Privy now facilitates nearly $25B of monthly transaction volume. @tryramp, @Deel, @Klarna, @felixpago, @HyperliquidX, and thousands of other businesses are building embedded banking functionality on Privy.

At Stripe, we're deeply integrating Privy into Treasury, @Link, and Connect. In each case, it's accelerating our global expansion, and enabling us to build better functionality faster. (Coming soon: @Link balances.)

We're also seeing that Privy's wallet infrastructure is the ideal substrate for agents to transact and earn -- live today with @merit_systems, @orthogonal_sh, @Nevermined_ai, @prlnet, and more. Developers prefer programmable financial infrastructure, but agents need it. We expect that the agentic economy will continue to grow extremely quickly.

The Privy team has maintained remarkable product velocity, with major launches this year including deposit addresses, earning on Privy balances, digital asset accounts, custodial wallets, and Stripe's own stablecoin cards.

It's also been neat to see how Privy has been accelerated by Stripe, with better onramps, @stablecoin payment rails and licenses, Stripe's fiat capabilities and issuing stack, and integration with @Tempo.

Together, we're building one API for holding stablecoin balances and earning yield, moving money in and out of fiat, and orchestrating spend with cards. We still have a lot of work to do, not least in integrating everything across Privy, Bridge, and the rest of Stripe -- there's been so much feature and functionality expansion that we haven't yet had much time to reconcile everything. Overall, though, I'm very happy with how things are going, and excited by where these capabilities are headed.

If you're interested in working on the future of stablecoins, agentic payments, and crypto's deployment in the real world, you should get in touch with @sternhenri (now leading all of @StripeCrypto) or others on the team.
