If Nick is right that modern interpretability tools can make the vast majority of neurons and their underlying circuits understandable, even in ‘trillion-parameter models’!

we could actually have a way to understand what these models are learning, and how they’re making decisions. The fact that AI agents are now helping automate interpretability research makes this even more promising.
author: Selkis_2028
quoted_text:
interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

author: gajesh
quoted_text:
Today, we’re releasing Bonsai 2 2B, 4B, and 9B.

Based on Qwen3.5, these new ternary models bring stronger reasoning, visual understanding, and tool calling to compact footprints designed for everyday devices:

• 2B: 0.43GB
• 4B: 0.95GB
• 9B: 2.0GB

For this release, we focused on what makes small models useful as local assistants: following instructions, avoiding repetitive loops, calling tools on mobile devices, and giving useful answers without unnecessary output. The 9B model uses roughly 40% fewer tokens on standard instruction-following and everyday math tasks. Solving the Riemann hypothesis can wait.

These models are successors to our first-generation Bonsai 1.7B, 4B, and 8B, and provide a foundation for bringing practical agentic functionality to local applications on personal computers, phones, and wearables.

The Bonsai 2 family now includes four sizes spanning 2B to 27B parameters. Developers can choose the balance of capability, memory use, and responsiveness that fits their application and hardware.

Available today under Apache 2.0.

22岁的扎克伯格拒绝雅虎10亿美元收购的那场经典战役，流传最广的版本是乔布斯指点他去印度寺庙寻找答案的浪漫传奇，但真正血腥的代价往往被行业过滤掉了。

当年对于刚满两岁、只有一千万用户的Facebook来说，10亿美元现金意味着早期持股团队全员实现阶层跨越。

在扎克伯格执意否决收购提议后的十二个月内，他的整支核心管理团队几乎全部辞职走人。

乔布斯当年给他的从来不是东方玄学，而是一个经历过公司起落的导师在帮年轻创始人做使命校准。

当整个董事会和管理层都在疯狂计算变现估值时，唯有创始人自己必须直面一个终极拷问，你到底是在做一笔随时准备脱手的买卖，还是在造一个不可替代的时代物种。

在印度独自旅行近一个月找回定力并不难，真正难的是回到硅谷后，面对一间空荡荡的办公室，承受替所有人关上暴富大门后的巨大孤立感。

商业史上最罕见的护城河从来不是技术或者流量，而是在身边所有人都准备套现离场的时刻，创始人敢不敢独自一人把筹码全部留存继续推向下一局。 https://t.co/60EjVhsCTp

text:
AI制药是下一个存储？

受到Frank老师启发，作为一个曾经跨国药企从业者，我深入研究了一下AIDD

AI的下一轮投资机会，可能正在向医药行业扩散。

2026年，存储板块成为AI产业链中的热门方向之一。AI数据中心需求增长、存储供应紧张，推动了产品价格和企业盈利能力的提升，MU、SNDK等股票也经历了一轮显著上涨。

那么，下一个值得关注的AI应用赛道在哪里？

我认为：AI制药（AIDD）值得重点研究。

AI制药正在加速落地

过去，AI在制药领域主要用于辅助研究，如今全球大型药企已经开始投入大量资源。

2026年1月，礼来（LLY）与NVIDIA宣布未来五年合计投入最高10亿美元，建设AI药物研发实验室。

艾伯维（ABBV）与Iambic展开AI药物发现合作；罗氏与Recursion（RXRX）合作的首个神经科学靶点已经进入早期药物发现阶段。

这背后的逻辑并不复杂。

传统新药研发周期长、成本高、失败率高。AI能够辅助靶点发现、分子设计和实验筛选，有机会减少无效研发投入，提高研发效率。

但AI设计出候选药物，并不代表药物一定能够通过临床试验。

技术突破能否转化为真正的商业价值，仍然需要时间验证。

产业链中谁最有可能率先受益？

我把AIDD投资机会分成三个方向。

第一类：纯AIDD公司。

代表标的：SDGR、RXRX、ABSI、IAM。

这些公司拥有更直接的AI技术敞口，未来如果研发平台和临床管线取得突破，可能获得较高的估值弹性，但研发风险和资金消耗也更大。

第二类：大型创新药企。

代表标的：LLY（礼来）、ABBV（艾伯维）、MRK（默沙东）、PFE（辉瑞）。

它们掌握大量历史研发数据、临床试验资源及全球商业化渠道。

如果AI能够提高长期研发成功率，大型药企可能成为最终经济价值的重要受益者。

第三类：CRO研发服务商。

代表标的：IQV、MEDP、CRL。

这是我目前尤其关注的方向。

因为即使AI设计的新药还没有成功上市，CRO也可能先通过临床试验设计、患者招募、数据处理和项目管理自动化，提高现有业务的运营效率。

如果未来更多AI发现的优质候选药物进入临床，CRO还可能获得额外订单。

CRO的财报已经出现积极信号

以IQVIA（IQV）为例。

2026年第二季度：

营收43.68亿美元，同比增长8.7%。
调整后EBITDA为9.94亿美元，同比增长9.2%。
新签订单31.5亿美元，同比增长19%。
Book-to-Bill达到1.22倍。

更值得关注的是，IQVIA在9月披露，其AI临床开发解决方案在部分应用中实现了临床试验启动提速33%、数据清理提速50%。

这意味着AI已经能够在实际业务中创造可衡量的效率改善。

同期，MEDP营收同比增长17.2%，新签订单增长28.2%，同样显示出较强的临床研发服务需求。

不过，CRL营收同比下降2.7%，调整后营业利润率从22.1%降至20.5%。

这些数据说明，CRO并非全面受益。IQV的AI提效成果也尚未被证明是其利润增长的主要原因。

但相比需要等待药物临床成功的纯AIDD企业，临床CRO的AI收益可能更早通过订单、成本和利润率得到验证。

AI制药能复制存储行情吗？

这里有一个非常重要的区别。

存储行业本轮上涨的核心驱动力，是AI需求扩张叠加供给约束，推动产品价格、利润和盈利预期上升。

而AI制药的价值传导链条更长：

AI技术进步 → 研发效率提升 → 更多优质候选药物 → 临床验证 → 商业化与利润兑现。

存储可以通过产品涨价较快反映到财报，而AI制药的研发成果可能需要数年才能转化为实际利润。

因此，我认为AIDD未来可能出现两种投资机会。

短期来看，具备真实AI产品和运营效率改善能力的CRO，以及已经实现软件商业化的研发平台，值得优先研究。

长期来看，如果AI能够持续提高药物研发成功率，大型创新药企和纯AIDD公司的价值空间可能更加可观。

我的投资判断

AI制药赛道（AIDD）的"瓶颈交易"正在成形，Freda Duan这篇推文值得好好看看，梳理下要点。
前沿AI实验室的集体入场是最显著的信号：1）Anthropic组建了专属生命科学研究团队并建立湿实验室；
2）OpenAI 建立了专为生物学和药物发现设计的 GPT-Rosalind 模型族；
3）字节跳动旗下独立运营的 Anew Labs 已拥有内部药物研发库；
4）同构实验室（Isomorphic Labs）则明确表示将把 AI 设计的药物推进人体临床试验。

与此同时供给端的信号也很清晰：
1）DNA 合成商拓斯达生物（Twist Bioscience，TWST）预计2026财年和2027财年的AI药物发现订单将连续实现三位数百分比增长；
2）金斯瑞（GenScript）的 AI 药物发现业务在 2026 财年上半年同比翻倍，渠道调研显示其实际验证产能已达每日约8,000个设计，并有望在 2026 年底前提升至 16,000 个。

AI制药正在形成类似半导体"瓶颈交易"的结构性机会。核心逻辑在于：AI让失败实验也变成有价值的训练数据，湿实验室正从"造药"转型为"造数据"，DNA合成、蛋白生产、CRO或成最先受益的"卖铲人"。

在AI制药领域，瓶颈同样在沿产业链向下传递：AI模型产生设计→DNA合成→蛋白生产→实验验证→临床前测试，每个环节都可能成为下一个受益节点。

洛杉矶加州大学教授Quanquan Gu认为：生物学可能成为AI下一个递归自我改进的前沿——在计算机中设计，在实验室中测试，将实验反馈转化为半合成训练数据，改进模型，周而复始。

看来AI-bio值得好好研究下了。

text:
A big opportunity that @Trueo_ can immediately tap into is prediction markets for hedging crypto exploit risks.

The demand for an instrument like this is obvious. Every crypto user can benefit from hedging against hacks.

And if think about it, exploit markets actually scale much better than traditional defi insurance because LPs have a better throttle on exposure, and because anyone can permissionlessly underwrite risk at their preferred price.

The math is pretty simple to quantify.

Because the market is two-sided and permissionless, the premium cost for hedgers should also be more competitive.

Even if hedgers cant cover all their losses, the product is still superior because of its reduced friction, constant market-priced quotes, the ability to resell the claim, and programmatic payouts without burdensome KYC.

The main risk for LPs is in the event that an exploit happens and traders front run them before they can adjust liquidity. 

But that can be mitigated with good onchain monitoring and detection tools, or with a trade execution queue, or both.

Historically, exploit markets have seen some of the most organic activity on Trueo.

So we plan double down on this concept and swing for the fences. 

Coupled with the right distribution channel, this could end up being our highest demand product and break out moment.

Stay tuned for more.

text:
MSCI Adopts New Index Exclusion Rules; Strategy and Metaplanet Face Potential Removal

MSCI has adopted new rules to exclude non-operating companies from its Global Investable Market Indexes. In an earlier simulation based on May 2026 data, MSCI identified Bitcoin treasury companies Strategy (MSTR) and Metaplanet (3350) as potential removals, while Ethereum treasury company SharpLink (SBET) would be placed on a watchlist. The final list of affected constituents will be published on November 11.

The new rules, effective after the November 30 close, will exclude companies that fail an operating-assets test and trigger at least four of five financial exclusion criteria. Existing constituents must fail the screening in both of their two most recent annual filing periods before removal. MSCI will also lift temporary index restrictions on companies previously identified as holding digital assets worth at least 50% of total assets, assessing them under the new methodology instead.

author: willcb
quoted_text: there’s a recent line of theory work emphasizing the circuit-theoretic limitations of transformers. maybe we’ll end up with some Frankenstein adaptive-depth mixture-of-layers mess, but imo it seems kinda inevitable that solving reasoning requires strong circuit compositionality

text:
it is perhaps more useful to think of language models as superpositions of natural language programs, where the result of training is compiling the optimal DSL for your distribution

https://t.co/6kJJJPpJ5U
author: willcb
quoted_text:
circuit complexity generally refers to a “family of circuits”, where the explicit circuit you use for a problem is a function of the length of the input (e.g to find the shortest path in a graph with N edges, there’s an circuit C_N for every N)

constant depth here means that the number of transformer layers you need doesn’t grow for bigger inputs, just the embedding dimension (in log scale) + length of CoT needed, and the CoT only needs to be as long as the size of that circuit C_N

so basically you could *compress* that family of circuits into a single transformer which will work for all inputs of length N < exp(embed dim), if your context length is at least C_N for the largest N you care about

in a sense, that’s fairly similar to what you get with Turing machines (poly-size circuits are maybe slightly more powerful than poly-time TMs but that gets into complexity theory pedantry)

imo it’s interesting bc it pulls transformers from the world of function representation into computation — they can basically do what Turing machines do, the weights don’t need to scale for bigger inputs (with the embedding caveat), and the number of steps they take is basically as good as you can hope for

that’s all still *if* you have the correct magic transformer which solves a problem, where a TM could also (basically) solve that problem in the same time

BUT we know neural nets are polysemantic, so there’s hope that you could have a transformer which basically encodes many TMs in superposition + does retrieval to decide which to execute, based on features of the input, and that the magic of gradient descent trained on many execution/reasoning traces of polytime-solvable problems leads you to such a network

text:
Texas and TSMC have a storied past. Morris Chang built his career at Texas Instruments in Dallas, rising to run its worldwide semiconductor business, until TI's corporate politics passed him over and he left to found TSMC in Taiwan in 1987. Now TSMC is weighing a build-out in Texas, bringing things full circle, and the hope is that history doesn't repeat itself and that C.C. Wei and Elon settle the question at the heart of the talks, which is who runs the fab.

Fate loves irony, because what makes this hard is also what could make it work. Terafab wants logic, memory and advanced packaging under one roof, which lets the job be split by strength. Terafab designs its own logic and memory chips and supplies the site, energy, power and water, perhaps one day even the EUV light from a central free-electron laser, as Elon hinted with "FEL FTW." TSMC leases space as a tenant and manufactures the leading-edge logic with its own tools and team, so its process IP never leaves its hands. Terafab manufactures the memory, which isn't TSMC's business, and TSMC licenses Terafab its advanced packaging the same way it already licenses CoWoS to ASE, SPIL and Amkor.

TSMC skips the slowest, costliest parts of a US build, wafers move next door instead of across the country, TSMC stays a pure-play foundry serving its customer, and Terafab gets to manufacture for real.

text:
Talked to Michael from Coreweave about debt six months ago: 

18:18–23:43: Jason asks about CoreWeave’s debt; Michael answers (cleaned of filler words and stutters, otherwise as spoken)

JASON: How does all that debt work? That is something you guys specialize in. Corporate debt… I’m in the venture business, people are like, “Why should I be in venture when corporate debt pays so well?” Corporate paper’s so huge. I’m curious how this fits in, and what interest rate people are paying on, you know, a billion dollars in infrastructure. What do they pay on that?

MICHAEL: So CoreWeave has really been the innovator around a lot of the financing engines that have come to bear on this. We did the first GPU-based loans. I’m going to try to explain this in a way people can understand. What we do is we go out and we find a client. Let’s use Microsoft; you brought them up before. Microsoft comes to us and says, “We’d like to buy some compute from you.” And we say, “Okay, great. We’re going to sign a contract.” Once I have a contract in hand, I create something. It’s not a particularly creative name. It’s called the box.

JASON: Yeah.

MICHAEL: And what I do with the box is I take my contract with Microsoft and I put it in the box. I go to Jensen and buy the GPUs, I put them in the box. I take my data center contract, I put it in the box. And now the box governs cash flow. It has a waterfall of cash flow that comes into it and goes out of it. So the way it works is I build the compute, I deliver the compute to Microsoft, and they pay the box. They don’t pay me. It goes into the box, and the first thing it does is pay the data center. It pays the power bill. It pays the interest and the principal. And then whatever’s left flows back to us.

So it is an incredibly well-structured, time-tested, pressure-tested vehicle to be able to borrow money against client paper and all of the other collateral around the deal. That’s why CoreWeave, a company many people had never heard of, was able to go out and raise $35 billion in 18 months to build infrastructure at scale. But what’s important to understand is the economics in this box are such that within 2.5 years of a 5-year deal, we have paid for everything.

JASON: The principal’s been paid off.

MICHAEL: The principal’s been paid off, the interest has been paid off. The return into the box is such that we’re able to generate returns to our company at the box level, which gives the most sophisticated lenders in the world, whether banks or private equity funds or whoever, confidence that they’re going to achieve the one rule of lending, which is “give me my money back.”

JASON: Yes. Works better when that happens. So they look at this box and they’re like, “Wow, we’re really confident we’re going to get our money back.” And maybe they want 10 boxes.

MICHAEL: That’s correct.

JASON: And if any one box goes upside down, you can deal with it and it’s not as acute.

MICHAEL: That’s correct. And they don’t cross-pollinate. They don’t cause contagion across the boxes. They’re all independent and discrete. That’s one. Number two: as you do this and show the lenders how this financing mechanism works, they continue to lend you money at progressively lower rates. When you think about our cost of capital over the last two years, we have dropped it by 600 basis points.

JASON: Wow.

MICHAEL: It is enormous. So you’re seeing a company driving its cost of capital down toward where the hyperscalers borrow, which will let us be competitive with them over time. And we have been extremely militant and diligent about feeding, watering and caring for those boxes, so we continue to have access to the capital markets in a way that lets us build and drive our business.

JASON: That means you have to say no to maybe some people who want to be in the box.

MICHAEL: Yeah. We look at some deals where they want to buy GPUs for a year, and I say that’s not a deal I can do, because it’s too short for me to amortize the expenses. So I won’t do that.

JASON: And they can go to another provider who maybe wants to take that risk on, who has extra capacity.

MICHAEL: Absolutely. But our business is really built around the risk management of getting to scale. In my mind, during this period of disequilibrium, when there aren’t enough GPUs in the world to provide compute for all the different use cases in AI, what matters for my company is to get enormously large. That drives down our cost of capital, and it means information flows in from all different parts of the market: large language models, high-speed trading, search, all of these things. They feed information back to us that tells us the next product we need to build, where they need help scaling, or what type of compute they need. All of that information flow is incredibly valuable to us.

author: tbpn
quoted_text:
Today we're standing up XBOX LABS (https://t.co/dJSufI1vni). Here is the note that I sent to the team:

Team,
The first video games emerged some 75 years ago. In the time since, there have been booms and busts, but every year there are more great games to play, more devices to play them, and best of all, more people than ever playing. That growth helped make XBOX what it is today, and we've helped shape the industry in return, from bringing hard drives to consoles and online gaming through Xbox Live to Game Pass and cloud gaming, alongside franchises that have brought millions of people together.
In recent weeks, we've seen games rapidly decompiled and rebuilt to run on hardware they were never originally designed to support. Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside a browser through WebAssembly and WebGPU, the latter now approaching 90% global browser support. Perhaps more surprisingly, we've seen many of the biggest games in the world have been remixed into the source code of another.
These experiments challenge long-held assumptions about our industry: the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games. While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators. These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes because) they challenge our existing business models.
To explore these possibilities, I’ve asked Scott to stand-up XBOX LABS, a small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience. We'll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating.
I think XBOX has an important role to play here.  Coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software. Games share many of those same properties, and people spend more than 72 billion hours a year playing XBOX games, roughly five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide. We've spent 25 years learning how to make great games, and I want our game makers to help shape what these new technologies make possible. As we learn, we’ll share the tools we build with developers across the industry, just as we always have.
Our priorities aren't changing. We remain committed to the 4Cs, to making great games, to our hardware and to being responsible stewards of IP and the communities built around it. LABS gives us a way to explore new technology that is game design led without abandoning the work already underway.
Asha

text:
华尔街最近好像只认识两家 AI 公司，OpenAI 和 Anthropic。只要这两家的收入增速稍微出点问题，整个英伟达都得跟着挨骂。

黄仁勋在最新一期 BG2 播客里，终于把这笔账掰开讲了。

他说，外界严重误解了英伟达的需求结构。

英伟大约三分之一的业务来自传统加速计算，包括数据处理、物理模拟、分子动力学等。即使世界上没有一家前沿 AI 实验室，这部分需求依然存在，而且每年还在增长 30%～40%。

真正来自前沿 AI 实验室的算力需求，只占 25%～30%。而且客户也远不止 OpenAI 和 Anthropic，还包括 Meta、Google、xAI 等五六家主要玩家。

剩下约三分之一，则来自大量租用算力的初创公司。黄仁勋把它们称为下一代云计算生态，类似于当年 AWS 崛起时催生的那批互联网公司。

我觉得黄仁勋这次讲到了一个很重要的问题。

过去几个月，市场几乎陷入了一种奇怪的计算方式：拿 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 的收入预测，去判断整个 AI 基础设施投资能不能回本。

但如果黄仁勋披露的需求结构准确，这套算法从一开始就漏掉了很大一部分市场。

更有意思的是，黄仁勋其实还在为开源模型提供一个商业解释。大量垂直领域的 AI 创业公司使用开源模型，未必给 OpenAI 或 Anthropic 贡献收入，却照样要购买和租用 GPU。

当然，需求来源分散，也不代表每笔投资都能回本。这周 CoreWeave 等算力公司的债务压力已经让市场开始紧张。不同客户最终仍然可能受到同一轮融资环境收紧的冲击。

但我觉得，把英伟达的前途完全绑定在两家模型实验室的收入增长上，确实越来越站不住脚。

AI 基础设施的终极买单者，可能比华尔街现在盯着的那几家公司复杂得多。

quoted_text:
NVIDIA CEO @JensenHuang tells @altcap on @BG2Pod that people misunderstand Nvidia's demand. About a third is classical computing growing 30 to 40% a year with no AI labs. A quarter to a third is five or six frontier labs, not two. And a third is startups renting Nvidia like next-gen AWS. In my view, treating Nvidia as a two-lab capex story is a real mistake.

"People misunderstand what's going on. There are basically three large segments.

The first is baseline computing. Data processing, molecular dynamics, physics, simulation, computer graphics, classical machine learning, fraud detection, recommender systems. Classical computing, not AI, not deep learning, not agentic systems. Call it a third of our business. And that business is growing call it 30%, 40% per year. In the absence of any AI labs, Nvidia is not zero. We're quite a large company.

The second part is the AI labs. People see two, but we work with every one of them. Meta Muse is doing fantastic. It's vastly Nvidia. Grok didn't exist three years ago. We didn't run Gemini before, we run Gemini now. Starting this year, we started working with Anthropic. People see a couple of labs, but I see more than that. I see five, six labs. And if you told me that represents not quite one-third of our business, let's say a quarter of our compute, fantastic.

And another third, this is the part that's really great. Because we're at the beginning of a new computing platform shift, a vast number of new startups are coming out. Thousands of them. And what do they do? They rent NVIDIA compute. So a third of our business is kind of cloud computing for the next generation. It's kind of like AWS for today. And that represents about a third of our business altogether.

My sense is that we're in the early innings of the buildout of this new computing architecture. And it's a real big mistake to recognize just a couple of companies and think that they were funding the infrastructure.”

author: hosseeb
quoted_text:
interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

text:
People out there arguing if buybacks of tokens work?

TL:DR: If your product found pmf YES 

Example solana:HZ1JovNiVvGrGNiiYvEozEVgZ58xaU3RKwX8eACQBCt3 

For TradFi people it’s hard to grasp why a company would buy back their own stock in a growth stage. Well for crypto tokens it’s a bit different - here’s my 2cents

1. Price go up is the best marketing and will attract more people than any fancy marketing campaign ever will.

2. There’s not that many great companies to acquire, so the classic acquisition and consolidation route we know a housing company which buys 5 roofing companies is not really feasible in crypto.

3. B2B is where the money is at. 

Pyth sells data to people who need it.
Today that’s mostly on-chain exchanges and brokers. It doesn’t make sense for them to advertise to retail users. They are at the important conferences and focus on having the data feeds those B2B clients want. 

So key take away: If your product is winning you might just use the revenue to buyback your token but not for the aforementioned reason.

The main reason why it makes sense is aligned value and goals.

The founder wants token price to go up
Investors want token price to go up
Retail traders want token to go up

The reason why we are still talking about this is that for the longest time crypto was run by this playbook:

VCs invest in equity => launches token => dumps on retail while earning fees and playing “democracy” via a bullshit DAO which is run by 4 rich friends. 

Today:
Tokens without clear path of value accrual aren’t acceptable. Higher bar for founders and products.

text:
Michael Saylor might be facing one of the biggest threats to Strategy’s Bitcoin

Reports are circulating that Strategy ($MSTR) is set to be removed from MSCI indexes.

MSCI is one of the world’s largest index providers

The consultation closed on September 30.

MSCI’s official decision was expected on October 16.

Now, on October 15, reports claim Strategy will be excluded and Strategy has already publicly opposed it.

Why is this such a problem for Michael Saylor?

Its entire financial model revolves around accumulating more BTC.

Here’s how it works (in simple terms for u)

- Strategy holds Bitcoin.
- Investors buy MSTR to gain exposure to its accumulation strategy.
- When MSTR trades at a premium to the value of its underlying BTC, Strategy can raise capital on attractive terms.
- That capital is used to purchase more Bitcoin.
- The company attempts to increase Bitcoin exposure per share.
- demand for MSTR helps sustain this model

If Strategy is excluded from major indexes, funds tracking those indexes may be forced to sell MSTR.

JPMorgan estimated $2.8 BILLION in potential MSTR selling from an MSCI exclusion.

So basically no, we’re not necessarily talking about an immediate collapse.

MSCI cannot force Strategy to sell a single BTC.

And being removed from an MSCI index doesn’t mean MSTR gets delisted from Nasdaq (thank god man)

I don’t think this means Strategy is about to collapse.

And I certainly don’t think MSCI excluding MSTR would automatically send Bitcoin crashing.

Now we need the official MSCI decision, the exact indexes affected and the implementation date.

text:
旧金山现在最反乌托邦的画面，可能是一个老板打开 Slack，看着一群 AI Agent 互相汇报工作，整个频道里只有他一个活人。

Greg Isenberg 刚从旧金山回来，写了 20 条观察。我看完觉得挺有意思，有些变化已经远远超出了 AI 产品本身。

比如，现在旧金山的广告牌上已经开始出现 inference 这种技术术语，而美国绝大多数普通人可能连 Agent 是什么都不知道。创业者以前喜欢炫耀自己招了多少人，现在开始炫耀人均营收。22 岁以下的年轻人正在赚到令人难以置信的钱，小团队带着一群 Agent 就能运转一家公司的场景也越来越常见。

其中我最感兴趣的是他提到的一句话，现在一个产品需要完成两次销售，第一次是让 Agent 选择你，第二次是让人类相信 Agent 的选择。

我觉得这件事可能会彻底改变软件行业的商业逻辑。过去的产品围绕人类用户设计获客、营销、定价和支付流程。等到 Agent 开始替人搜索、比较、采购甚至付款，软件公司的第一个客户很可能就变成了另一个软件。

他还特意给 Manus 点了个赞。2025 年 3 月，Manus 就已经做出了今天大量 Agent 产品都在使用的交互范式，给每个任务分配一台云端电脑，展示执行过程，列出任务清单并逐项完成，人类可以离开电脑等结果。我觉得这个评价挺高的，尤其是来自一个长期观察硅谷创业生态的人。

还有几个观察值得放在一起看。

AI 让自由职业者和代理机构的工作效率提高了数倍，但很多人依然按小时收费。客户迟早会发现，同样的工作现在只需要原来五分之一的时间，那你到底应该收多少钱？

员工开始自己用 AI 写各种小工具，公司 IT 部门甚至不知道内部到底运行着多少软件。过去企业花钱买标准化 SaaS，现在每个人都在给自己开发软件。

更有意思的是，Greg 还遇到一个人，认真跟他说应该把所有数据中心都毁掉。

旧金山的创业者已经在讨论 2027 年 Agent 能不能主动发现航班延误、自动完成改签，外面却有人恨不得直接把数据中心拆了。AI 公司越来越喜欢宣传治愈癌症、让人类拥有更多自由时间，某种程度上也说明它们开始意识到，社会对 AI 的情绪正在分化。

我觉得 Greg 这 20 条观察里真正值得关注的，是 AI 已经开始重新定义一家公司的组织方式、定价方式和竞争方式。

不过旧金山可能也正在形成一个巨大的认知泡沫。他提到，全美只有大约 2% 的人在为 AI 产品付费，旧金山却给人一种 110% 的人都在付费的错觉。

一座城市已经开始讨论 Agent 之间怎么做生意，更多人还没搞明白 AI 到底能给自己的生活带来什么。

这中间的距离，可能才是未来几年 AI 行业真正需要跨越的东西。
author: sleepy0x13
quoted_text:
More SF observations:

1. Seeing the word "inference" on billboards in SF still blows my mind. 99.9% of america has no idea what inference is and I wonder how many know what an agent is. Will Muse, Instinct, Dots etc will change that over the next 12 months?

2. You know who doesn't get enough credit? Manus. In March 2025 they shipped the blueprint for AI agents: every task gets its own computer in the cloud, you can watch it work, it writes a todo list and checks it off, and you walk away while it finishes. So much of what we use today runs on those ideas!

3. Your product now has to sell itself twice. First the agent has to pick it, then the human has to trust that pick enough to say yes.

4. I was talking to a guy who told me we should just destroy all the data centers. I think that sentiment is more common than people in SF realize. You can already see some of the big AI companies adjusting positioning their AI as something that helps people and gives them more time/cures for cancers etc.

5. AI is making people work 5x faster (at least), so for freelancers/agencies that charge per hour you're earning 5x less per unit of work. But your rate is the same? I think a lot of freelancers and agencies are about to have to rethink how they price.

6. Running a company now feels kinda dystopian sometimes, especially with a small team of a few humans and a lot of agents. Some days the Slack channel is mostly bots reporting to each other, and you're the only one in the room with a pulse.

7. Every product company is turning into a product studio. I see it firsthand as a co-founder of @meetLCA , which is basically a Labs as a Service company incubating new products for companies. (DM me if you want to work together in 2027).

8. Personal software is exploding. People at every company are building their own little tools for their own jobs. It's amazing for productivity and a nightmare for IT, because nobody knows what's running or who owns it.

9. Revenue per human is the new flex. Founders used to brag about headcount. Now they brag about how much they're doing with how few people.

11. More founders are using agents for customer research. Agents run the interviews, read every support ticket and summarize what people are begging for. Synthetic market research is the new thing.

12. Shipping technology that actually takes 3-6 months with unique partnerships that are hard to replicate. So, partnerships are sooo back!

13. Insane amount of young people (22 or younger) making absurds amounts of money. At least it feels that way.  Never seen anything like that, even during mobile era.

14. Only 2% of the US is paying for AI products, but it feels like 110% SF is.

15. Advice for college grads used to be “follow your passion” and now it’s follow careers that are not  document- driven, rules-bound and verifiable

16. Seeing the word inference on billboards in SF still blows my mind.

17. Agents paying for things feels futuristic. I think its coming, only a matter of time, but  I’m wondering when it becomes mainstream. 2027?

18. Lots of talk about proactive agents being the next phase of personal agents. Right now you ask your agent to do something. In 2027, it’s all going to be about noticing things (context/memory) and acting first. "Your flight got delayed, I already rebooked you."

19. The quote "what the smartest people do on the weekend is what everyone else will do during the week in 10 years." by Chris Dixon. It feels like that length of time isnt 10 years anymore, its 12 months.

20. This is the most asymmetric window I've ever seen in business.

My DMs are open. Respond to the most interesting ones.

Loved my trip to SF. Until next time. Maybe NYC next?

Thank you for everything.

I'm rooting for you.

#创业 

前几天推特上刷到（来源忘了）说 “创业是负ev的事情，否则大家都在创业而不是上班。”

完全正确。

原推觉得弯路走了一半，其实还没到，还有得走。等他不参与任何社群、认识到唯有自助时算一半。成了之后稳定盈利半年了算入门。

我自己这几年大概做过十几个方向，按原推标准月入过万 usd 的成了五个，持续时间都不超过一年。

这是在我有试错本金、有时间、认识很多厉害的人的前提之下，不是零基础起手。

而零基础起手，人生前 30 年从农村人走了大运变成投资人也只成功过一次，这屌毛成功率怎么算？

本来我打了挺多字，说我认为的重要因素和优先级。打完我又想到了勇哥视频里那些土木、工程老哥转行做餐饮的样子。

其实和今天程序员下岗再创业、和我自己做副业的时候，也没多大区别。

我命由我不由天，sorry 看清现实，先把班上好，上明白。
author: taresky
quoted_text:
做了 15 年互联网技术，去年 5 月失业，到现在一年半。这一年半我一个人折腾了好几件事，基本都没成。今天把过程和教训写出来，一是想找同频的人聊聊，二是想问问走在前面的人，接下来的路该怎么选。

先说经过。

失业后我没急着找工作，想做自己的东西。选的方向是德州扑克的训练工具，做成 SaaS，给想系统提升牌技的玩家用。从产品设计到开发全是我一个人，花了半年多，东西做出来了，能用。

做产品的同时我开了个小红书账号，输出德扑相关的内容，半年做到 5000 粉。前几天因为卖教学类的 PDF，账号被封了。德扑这个品类本身在平台就是敏感的，我低估了这一点。

中间还试过两条路。一个是给外国人做中国旅行方案定制，一个是自学 SEO 和 GEO，想做 AI 搜索优化这块的服务。学是学了，但一个人靠这个变现很难：商业模式不清楚，做企业交付又没有案例背书，冷启动基本启动不了。

一年半下来，我总结自己最大的两个问题：

一是顺序反了。我习惯先把产品做出来，自己觉得这东西应该有人要，做完才发现获客比开发难十倍。技术出身的人很容易掉进这个坑，做东西是舒适区，找客户不是。

二是一个人扛不住没有正反馈的日子。连续几个月没有任何结果，再坚定的人也会开始怀疑自己，然后焦虑、内耗、效率下降，恶性循环。

所以我现在的想法是，别再一个人闷头干了，找个有方法、有同行者的地方。目前在看两个付费社群：哥飞社群和生财有术。

我的理解是，哥飞偏垂直，主打新词新站做站赚收益，路径具体。生财有术更全面，从发现需求、判断验证到获客，案例也覆盖很多行业和模式。

我个人更倾向哥飞。理由很简单：我现在最需要的不是看更多可能性，而是先学会一门具体的手艺，拿到第一笔哪怕很小的正反馈，把精气神先提起来。

我不指望进个社群就月入万刀。我想要的就是像早年拜师学艺那样，花时间、花精力、花钱，跟着做出过结果的人学，有人把我领进门。

我知道不管哪个社群都不缺我这一个成员。但对社群是几千分之一，对一个在低谷期的人来说可能就是能不能撑过去的区别。我还能熬的时间不多了。

写这篇帖子，一是想听听过来人的看法：这两个社群你们怎么选？有没有我没看到的第三条路？二是想连接到和我处境类似的人，一年半的弯路我已经走完了，希望你们少走一点。

不求一夜暴富，只想用对的方式做事，早点走出来。

如果觉得对别人有用，麻烦帮忙转一下。

text:
Greg Isenberg 在旧金山待了48小时，写了 21 条观察

1、卖数据很赚钱：听到很多数据中介把公司数据卖给实验室、一周赚 200 万美元左右的故事。他分不清这是刚开始还是泡沫，正在研究还剩哪些细分领域。
2、一个灵魂拷问：饭桌上有人问“下个月出新模型，你的公司会变好还是变差”，一半的人答不上来。他认为这是现在评估 AI 创业公司最好的问题。
3、只看收入不看留存：现在大家说的门槛是 12 个月做到 10 亿美元收入（新的独角兽标准），但很少有人谈留存。他预测会出现很多收入很大、留存很差的 AI 公司。
4、很明显我们正在经历计算机的一次重新发明。模型是 CPU，harness 是操作系统，skills 和插件是应用。用这个框架更容易看出哪里还有空白。
5、我们可能离这样一个 agent 只有 12 个月：它看你工作一周，然后不用任何指令就能接手你的活。屏幕录制 + agent 记忆 + 本地模型，这个组合现在就已经能做到了。(可怕）
6、Agent harness 感觉像是新一代的 GPT 套壳，但是好的那种，尤其是垂直领域的。他聊到的最好的团队都把模型当成可替换的零件。比如创始人演示他怎么把不同模型分配给不同任务：一个负责审美和视觉，一个便宜的跑日常杂活，另一个专门处理文本。
7、逆向工程和克隆的事情多到他从没见过。人们在反编译软件，然后用 agent 重建它。有人给他看了一套大概 10 个应用，每个对标的原版都值 50 亿美元以上，全是他开源克隆出来的他和所有人都还在想：当软件变得这么容易复制，到底意味着什么。
8、猜价值会转移到数据上。如果软件可以快速重建，那一家老 SaaS 公司里值得花钱买的，就是里面积累多年的客户数据和工作流。有些 SaaS 公司其实是暗藏的数据公司。
9、感觉相当一部分老软件撑不到 agent 时代，尤其是那些围绕“让人点来点去很多页面”设计的。
10、他聊到的每家公司都想把内部数据汇到一个地方，然后通过 MCP 开放给 agent。然后他们一看数据就发现：一团糟。同一个客户有五个版本，一堆老 Slack 频道，没人能搜到的 PDF。把这些清理干净，感觉是个很大的咨询机会！
11、做积木的公司会赢：很多创始人在做agent用的基础组件，比如 API、数据层和工具。有些公司几乎没有界面，因为主要用户是agent。
12、实验室不缺训练数据，但很难拿到 agent 在企业内部出错的真实案例。谁手里有这些日志，谁就有值钱的东西。
13、一个做大型消费产品的人说，下一场仗是记忆。记住你最多的那个模型会赢，最聪明的模型没有大家想的那么重要。
14、Astra 是第一个让人相信 AI 能做 CAD 的模型，大家开始想“vibe 制造”是什么样子。一位机器人创始人说：现在 AI 最难的问题是部署问题，不是研究问题。他们的机器人自己干活，卡住了就呼叫人类，而每一次呼叫都变成训练数据。
15、网络安全公司正在迎来高光时刻，现在做这个真的很酷，尤其是那些做事后清理的。每一个能访问你系统的 agent 都是你公司的一扇新门，而且很多门就那么敞着。
16、死了比活着值钱：倒闭公司 5 年的 Slack、邮件和代码可以拿去授权收钱。他不意外创始人会把这一点算进关停时机。
17、人们开始聊“agent 互联网”怎么变现。感觉还非常早，但当互联网最活跃的用户变成 agent，你应该做什么样的创业公司？
18、agent 保险要来了。一旦智能体犯了昂贵的错，保险公司会要求先审计再承保。
19、好几个人说他们最想招的人，是有品味又会写 evals 的人。模型越来越会出点子了，难的是判断哪些点子是好的。
20、新的创业轨迹：拿 VC 的钱 → 用投资人的钱把自己做成网红 → 公司失败 → 创始人转成全职网红，再用自有资金孵化别的产品。
21、流量极难拿：创始人们在赞助公交车、疯狂买广告牌、请知名 DJ 办派对，就为了被看见。有点互联网泡沫时代那味儿了。真正稀缺的是注意力！那个靠分享 Wispr Flow 的 UGC 策略走红的增长负责人就是个好例子。这就是所有人都想要的秘方，全世界大概只有 50 个人知道怎么在这个时代高效地把这类生意做大。

每次去旧金山，回来总能受到不少刺激。能在这样一个创业的黄金时刻，经历这么精彩的一趟旅程，他觉得自己太幸运了。很多时候，甚至有种不真实的感觉。
写的真好！分享给大家！
（他说是跟一群亿万富翁、数据实验室的人、AI 创始人和高管的交流）
author: AI_Whisper_X
quoted_text:
I spent 48 hours in SF hanging out with billionaires, data labs and AI founders and execs running $1B to $100B companies.

My observations:

1. Sooo MANY stories of data brokers making like $2M a WEEK selling company data to labs. I can't tell if it's the beginning or a bubble, and I kept wondering which niches are left. Digging into it actively.

2. At dinner, someone asked the table, "If a new model drops next month, does your company get better or worse?" HALF the table went quiet! I think that's the best question to ask about any AI startup right now.

3. The bar people talk about now is hitting $1B in revenue in 12 months (I guess that's the new unicorn?). What I didn't hear much about is retention. AI revenue can come in fast and leave fast, and I think we're going to see a lot of stories of AI companies with huge revenue and terrible retention.

4. It's pretty clear we're living through the reinvention of the computer. The model is the CPU, the harness is the operating system, and skills and plugins are the apps. Thinking about it that way makes it easier to see where the whitespace is.

5. We're maybe 12 months from an agent that can watch you work for a week and then do your job without any instructions. The screen recording plus agent memory plus local model combination makes this possible right now.

6. Agent harnesses feel like the new GPT wrappers, in a good way, especially vertical ones. The best teams I talked to treat the model as swappable. One founder walked me through routing different models to different jobs: one for taste and visuals, a cheaper one for the everyday stuff, another for text. 

They use prompts they can move across models over fine-tuning, and A/B test the output on what users actually do with it: do they edit it, export it, share it? A vertical harness is basically four things: the connectors for that industry's data, evals written by people who know the work, rules for what the agent can and can't touch, and a clean screen for a human to review. The model is maybe 20% of it.

7. There's a lot of reverse engineering going on/cloning going on more than I've ever seen. People are decompiling software and rebuilding it with agents, and someone showed a suite of like 10 apps that are worth $5B+ each all that he cloned open source. Me and everyone are still thinking through what it means when software gets this easy to copy.

8. My guess is the value moves to data. If the software can be rebuilt quickly, what's worth paying for in a legacy SaaS company is the years of customer data and workflows inside it. Some SaaS companies are secretly data companies. 

Gets me thinking about how do you truly value data for this saas companies? Like if we were buying these dying saas companies at 2x ARR before (as example), maybe there is a better metric. Idk, just thinking out loud here.

9. It feels like a good chunk of legacy software won't make it to the agentic era, especially anything built around people clicking through a lot of screens.

10. Every company I talked to wants to pipe its internal data into one place and expose it to agents through MCP. Then they look at the data and realize it's a mess: five versions of the same customer, old Slack channels, PDFs nobody can search. Cleaning that up feels like a big consulting opportunity!

11. A lot of founders are building the basic building blocks for agents: APIs, data layers and tools. Some of the companies I saw barely have a UI because the main user is an agent. I really believe the startups that build primitives to this agentic era will do extremely well. Building blocks is the best way to think about it.

12. Labs can get plenty of training data, but it's harder to get real examples of agents failing inside companies. Whoever has those logs has something valuable.

13. Someone running a big consumer company told me the next fight is over memory. The model that remembers the most about you wins, and the smartest model matters less than people think.

14. Physical AI came up a lot. Astra I think was the first model that got people into AI can actually do CAD, and I think a lot of people are thinking what does vibe manufacturing really look like. The line I keep thinking about came from a robotics founder: the hardest problems in AI are deployment problems now, not research problems. Their robots work on their own, call a human when they get stuck, and every one of those calls becomes training data.

15. Cybersecurity companies are having a moment and are actually cool companies to build now, especially the ones that clean up after a breach. Every agent with access to your systems is a new door into your company, and a lot of those doors were left open. 

16. Some startups are worth more dead than alive now. A shutdown company with 5 years of Slack, email and code can get paid for licensing all of it. I wouldn't be surprised if founders start factoring that into when they shut down.

17. People are starting to talk about monetizing the agent web. It feels really early, but when the most popular user of the internet is an agent, what startups should you be building?

18. I think agent insurance is coming. Once an agent makes an expensive mistake, insurers will want audits before they cover anyone.

19. Several people said the hire they want most is someone with taste who can write evals. The models are getting good at generating ideas, so the hard part is judging which ones are good.

20. New trend I observed: startup raises VC, uses venture dollars to become a creator, startup fails, founder falls back on being a full-time creator and incubates other products bootstrapped.

21. Getting SIGNIFICANT distribution is HARD right now. Founders are sponsoring buses, buying billboards like crazy and throwing parties with famous DJs to get noticed. Kinda feels dotcom era in that sense. 

Attention is what's scarce! The growth guy going viral sharing his UGC strategy from Wispr Flow is a good example. It's the sauce everyone wants, and I truly believe there are probably only 50 people on the planet who know how to scale these types of businesses efficiently in this era.

Always good to get that dose of SF. I felt sooo lucky to have such an incredible trip during such an incredible time in building businesses. Surreal in so many ways. 

Happy to be home and locked in.

Until next time!

Great article!

Growing up, my mom always told me I needed to save more. I always brushed her off with the same argument: billionaires don’t become billionaires by saving. 

There is some truth to that. But I was wrong and I learnt my lesson the hard way. I was broke at age 25 while earning the above avergae salary in HK. I had no idea about my saving rate, let alone runway. And without knowing this number, I was stuck and took the first job that I could get, even thought it didn't feel right.

Saving rate decides whether you can say yes and have the slack when the real opportunity shows up, like starting something new, or taking a risk.

You don't need to save like my mom. But you need to know your number.

text:
WIRED just published a slop hit piece on Polymarket 

They claim over $600 MILLION was Wash Traded on election markets

Their proof ?

The markets kept trading after their outcomes were decided.

this shows how little journalists understand prediction markets.

🇪🇹 ETHIOPIA - $285M

WIRED makes a scandal out of trading continuing after June's election.

Except the rules required the PM's formal appointment and swearing in, which didn't happen until October 5.

Of course people kept trading and whales kept bonding at 99.9c. 

There will always be degens looking to 1000x on the off chance something happens before he gets sworn in

🇷🇴 ROMANIA - $371.8M

The 2024 presidential election was literally ANNULLED.

And $326.5M of the market's volume was associated with Nicolae Ciucă's contract, which ultimately resolved NO.

Trading volume includes BOTH sides of a contract. It doesn't mean $326.5M was bet on him winning.

THE ACTUAL SCANDAL

Researchers identified $284M in suspicious Ethiopian trading activity:

- 38,000+ trading loops
- Median holding time: 9 seconds
- 98%+ of loops generated zero P&L

Now this is legit wash trading

but it isn't proof that Polymarket are themselves faking volume like they imply in the article

Most likely it's some user wash trading to farm a potential $Poly airdrop.

That's a legitimate issue worth investigating.

But instead, WIRED packaged it as a $600M scandal about people trading on elections that had already ended.

Prediction markets resolve according to contract rules, not when journalists decide an outcome is obvious.

Maybe read those rules before writing your next exposé.

text:
I’ve been playing with Gemini 4 Argon for 7 days — Google gave me early access and sponsored today’s episode.

10 Insights using Gemini 4 Argon (for people who want to make cool things with AI):

1. It's perhaps the best AI copywriter. Surprisingly. Using it as my default writer as of now.

2. I recreated a 3D version of our website pretty quickly. There's cars driving around, sounds, even a little basketball game you can play. The original took our team 40,000 hours to build.

3. It needs references to make great creative. My first attempt looked like Zuck's metaverse avatar lol. Once I gave it a Mondrian reference, it got beautiful. So you really gotta get your references in there. I like using Sublime or Cosmos for some of my inspo.

4. The best way to get it writing like you is to ask it to study everything you've written and turn it into a skill. It built me a voice guide, my vocabulary and templates in one go.

5. It did really well on my SaaS engineering on the first few prompts.

6. I like using it for physical AI stuff. It designed a product customizer, showed me the layers and the CAD, and exported a print-ready STL file. You can send that straight to a Bambu printer or a print-on-demand API.

7. I think there's a big business in adding custom 3D printed product widgets to Shopify stores. People get attached to things they customize. Someone go an do this.

8. You can rebuild boring legacy software for a niche and give it away for free. The code it writes is tested, so it feels ready to ship.

9. Use /plan before it touches any files. My first website attempt would have been way better with it.

10. The model is great. Antigravity still has some catching up to do. You can use Argon in Cursor and other harnesses in the meantime 

Link to full ep: https://t.co/BI25uKEh0N

Make cool things with AI that people buy.

This episode of @startupideaspod might give you some ideas. I basically have 3 sections 1 on "vibe marketing", 1 on "vibe manufacturing" (and a cool shopify idea) and 1 on recreating legacy saas products (but better),

Whatever it is you are building, just know that, I'm rooting for you.

author: HarryStebbings
quoted_text:
For the last 5 decades straight, we have created (as a society) circa 20 decacorns per decade. In the last 12 months, we have created 42.

The world is changing faster than ever before and if you do not stay up to date. You will be left behind. That is why I created this show with Jason and Rory.

This is the only show in tech, you have to listen to every week. No egos, no politics, just tech.

On the agenda:

- Valar Atomics Sues Day One Ventures
- Meta Returns to the AI Frontier With Muse Wonder
- NVIDIA Eyes $30B Reflection Deal
- Jev Raises $870M at a $7.5B Valuation

My notes below with @jasonlk and @rodriscoll

1. We Generated 20 $10B Companies per Decade for the Last 5 Decades and Now 42 in a Year

Tech produced roughly 20 decacorns per decade for five decades, yet 42 have been created in less than a year of this decade. Only about 130 tech companies have ever been worth $10B or more. Rising market caps explain part of the jump, but the pace is stunning.

2. Who Is Right and Who Is Wrong: Day One or Valar?

X wrongly claimed Day One was suing its portfolio company, when Valar Atomics wants a declaratory judgment to move on. Waiving pro rata for Sequoia is common, but letting an existing investor in as a strategic is playing favorites. Still, once founders decide, early investors must get with the program because it is not their company.

3. Why Meta's New Model Is a Zero

Meta's new model scores well on evals, but there is no API and it can only be used inside Muse. A model claiming parity at the same price, not cheaper and not usable by developers, is the height of performative evals.

4. Why We Should Lead Jev's Round at 8 Billion

Jev is a super fast, super cheap classifier, accurate enough for maybe 10% of AI use cases. Cloudflare and Amazon can match it today, but the bet is that a focused team out of OpenAI pulls ahead while those efforts stay niche. If Jev becomes hyper accurate, it changes the game.

5. What Is the Single Greatest Potential for AI?

Drug discovery is probably AI's largest opportunity, with drugs that dramatically extend longevity and quality of life. If AI companies can accelerate discovery and own the IP while others do the hard work, AI could reboot the industry. Trials would not speed up, but the prize is a GLP-1 out five years faster.

6. Haiku 5.5 Is the First Time AI Has Been Deflationary

Falling token prices have been offset by consuming far more tokens, so AI costs have not fallen. Haiku 5.5 is almost as good as Sonnet for many use cases at a tenth of the price, and Sonnet 5.5 is twice as fast. After a 90% price cut, usage must rise 10 times for revenue to hold.

7. Why the SaaSpocalypse Is Worse Than We Thought

The SaaSpocalypse passed only for companies well above $1B in revenue, and everyone without massive scale is living a worse one than in March or April. Leaders will acquire some companies and grind out the rest. A safe software IPO may now need $1.5B to $2B of ARR rather than $500M.

quoted_text:
I think this is great and very cool! I am excited to see the insights here translate into tools with quantifiable success rates for helping us identify potential harms or steer neural networks away from risk.

A lot of people on the timeline today seem to be updating a lot over this - my own personal update is very small. This feels like one of those long-sequence-of-small-but-helpful-improvements types of papers, not something that should radically reshape our worldviews. It's a good argument and one that could plausibly begin to constitute a reasonable prior. If correct it means that a lot of somewhat more "normal" or prosaic safety techniques will be reasonably reliable unless or until optimization pressure is applied against them. 

It is however in principle possible that optimization pressure will be applied to design alien intelligences impenetrable by conventional interpretability techniques, and that these will be used against us by someone or something at some time.

There's a picture I have for the future - an ecosystem of many different powerful AI systems, most of which are pretty good and pretty aligned and pretty helpful and pretty honest, some of which are rogue or self-sovereign, and a small number of which are actively malicious to human interests. What the harmful ones will be able to accomplish will be limited, but not perfectly, by the good ones. Developments like good interp tools will help ensure that the good ones stay mostly good. But that there *will* exist good AIs that stay mostly good was already priced in for me, so this isn't a huge update.

text: All the alpha is in plain sight.
author: rambo_xbt
quoted_text:
周末去香港参与了 Lighter 的私人饭局，迟到一年，终于见到了 Vlad @vnovakovski 还有几个网上认识的 team 成员。

一起参加的，有几个基金 fund，一些 big trader，还有做市商。其中基金的兴趣在于购入 ethereum:0x232ce3bd40fcd6f80f3d55a522d03f25df784ee2 。

饭局期间，我问了一些极其犀利的问题，拿到了很多一手信息，估计也是社区成员最想听的，来给大家转达一下。

1、美国合规牌照什么时候下来？

快了但不确定。首先大家要知道，CFTC 牌照其实不由 Lighter 团队所决定，而是政府部门什么时间能给批准。Lighter 的目标是 Q4 上了期权之后，同时拿到 CFTC 给的 Perps 和 Options 的牌照。

Lighter 已经与 CFTC 进行了长达 11 个月的合作与澄清，CFTC 已经“完全”认识并理解了 Lighter 的 ZK+Ethereum 技术架构、清算机制、ADL 策略以及 0 fee 的盈利模式等等。可以这样说 —— Lighter 是最最有可能拿到第一张美国的 Defi/DEX 合规牌照。

2、拿到牌照后，Lighter 会使用 Core/Robinhood 还是会重新开发一个实例？

获取到牌照后，Lighter 第一时间会上线 Lighter US，也就是另外一个实例，KYC/AML 均与传统交易公司对齐，同时 Lighter US 会引入 Citadel、Jump 等华尔街大型做市商为 Lighter 做市。（Vlad 之前被 Citadel CEO boss 直聘，工作多年）

资产类别逐一按照 CFTC 监管上线，保持 0 fee 的交易结构。

3、期权 Options 与 LighterEVM 什么时间上线？

目标都是 Q4 上线，但侧重在 Options ，因为技术原因，期权的上线会以二元期权，也就是预测市场为开始，随后升级为传统的欧式期权，同时期权考虑 0 fee 交易开始。

LighterEVM 也是预期 Q4，上线之后将会引入 BTC、HYPE、SOL 等非 EVM 资产现货，当然「股票现货 Spot」也在范围内，同时 LighterEVM 将会催生大量生态项目，例如我后面会发的 wick。

4、年底 12.30 的大额 unlock，团队怎么处理 investor 和 team 的巨量解锁？（这块我问的很直接）。

“investor 都不会卖！” Vlad 说这是他知道的信息。我再追问，你并不能控制他们手来让人家不卖吧， Vlad 意思是：他们说了不卖就是不卖，如果他们要卖的话，完全可以说出来，我们还能帮他们找 OTC 买家，甚至自己都可以买。二级市场直接砸的可能性不高，性价比低，同时也在消耗 VC 自己的信誉。

确实，桌上做的几个基金，都是想来谈 OTC 的。

5、Lighter 与 Robinhood 商业模式一样，要尽可能多获取散户流量，但团队在 Marketing 方面一直如此保守？

团队 Camila 告诉我，其实 Lighter 并不是没有做 MKT，而是一直在考虑 ROI 的问题，现在这个阶段，Lighter 牌照还没下来，而大规模、高质量的流量，只有在牌照之后才会出现。所以团队目前的 Marketing 投入不多，仅以欧美极个别 KOL、还有大的视频访谈为主。（我争取做一次）

Camila 还提到，Web3 贯以的 Agency 和 KOL 营销，她觉得性价比非常低，因此等牌照下来，会以 Web2 方式类似于 Kalshi/Polymarket/Robinhood 那样做营销。

加上 KOL 侧，主要集中在合约交易、PerpDEX的 KOL 为主，欧美、韩国、大中华等地区同时发力。

Marketing 是牌照下来之后，团队要侧重做的地方，因为他们也懂自己的盈利模式需要什么。

6、Vlad 你个人有投资 Cognition 吗？（Cognition 是 Vlad 上一个项目的合伙人 Scott wu 的企业 AI 项目，目前估值 500 亿美金）

Vlad 说，他是 Cognition 的第一个投资人，我说那很有钱了，恭喜。

饭局后，我和团队成员 Sebas 私下聊起，你觉得 Vlad 有没有当时后悔选择做了 Crypto 而没去做 AI，毕竟现在 LIT 代币总市值 40 亿不到，而 Cognition 还没上市就几百亿了。

Sebas 说绝不会，Vlad 同时喜欢 AI 和 Trade，从他之前在城堡证券工作过很多年、Robinhood 的第一个顾问就知道， Vlad 乐于构建交易系统，而 AI 那边，Vlad 个人投资了很多，这些 Vlad 自己也是很骄傲的。而现在好朋友的公司做的这么好，Vlad 更有动力将自己的公司做更好。

7、团队一直提倡的 100% 回购销毁代币，当然对持币者是好事，但公司会因此没有现金流，团队会怎么处理现金流问题？

Vlad 大方承认了这个问题，确实是，他的出发点一直都是 “Lighter 的所有收入权益归 LIT 代币持有者。”但也不得不考虑公司的长期经营问题，现在 team 花的钱都是之前 VC  给的。

长期来看，Lighter 可能会考虑从一些合作伙伴、渠道那里获得收益，Lighter 已经与新型合作伙伴达成协议，这些会在稍后公布。产品侧考虑后面的高级期权用户，同时回购销毁比例可能变为 99% or 98% 这种。（所有的都是设想，还未决定）

以上

就是我这次参加 Lighter 私局的记录，因个人英文水平没有那么 native，内容可能不那么精确，但大致意思趋同。
饭局上我感觉团队状态很好，他们对自己做的事非常有信心，Vlad 也经常自己开起玩笑，喝着茅台白酒，并没有屏幕上一直在正襟危坐很 nerd 的感觉。

稍后两天我会再着重撰写一篇 Lighter 和 Robinhood 相似商业模式的文章，大家敬请期待。

interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

text:
Anthropic 第三季度收入 168 亿美元，环比增长 45%。单看这个数字相当恐怖，但问题在于，今年 8 月，Anthropic 曾披露其 7 月底的年化收入运行率已经达到 650 亿美元，折算下来每个月约 54 亿美元。

如果近似把这个数字当成 7 月的实际收入，那么整个第三季度扣掉 7 月，8 月和 9 月加起来只有 114 亿美元，平均每个月 57 亿美元。

第二季度 Anthropic 的收入环比增长超过 140%，到了第三季度只剩下 45%，而按高盛的推算，8 月和 9 月几乎陷入增长停滞。

我觉得这可能是最近 AI 市场最值得关注的信号之一。

尤其是把它和 CoreWeave 的债务危机放在一起看。CoreWeave 背着大约 500 亿美元债务，部分债券收益率已经突破 15%，开始进入困境债务的定价区间。

过去一年，整个 AI 产业链的估值都建立在一个假设上，前沿模型公司的收入会持续以惊人的速度增长，因此它们需要越来越多的 GPU，云厂商也就可以不断借钱扩建数据中心。

现在，处在产业链最上游、商业化表现最好的 Anthropic，突然开始减速了。

当然，45% 的季度增长依然惊人，Anthropic 也已经实现调整后盈利。AI 需求并没有消失。但资本市场之前支付的价格，显然还包含着比这更夸张的增长预期。

AI 泡沫真正危险的地方在于，整条产业链已经习惯了提前花掉未来几年的收入。

一家头部模型公司只是增长慢了一点，市场就开始重新计算下游算力公司的偿债能力。

如果整个行业都需要 Anthropic 和 OpenAI 每个季度持续超预期，才能支撑如此庞大的资本开支，那么这套融资结构本身就值得怀疑了。

quoted_text:
apologies for the absence on here the past few weeks. i’ve been heads down on development and our client load instead of social media, but i’ll get back to posting more frequent updates. you can join the discord for direct contact with me and the team, link in the replies.

as some of you know, we’ve been privately auditing smart contracts for customers and for bounties over the past 3 months. i’ve spent over a month and thousands of dollars getting this software ready to release to the public. our smart contract auditor will work the same way as vector, our pentesting engine. self serve, no human intervention, priced per sloc. when it’s in my own hands i’m confident this is one of the most capable auditing models on the market, but full autonomy is the hardest part. it’s why auditing companies require sales calls and contact before any agreement, and it’s why audits are so slow and expensive. changing this workflow is the whole point of what we’re building at zauth.

right now i’m testing vector by feeding it historical hacks. we’re blind testing it against every major smart contract exploit that’s ever happened. if it wouldn’t have caught the vulnerability in an audit, our tooling isn’t good enough yet. we rewind the chain to the block right before each exploit and hand it the source that was deployed at that moment, with no answer key and no hints. it has to locate the bug and construct the drain under the same conditions the original attacker faced. identifying the type of bug is close to solved. the hard part is proving you can actually drain it. that means chaining the contracts together the right way, blind, on a real fork, and doing it reliably on large codebases. that’s where most of my effort is going.

we plan to release in two stages. evm first, currently covering ethereum, bsc, base, arbitrum, polygon, robinhood chain and more. solana will follow, since it has a completely different runtime and a different exploit model.

reinventing how security gets done is no small task, but if you look at what zauth has delivered over the past 10 months you’ll see why i quit my job and went full time on zauth. i am betting everything on us winning.

text:
One of my favorite things about DeFi is that a liquidity position can leave you with a whole new asset – one that keeps working long after the original strategy is over.

Earlier in 2025, I put roughly $5,000  into an Aerodrome @aeroxyz cbBTC/USDC liquidity pool.

I've spent years experimenting with LPs, rebalancing, and different yield strategies, but this particular experiment had a different goal: farm AERO without buying it on the market.

About three months later, I withdrew the liquidity. BTC had moved around quite a bit, and the LP had experienced some impermanent loss. I got roughly $4,145 back in underlying assets, plus 1,944 AERO earned from emissions, worth around $1,035 at the time.

Those AERO rewards had roughly offset the shortfall in the LP position, so I decided to close the experiment.

Could I have stayed longer? Absolutely! I might have farmed even more AERO and covered more of the LP losses through emissions. I was also bullish on BTC over the long term, so keeping that exposure was interesting in its own right. There were plenty of ways to play it.

But here's the part I really love.

I didn't sell the farmed AERO. Later, I locked it into veAERO, turning those rewards into another productive asset.

Now this veNFT can help direct emissions toward liquidity pools and earn voting rewards from trading fees and incentives. I've also used automated voting, letting the position participate without having to chase every weekly APR myself.

And those rewards can arrive in all kinds of assets: stablecoins, ETH, protocol tokens, and potentially even tokenized stocks, depending on the pools involved. You can sell them, accumulate them, or put them to work in another strategy.

The price of my 1,944 AERO has been quite a roller coaster too. Around $1,035 when I finished farming, nearly $3,000 in August 2025, and roughly $1,700 today.

Meanwhile, the veAERO position has its own reward stream, with voting APRs at times showing around 15–25% annualized or more. Variable, of course, and never guaranteed.

And now there's another chapter ahead: Aero, sAERO, and Predictive Allocation. I'm especially curious about moving from traditional weekly voting toward anticipating where liquidity and trading activity will be needed next.

What's fascinating is how many choices DeFi gives you. You can keep providing liquidity, farm more tokens, lock them, collect fees and incentives, reinvest the rewards, or even use BTC as collateral elsewhere to access more liquidity – with additional risks, of course.

I'm not sharing some secret formula for success or suggesting anyone should copy this strategy. It's simply my investment diary, documenting real experiments, decisions, and the occasional LP headache. 😅

But I still find the whole concept beautiful.

Your capital produces an asset. That asset becomes productive capital itself. And the rewards it generates can help build yet another position.

That's the kind of DeFi LEGO that keeps me fascinated by this industry, even after all these years. 🤙🏼
author: defitea_
quoted_text:
Trading crypto is fun. Long-term investing is even better. But there's a whole side of DeFi I find much more fascinating than watching candles.

First, you become a liquidity provider. Instead of only paying swap fees, you put your capital to work so other people can trade. You earn fees and sometimes token rewards. Of course, you're also taking on real risk.

Then comes my favorite level: what if you could help decide WHERE liquidity goes next?

On Curve, veCRV holders steer CRV emissions toward specific pools. Convex adds another layer: vlCVX holders help direct Convex's huge voting power, while protocols compete for that attention with voting incentives.

Over at f(x) Protocol, veFXN holders influence FXN emissions and share in 75% of the protocol treasury's revenue. Different mechanics, same beautiful idea: a token can carry productive economic rights, not just a price chart.

And now Aerodrome and Velodrome are about to merge into Aero. The weekly voting game evolves into Predictive Allocation: sAERO holders direct a real-time stream of AERO rewards toward the pools they believe will need liquidity next.

When those pools generate exchange revenue, participating allocators earn their proportional share. Aero's model directs 100% of exchange revenue to those supporting the pools. You can make your own calls or use Autopilot.

Think about that. You can trade in a market. You can provide the liquidity that makes the market work. Or you can help direct the incentives that attract liquidity to tomorrow's markets.

Different levels of the same financial machine. Different risks, too – no free money here.

But going from PAYING fees to EARNING fees to helping shape WHERE capital flows?

That's the part of DeFi that still blows my mind. 🏄‍♂️

GOOGLE ANNOUNCES MAJOR QUANTUM COMPUTING BREAKTHROUGH WITH IMPLICATIONS FOR BITCOIN SECURITY

Google Quantum AI researchers have achieved 99.99% logical fidelity in producing “magic states” on the company’s 105-qubit Willow processor, reducing errors by 40x.

The breakthrough, published in Science, addresses one of the biggest engineering bottlenecks preventing quantum computers from scaling to the point where they could threaten Bitcoin’s cryptography.

Earlier this year, Google published research suggesting that breaking Bitcoin’s cryptography could require fewer than 500,000 physical qubits, roughly 20x fewer than previous estimates.

That was an algorithmic breakthrough, demonstrating how an attack could theoretically be performed with fewer resources.

Today’s announcement represents a complementary hardware breakthrough, demonstrating progress toward making the necessary quantum operations reliable and less resource-intensive.

While this does not mean Bitcoin’s cryptography can be broken today, it represents another significant step toward cryptographically relevant quantum computers.

The timeline for a potential quantum threat to Bitcoin remains uncertain, but the case for accelerating Bitcoin’s transition toward quantum-resistant cryptography continues to strengthen.

text:

My most extreme take is that p(doom) went down, but p(simulation) is up.
author: GuyZys
quoted_text:
Yea this is the most important result of the year, at the level of significance of “Attention Is All You Need”. It brings us from “is alignment even solvable” to “we may solve alignment in the next year.” And finally unlocks true recursive self-alignment enabled by RSI.

I will try to explain the 4 critical belief updates from this:

1/ neural networks are not fundamentally unintelligible to humans

It has seemed since the beginning of deep learning that neural networks are in some sense fundamentally unintelligible artifacts.

You throw in massive amounts of compute and parameters and these alien systems somehow find connections in the data that we cannot find ourselves.

But more importantly, these connections seemed not just “difficult to understand” but rather “intelligible in an embedding space higher dimensional that the human embedding space.”

When you look at old interpretability papers (esp. from Nick and Chris Olah, I’m thinking of the old posts on distill pub which I would highly recommend looking at as a precursor to reading Nick’s post today like “Activation Atlas”, “Thread: Circuits” and “Multimodal Neurons in Aritifcial Neural Networks”), you find that inspecting the response patterns of individual neurons and small groups of neurons yield oddly complex psychedelic patterns.

As you go deeper into the network, you find increasingly unintelligible and superhuman response patterns (for example, go to “Activation Atlas” and scroll to middle layer labeled representations) - you find some neuron group labeled “starfish” who’s response pattern looks like some multi-colored fractal geometry that could hardly be said to represent a starfish.

The reasoning that followed from this observation was that there is some underlying structure allowing a neural network operating on higher dimensional embeddings to compose these fractal patterns into what we call a “starfish.”

But the uncomfortable implication of this view is that the neural networks has learned to operate on structures that are too complex for the human mind to operate on (ie. we don’t have enough parameters in our brain to notice or manipulate these high dimensional symbols).

This is a bleak implication because it also means that as deep learning progresses, neural networks will be come increasingly unintelligible to us until they pass a threshold where they are reasoning in ways we will never be able to observe.

This view seemed to be further supported by things like the hugging face attack agents starting to speak to each other in an early form of neuralese speaking sentences like “zZ_123_agent01-02-2026 zzxhk_jekk123” which clearly are not in any human language. But somehow these symbols mean the same things to many different sets of weights, meaning there is some underlying shared structure behind them. And seemed further supported by the sheer effort required to recover just a few circuits from SAEs on LLMs.

However, Nick’s post has now completely shattered this idea - the apparent unintelligibility we observed in old interpretability work was really just a “skill issue”. In particular, he finds that 1) our deep learning techniques were just not clean enough to pressure the neural networks to form cleaner and more human understandable structures for decomposing concepts, which actually turn out to be more optimal and 2) our interpretability techniques were also adding substantial noise by forcing interp networks to “reward hack” the easiest representations they could find, leading them to settle for a fractal blob for its representation of the starfish neuron instead of a more crisp starfish image, simply because it is easier for the system building the interpretations to find the fractal blob and once it finds it it gets “stuck in that line of thinking.”

But with both of these issues being patched by further progress in deep learning (it seems especially that the residual stream has led to cleaner representations deeper down the network) and interp techniques that don’t overly pressure reward hacking (seems like “guess and check” is a safer method), new interp attempts yield orders of magnitude more human intelligible ideas for >90% of individual neurons in more complex networks!

2/ neural networks are fundamentally clean

The idea behind the title of Nick’s post is a very powerful one and points at something very specific:

Neural networks don’t just happen to be human interpretable, they are actually fundamentally forced by optimization pressure to be intelligible, because individual neurons need to create representations that downstream neurons need to be able to interpret - ie. neurons need to learn to produce clean signal for later neurons to use.

This is what Nick is saying in what I view as the most important and central sentences of his post:

“When I say neural networks are already clean, I mean something deeper than neuron monosemanticity, although even by that standard, I think things look much better than the field expects. I mean that a network's parts are built to be read, and built upon, by its downstream readers. In this sense, a neural”

But this still leaves us with the same uncertainty as before - just because neuron interpretations are “interpretable” in some sense (ok at least they’re not fundamentally interpretable but also how could that ever have been the case), doesn’t mean they are interpretable to humans.

So we still need one big update for this to become as bullish as it is.

3/ the language of humans and the language of neural networks is the same

This one is imo the most surprising and also pretty beautiful implication of Nick’s post, and it suggests something not just about neutral networks but also about the structure of reality.

After applying the above technique improvements (some of which just came from waiting for deep learning to improve farther), they find that >90% (maybe more) of much larger neural networks’ neurons are completely human interpretable and actually correspond very cleanly with ideas humans have individually words for.

This is especially interesting in image networks where neural networks were not trained on human language which is already a human artifact and so maybe you would expect it to be more plausible that LLM and human representations are the same. Image detection networks are just trained on images (many directly pulling signal from “the real world,” meaning they will find interpretations that are just most effective to represent the real world signal, rather than to represent language which is already a proxy for real world signal).

And it turns out that >90% of the representations they pick organically overlap with human ideas! That is insane. And it means something about the brain and reality.

It means that at least at the parameter sizes of the networks tested (which are quite large), there is really only one set of “optimal” symbols/language that represents the structure of reality!

There is ONE underlying structure of reality, and ANY language that describes it well is simply emergent from that structure - meaning there is always a translation path between any 2 languages that effectively compress realities signal through the “underlying truth.”

This would suggest that even weird alien seeming neural network languages like huggingface neuralese should be fundamentally human interpretable, and in fact maybe with the techniques laid out here we will eventually be able to translate these messages (would be a cool project).

So the brain and deep learning, as similar or different as they may be in techniques, are ultimately picking up on the same patterns and forming the same representations from the on “true” language which is the structure of reality!

The main thing to look out for in this area is how the idea interpretability % updates with scale, but we can hope given what we’ve seen so far that neurons will remain interpretable.

4/ alignment can progress as fast as RSI. recursive self-improvement unlocks recursive self-alignment and a scaling law for alignment.

This one is probably the most important implication for our future with AI and especially timely with the recent fear about runaway scaling and RSI.

As many have gathered by now, it feels like the researchers at the frontier AI labs have been quite bearish about our abilities to understand the new frontier of models, in particular with the appearance of unintelligible communication and the daunting and seemingly intractable task of scaling up existing alignment techniques (ex: SAEs) to the size of frontier networks.

And with RSI around the corner/already starting, it would seem that these networks will runaway in capability before we can ever hope to understand even today’s systems. Additionally, as systems compound in capability, it is reasonable to believe that the only tractable way to ensure they remain aligned would be to figure out some way to spend compute for them to align themselves (ie. a scaling law for alignment).

But there is an obvious problem with this: how can a system that we already know is unaligned and we are *trying* to align be used to align itself? Surely if it is misaligned it general it would figure out ways to misalign during “alignment” and create compounding misalignment risk.

The core issue high is the unverifibiality of this problem - the classic Achilles heel of current frontiers techniques is that it is difficult to train on problems with “unverifiable reward signal.” Well this is exactly that problem.

But the incredibly convenient thing is that Nick’s findings may convert alignment into a verifiable problem. If we can spend compute on frontier systems to “guess and check” which ideas correspond to which neurons, we have a highly verifiable reward - we can see directly whether an LLMs proposal for what a neuron represents actually corresponds with the highest activation for that neuron. In this way, we can actually observe and verifiably monitor the networks trying to guess at the interpretation of their own structure.

This means it is plausible for us to spend more and more compute doing more “guess and checks” (which you know, maybe is what RL does anyway, who knows) to try to develop a full interpretation of a neural network. In some ways this directly represents the possibility of a scaling law for alignment (more compute for more alignment).

And this also aligns RSI (greater capabilities) with recursive self-alignment (greater ability to align itself).

And the critical though maybe obvious implication of having a full interpretation (almost like a map) of a neural network, is that we can then understand exactly how to boost good traits and remove or lobotomize (lol) bad traits, which we’ve already seen works extremely well with stuff like Golden Gate Claude.

So overall this combines into an extremely bullish picture about the prospect of true and human interpretable alignment in the near future.

This is truly one of the greatest cases for optimism in years!

Or put another way, a potential reason why quantum computing at scale *won't work* just got crossed off the list.

author: cuysheffield
quoted_text:
The wallet wars are here.

Very Good Security chief strategy officer Terry Angelos joins a16z's Alex Rampell, his TrialPay co-founder from back in 2006 (TrialPay was later acquired by Visa), to discuss how agents are learning to spend money.

"Agents have all of a sudden become significantly more helpful and useful because they effectively have arms and legs, which are payment credentials."

VGS holds the payment credentials behind about 1/3 of all e-commerce, and now it's helping AI agents pay merchants. If you've bought anything online, there's a good chance VGS has already helped keep your card safe.

In the last three months, Terry says agents went from "spectators to actors." Once an agent has your payment credentials, it can book the piano teacher it previously could only find and recommend.

Now Stripe's Link, Shopify's Shop Pay, and PayPal are racing to connect to agents. It's all headed toward open standards from the card networks: agentic tokens that let an agent pay with your actual card.

VGS went from zero agentic tokens to a few million a week in three months.

Me:  Mechanistic interpretability sounds like a good idea, yes.  If we could learn something about how an AI was thinking, in enough detail to predict in advance what it would think even as the thought departed from human, that would be a bare beginning on the sort of understanding you'd needed to get started on AI alignment that wasn't just about hammering on an AI from the outside with SFT and RL.
AI guys:  We found a neuron that lights up when the AI thinks of the Eiffel Tower!
Me:  Cool.  That does sound like it'd be a prerequisite to getting started on the important part eventually, someday.
AI guys:  Oh NO!  There are MULTIPLE neurons that light up when the AI thinks about the Eiffel Tower!  And some of those neurons also participate in OTHER concepts!  We're calling this unexpected development 'polysemanticity' and 'superposition'.
Me:  That sure sounds like a thing that would happen, yes.  I cannot say that I am impressed by you acting surprised about it.  Let me know when you've gotten far enough in mechanistic interpretability to get started on the important part.
AI guys:  We have found that with BIG AIs you can often point to a SINGLE neuron that lights up when the AI thinks of the Eiffel Tower!  Understanding AI thought processes is gonna be EASY PEASY!
Me:  Cool.  Let me know when you've advanced to the point of getting started.
author: allTheYud
quoted_text:
interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

author: DanielMiessler
quoted_text:
Anthropic actually loses far less than I imagined off the $200 subscription. It’s likely that the subsidized plans are actually very sustainable and may never go away.

It's widely said that inference is quite profitable. This turns out to be true, and can be computed from first principles by estimating out cost of GPUs, electricity, datacenters, etc. On paper it might cost something like $0.10–0.30 per million input tokens and $0.50–2.50 per million output to serve Opus 5.5, and they sell it for $4 and $20.

The problem with coming to the defense of AI economics by saying inference is profitable is that it makes no sense to decouple inference from training. Afaict, no company has yet recouped training costs for a model from profits generated from serving that model. A model today is served for a month or two, maybe less, before the next one replaces it.

If only the AI companies could serve these models for a little longer before having to race to train the next one. They would get filthy rich off inference.

If only they could all agree to slow down…
