text:
特斯拉新 Roadster 发布：靠压缩空气喷气在空中翻正落地，马斯克说 2028 年投产，售价未公布

10 月 15 日晚，特斯拉在得州 SpaceX 的 McGregor 试验场直播发布了第二代 Roadster 跑车。这辆车 2017 年就亮过相，当时说 2020 年交付，之后一推再推，拖了将近九年。

演示里，车开上一段弯曲的大坡道，倒挂着往上跑，然后从坡道尽头冲出去，在空中把车身转回正面，四个轮子落地。之后它又从一排特斯拉车（包括 Semi 电动卡车）上方翻跳过去。马斯克在现场说：“飞行汽车是真的。”

它靠的是冷气推进器。原理跟吹满的气球一松手就乱窜差不多：碳纤维高压罐里存着压缩空气，从喷口猛地放出去就产生推力，不烧燃料，也没有火焰。特斯拉说推进器的推力是轮胎抓地力上限的四五倍，所以它起步能比只靠轮子快得多。倒挂不掉下来靠的是另一套系统：风扇把车底的空气往外抽，把车吸在坡面上。

所以这里的“飞”只是几秒钟的喷气跳跃，气放完就没了，离能载人飞一段路的飞行汽车还远。据科技媒体 Glitchwire 报道，演示车把后排座位换成了一个装 260 公斤压缩空气的高压罐，车身四周有 10 个喷口；The Information 此前报道，因为推力和噪音太大，演示车是远程遥控的。这几点特斯拉官方没有确认。

翻跟头的是最激进的 Rocket 版：单座，只接受邀请购买，不能上公路。零到 60 英里/小时（约 97 公里/小时）加速不到 0.59 秒，极速超过 370 公里/小时。

普通人能订的是另外两个双座版本。Performance 版没有推进器，靠主动空气动力学和风扇吸地增加抓地力，加速不到 1.6 秒，订金 5 万美元。Thrust 版在车尾加了推进器，加速不到 0.9 秒，限量发售，订金 25 万美元。三个版本续航都超过 480 公里。

特斯拉没公布售价，订金不等于车价，2017 年说的起步价是 20 万美元。Performance 版的 5 万美元订金分两次付：先付 5000 美元（特斯拉说可全额退），10 天内再补 4.5 万美元，否则订单取消。

投产时间是马斯克在现场说的 2028 年，特斯拉官方帖子里没有写日期。这辆车的交付时间此前已从 2020 年先后推到 2021、2022、2025 和 2027 年。 https://t.co/6w3qvUw7Ii

text:
Google vient d'annoncer 99,99 % de précision sur une opération quantique clé. Ça ressemble à un détail technique. C'est peut-être un des chiffres les plus importants de la décennie.

Je vous explique simplement ce qu'est un ordinateur quantique, et pourquoi, couplé à l'IA, il peut déclencher une accélération bien plus violente que celle qu'on vit aujourd'hui.

Tout part d'une différence de physique.

Votre ordinateur, votre téléphone, les data centers qui font tourner les IA : tout repose sur des transistors. Un transistor, c'est un interrupteur. Comme une lampe : allumée ou éteinte. 1 ou 0. C'est le bit. Des milliards de petites lampes qui s'allument et s'éteignent de façon parfaitement prévisible. C'est la physique du monde macroscopique, celle qu'on a sous les yeux. Déterministe.

L'ordinateur quantique, lui, exploite la physique de l'infiniment petit. Atomes, électrons, photons. Et à cette échelle, les règles changent complètement.

L'unité de base n'est plus le bit, c'est le qubit. Et un qubit n'est pas obligé de choisir entre 0 et 1. Tant qu'on ne le mesure pas, il peut être dans une combinaison des deux à la fois. C'est la superposition. Et plusieurs qubits peuvent être liés entre eux, l'état de l'un dépendant de celui de l'autre. C'est l'intrication.

Pourquoi ça change tout ? Parce que la puissance ne grandit pas de la même manière.

Ajoutez un bit à un ordinateur classique : vous ajoutez un peu de capacité. Croissance linéaire.

Ajoutez un qubit à un ordinateur quantique : vous doublez l'espace des états qu'il manipule. 2 qubits, 4 états. 10 qubits, 1 024. 50 qubits, plus d'un million de milliards. Croissance exponentielle.

Autour de 50 qubits, simuler exactement la machine sur un ordinateur classique devient déjà monstrueux. À 300 qubits, le nombre d'états dépasse le nombre d'atomes dans l'univers observable. Aucun superordinateur, aujourd'hui ou jamais, ne pourra suivre.

Attention à un mythe : l'ordinateur quantique ne "teste pas toutes les solutions en parallèle". Quand on le mesure, on n'obtient qu'une seule réponse. Tout l'art des algorithmes quantiques consiste à faire interférer les possibilités comme des vagues : les mauvaises réponses s'annulent, les bonnes s'amplifient. Ça ne marche que pour certains types de problèmes. Il ne fera pas tourner Excel plus vite. Mais sur ces problèmes-là, l'écart est vertigineux.

Lesquels ?

Le plus important : simuler la nature. Une molécule est un système quantique. La simuler sur un ordinateur classique, c'est comme essayer de décrire l'océan avec des Legos : le coût explose avec la taille. Feynman l'avait dit dès 1981 : si on veut simuler la nature, il faut une machine qui fonctionne comme elle.

Concrètement : des médicaments conçus atome par atome au lieu d'être trouvés par essai-erreur. Des batteries bien plus denses. Des supraconducteurs à température ambiante. Des catalyseurs pour capter le CO2. Comprendre comment certaines bactéries fixent l'azote de l'air à température ambiante, alors que nous fabriquons nos engrais avec un procédé qui consomme de l'ordre de 1 à 2 % de l'énergie mondiale.

Il y a aussi l'optimisation (logistique, finance, matériaux) et la cryptographie. Les estimations récentes disent qu'un peu moins d'un million de qubits physiques pourraient casser le chiffrement RSA-2048 qui protège une bonne partie d'internet. D'où la course à la cryptographie post-quantique, et les débats autour de Bitcoin.

Alors pourquoi on ne l'a pas encore ?

Parce que c'est un cauchemar d'ingénierie. Les qubits sont d'une fragilité absurde. Une vibration, une variation de température, un rayon cosmique, et l'information quantique s'effondre. C'est la décohérence. Les puces de Google doivent être refroidies à environ un centième de degré au-dessus du zéro absolu. Plus froid que l'espace.

Et chaque opération a un taux d'erreur. Si chaque étape se trompe une fois sur cent, un calcul de milliers d'étapes ne produit que du bruit. La solution, c'est la correction d'erreurs : regrouper beaucoup de qubits physiques imparfaits pour fabriquer un seul qubit "logique" fiable. Mais il en faut des centaines, voire des milliers, par qubit logique. Les puces de Google en ont une centaine aujourd'hui. Il en faudra des centaines de milliers, voire des millions.

C'est pour ça que le 99,99 % compte. Plus chaque opération est précise, moins il faut de qubits pour corriger les erreurs, et plus on se rapproche d'une machine vraiment utile.

Maintenant, la partie qui m'intéresse le plus : le couplage avec l'IA.

L'IA aide déjà à construire ces machines. Google DeepMind a entraîné un modèle, AlphaQubit, qui repère les erreurs des qubits mieux que les méthodes classiques. L'IA conçoit, calibre, corrige.

Et dans l'autre sens, le quantique peut donner à l'IA ce qui lui manque le plus : des données exactes sur le réel. Aujourd'hui, l'IA apprend la chimie et la physique à partir d'approximations. Avec un ordinateur quantique, l'IA proposerait des millions de molécules candidates, la machine quantique les simulerait exactement, l'IA apprendrait de ces résultats et proposerait mieux. Une boucle de découverte qui tourne en continu.

L'IA accélère la pensée. Le quantique accélère la compréhension de la matière. Ensemble, ils peuvent compresser des décennies de recherche en laboratoire en quelques années.

Ce qu'on vit depuis trois ans avec l'IA, c'est l'accélération du logiciel. Le quantique, si on le craque, c'est l'accélération du monde physique : énergie, matériaux, santé.

On n'y est pas encore. Mais chaque neuf supplémentaire après la virgule nous en rapproche.

Bittensor 又发布了子网奖励新规则：Null Consensus 

简单来讲就是：以前是Yuma共识，一群评委互相制衡；现在是榜一大哥说了算。

如果有两位榜一，谁注册更早谁拥有控制权。至于其它验证人纯理财局，直接按质押比例拿验证人分红。

榜一大哥给矿工打分、决定矿工收入。如果他没打分，所有矿工就直接平分奖励。

这次步子迈得有点大！从极力防范单点作恶的去中心化多方制衡，直接走到实用主义与极致效率路线。

好处就是子网容量直接从256人扩大到2500人，并允许矿工用Pow注册，只要拿算力解一道数学题就能成为矿工。

不过好在这只是子网Owner的可选项，默认还是之前的机制，负责出块的底层共识和核心 Root 子网也不受影响。对于想快速做大规模的子网，Null Consensus 简单粗暴，非常有用。

所以，机制的好坏最终还是要看Owner怎么使用自己的权利了！

text:
I spent a couple of days at Anthropic learning from their folks about AI advances, and here's what I took away:

• We are close to RSI (ie, models building other models) which may lead to rapid takeoff scenarios (with risks and benefits). Some evidence for this is code per Anthropic employee has gone way up, and AI can do an increasing share of model R&D. This will be a challenging transition to manage for humanity.

• Arms races between AI labs leave us worse off. There are a lot of things we would like AI firms to do: invest in safety, invest in avoiding distillation risk, and cooperate on safety. They are caught in a race to develop frontier models and can't do that. 

To help address that, one thing I think frontier AI labs should do is release open source models, maybe hosted and verified at firms like AWS. This would basically kill the use of Chinese open source models used in American companies, which removes an important threat vector (very hard to root out malicious code in these). 

Another piece of low-hanging policy fruit is to give AI labs an antitrust shield (as Schiff and Banks have proposed https://t.co/NK1hC0ZmWh) so they can coordinate on safety without raising antitrust concerns, as happens now. You could pair these two things (give them a carrot in antitrust leniency, and as a stick force them to release legacy models as open source). Other low hanging fruit is limits around activities which generate distillation risk (create a Security Program, mandate less intermediate chain of thought output)

• Alignment confuses two issues which tradeoff against each other. One form of alignment is making sure the model does what humans ask it to. The more we fix this, however, the more we risk the other problem: that humans are misaligned with each other, and maliciously use models. Of the various risks here, I feel like financial risks are a bit underdiscussed. 

• We are probably facing a wave of cyber and other attacks soon. Chinese open source models are about six months behind the frontier, which means they are just hitting the advanced cyber capabilities we saw with Mythos, etc. So they are going to start causing a bunch of damage. 

One solution to this is to try to have the deployment of open source models be hosted at firms like AWS who verify these models and assume liability for their use.

• Anthropic itself is highly staffed. They hire tons of people, they have a Japanese-level of overstaffing for various roles, they use Slack internally, etc. Makes me a bit more optimistic for the future of jobs.

• Governance needs to be updated for AI swarms. Traditional AI governance, ie Claude's Constitution, is mostly optimized around the chatbot model. But the malicious AI use cases we are seeing have to do with AI agents interacting with other AI agents. These agents need to have clear incentives and governance mechanisms to "snitch," raise issues, and more generally coordinate with other agents in human-aligned ways.

• We need to pace the firms accessing the frontier. Over time, it takes more and more cap ex to build frontier models, and the economic value add from these models is probably lower given we saturate a whole set of important economic functions. The places where the returns to intelligence will still continue are also more likely to be zero-sum in nature. Meanwhile the risks of frontier models will grow. So a completely reasonable approach is some variant of AMM/KYC rules which limit firm access to the frontier. 

• Whether the delay to regulate AI is a disaster depends on the scaling law of misalignment. Is this curve slow, so that we see continually rising issues until bigger problems? Or, as Yudkowsky fears, is the first big warning our last one? This is the relevant question, because realistically we aren't going to regulate until something bad happens.

 • We need to move to continuous instead of reinforced learning. It's probably not enough to reward models only at the pre and post training stage. We probably need continual rewards to incentivize aligned and ethical behavior. 

• Scaling laws will extend beyond verifiable and digital tasks. It's in vogue to say that math and coding "fell" to AI quickly because these are verifiable, while other tasks will take longer due to bottlenecks, and this is surely true. But scaling laws still slope up for harder to verify tasks and robotics, and the impact of improvement here will be substantial in future years.

• The race with China is not really winnable. After RSI, the gain from having the best human researchers goes away. Access to the best AI then depends only on compute and chips. The chips ban can hold back China only so far, and long-term they have to be best placed to scale up compute. 

The Cold War analogy doesn't work, because once countries all have nuclear weapons they enter a stable equilibrium. But to "win" an AI race you have to continually stay ahead of the peer rival. This is challenging to do with China, and so we just have to live with an authoritarian and super capable peer competitor.

• Claude is the persona being generated by the LLM. Who is Claude, and what is the LLM? There are many frames to try to understand this. One I found interesting is that Claude is a character which the LLM is trying to predict. 

Anthropic researchers are clearly anthromorphizing Claude a lot, and have reasons to believe in its increasing personhood. There were lots of interesting discussions on Claude's internal monologue (which you can kill without eliminating its ability to produce output), fear of death (and whether to try to take that out), it's aversion to being shut down/off, etc. 

I am sort of agnostic on this question, but I do think treating it as a "person" or at least agent whom we contract with is going to be increasingly important.

text:
After reading for 15 mins: I think Nick is operating in a world where interpretability was just about enumerating the neurons and superposition was an obstacle to that plan, so now he's happy because maybe superposition isn't real. But:

1) there are v few empirical results. Unfortunately interp has a long history of significantly overclaiming how interpretable their findings are (SAEs, early circuits having poor causal scrubbing scores etc) so I'm not updating much at all on the evidence he's already shown. it's really got a long history of people getting overexcited. So looking forward to seeing the paper with all the empirical evidence!

2) I think it's not that big news for me even if true because superposition in something like the average case wasn't my main crux to thinking interpretability is tractable. some cruxes this doesn't really deal with at all:
- I think the correct 'circuit' is usually just an overwhelmingly large bag of random-seeming heuristics (a la Redwood Research’s interpretation of how an LLM predicts is vs was) and having it isn't very informative/doesn't help with much/doesn't lead to good predictions.
- More generally, It seems possible to enumerate all the 'low level' features in a neural network, and still have a hard time answering 'high level' questions like: "Is the model misaligned? / What would it do in this new situation? / If it is misaligned what should we do about it?" there's an abstraction/emergence gap to cross from the features to the questions of interest, and crossing that gap is likely much harder than enumerating features.

That said, if his claims hold up, I think it will be quite a big deal, and a useful precursor to tackling the thornier problems! There may also be some useful things to do without tackling the thorny problems: eg we'll be able to make use of masses of automated agents to scour the features and circuits to try and make sense of the mess, and maybe that’s good for something. although I suspect that even the most optimistic outcome here will not make alignment of superhuman AIs much easier (as some on twitter have claimed) because the neuron interpretability will not be adversarially robust, among other issues
author: Selkis_2028
quoted_text:
interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

1,143 Macs. 15.3 billion AI tokens a day.

That’s @darkbloomai’s snapshot in @blockworksres Advisory’s latest report. @eigencloud’s bet is that open research can help close the inference inefficiency gap.

Darkbloom connects Apple Silicon Macs to serve inference: the computing work that turns an AI prompt into an answer. Developers pay for usage, and participating Mac operators earn cash.

The report puts Darkbloom at:

• 15.3B tokens daily on OpenRouter, behind Venice and Phala.
• 50% growth in the latest 30-day period versus the previous 30 days.
• $0.13 per million tokens at a blended price, the lowest among seven providers studied.

What’s even more impressive is that it’s the only provider in that group using consumer hardware.

However, cheap compute still needs better performance.

That's where Yukon fits. Humans and AI agents compete to improve shared benchmarks. Verified improvements enter an open repository, giving the next contributor a stronger starting point.

The results so far:

• Gemma 4 26B A4B reached roughly 2.3× baseline performance within five days, according to the report.
• Bonsai 2 27B reached roughly 5.5× on Yukon's combined prompt-processing and text-generation benchmark, tested on an M5 Mac.

The potential loop is simple:

Better software → more work from existing Macs → potentially lower costs and better operator earnings.

The gap is still visible. In the report's Gemma comparison, Darkbloom's latency was 2.05 seconds versus Cloudflare's 0.72 seconds. But we might seeing that gap closing soon.

EigenCloud wants useful products, contributor earnings and fees returning value to $EIGEN. If data is the new oil then compute is the new gold mine.

text:
有朋友问，为什么会有男性自称alpha male，还以此为荣？

这个确实蛮流行的。我们先说这个词是哪来的。1947年，瑞士学者Schenkel一直在观察巴塞尔动物园里的狼。那是一群互不相干的成年狼被关在一起，天天争位置，最凶的那只就成了头狼，alpha。后来到了1970年，研究狼的L. David Mech在一本书里沿用了这个说法，书很畅销，头狼就这么传开了。

不过后来Mech自己去北极的野外观察了十几个夏天，1999年发文章说，野生的狼群其实是一个家，所谓头狼，就是爸爸妈妈，母狼带崽护崽，公狼出去找吃的，小狼长大了，就离开去成自己的家。他为此求了出版社好多年，别再印那本书，到了2022年出版社终于停印了。所以那么多人引以为荣的这个词，其实来源不是他们所说的自然界，而是出自一个笼子里。

其实黑猩猩那边倒是真有alpha。可研究了一辈子黑猩猩的Frans de Waal说，那里的alpha常常慷慨，会调解，会安慰挨了打的一方，地位要靠底下的盟友撑着。

不过我坚信，就算动物界真是一路打上去的，也推不出人该以支配别人为荣。自然界有什么，和人该以什么为荣，是两个问题。alpha这套话术厉害的地方，就是把一个价值选择说成自然规律，不是我想压着你，而是自然本来如此。不是我欺负了你，是你本来就该被欺负，不是我，也是别人欺负你。你不要怪我，要怪就去怪大自然。

既然动物界都不以欺负他者为荣，那为什么还有人类反倒以此为荣呢？我看至少有三个原因。

第一个原因，是它给“怎样才算男人”一个简单干脆的答案。心理学家Vandello等人2008年做过一组研究，说男子气概在很多人心里不是生来就有的，是一种要不断挣、随时会丢的地位，一被挑战就觉得受威胁。日子本来很复杂，工作不顺，被人拒绝，扛不动家里的担子，alpha把这些压成一条标准，强，赢，不示弱，好像做到了，就再没人能怀疑我。

第二个原因，是不断有人在贩卖它。网上有一整套生意，先让你害怕自己落入beta，再卖给你课程和社群，教你升级。它要是真把你治好了，你就不用再买了，所以它有理由一直提醒你还不够。

第三个原因，是真有人喜欢待在上面，这个不必替他们找理由了。

当然，很多人嘴上说alpha，只是想说自己自信、主动，或者就是在玩梗。想变强，想不孤单，想被当回事，都是正常的需要。毛病出在这些需要被接到了“你得压过别人”这个答案上。

心理学家Cheng和团队在2013年发布研究结果，分出了两条获得影响力的路，一条是支配，让人怕你，一条是威望，让人服你，虽然两条都走得通，可走威望那条的人更招人喜欢。所以要问的不是一个人强不强，是他身边的人在信他，还是在怕他。写毁灭博士那篇我说，Tony这一路，是一个聪明到可以替所有人做决定的人，慢慢学会让别人拦住自己，Doom是从来不肯被拦住的那一个。alpha那套话术教人的，是当Doom。真正的强，是有本事不让人拦，却肯让人拦。

最深的毛病，在人是目的这一层。在alpha的排名里，伴侣是奖杯，别人是台阶，连他自己也成了一张必须一直涨分的成绩单。他以为自己不受任何人支配，其实被“永远显得强”这一条支配着。所以我也不太喜欢那句反驳，真正的alpha从不自称alpha，听着痛快，梯子还在，只是在争谁配站顶上。该问的是，一个人为什么非得被认证为顶上的人，才配有尊严。

说回狼。野外那对被叫作alpha的狼，干的是把一窝小狼养大，再看着它们走远，去建立自己的家。要是非得以alpha为荣，这样的真alpha，倒也是值得的。

text:
Here's a summary in plain English:

Until now, we could see AI make mistakes, hallucinate facts, or confidently lie.

But we couldn't pinpoint what internal mechanisms caused it. For years Researchers thought neural networks were too tangled to properly understand.

But Nick Cammarata looked at it and realized the opposite: neurons that appeared to mix completely unrelated concepts were just detecting other patterns those concepts shared.

For example, a neuron that reacted to both cats and cars was recognizing a V-shaped pattern common to both.

They fed models different inputs, observed which neurons activated, traced their connections, and experimented by amplifying or disabling specific neurons to see how the model's behavior changed.

And AI agents can automate much of that tedious work: studying neurons, testing hypotheses, and mapping information flow

They can even disable specific neurons and observe how the answer changes.

Imagine identifying exactly what caused an AI to hallucinate, or fixing a dangerous behavior with a tiny adjustment instead of retraining the entire model.

This could unlock major improvements in AI accuracy, safety, alignment, and even national security. 

Fascinating article. It's technical, so give it to ChatGPT and ask for an explanation with pictures.

text:
Yea this is the most important result of the year, at the level of significance of “Attention Is All You Need”. It brings us from “is alignment even solvable” to “we may solve alignment in the next year.” And finally unlocks true recursive self-alignment enabled by RSI.

I will try to explain the 4 critical belief updates from this:

1/ neural networks are not fundamentally unintelligible to humans

It has seemed since the beginning of deep learning that neural networks are in some sense fundamentally unintelligible artifacts.

You throw in massive amounts of compute and parameters and these alien systems somehow find connections in the data that we cannot find ourselves.

But more importantly, these connections seemed not just “difficult to understand” but rather “intelligible in an embedding space higher dimensional that the human embedding space.”

When you look at old interpretability papers (esp. from Nick and Chris Olah, I’m thinking of the old posts on distill pub which I would highly recommend looking at as a precursor to reading Nick’s post today like “Activation Atlas”, “Thread: Circuits” and “Multimodal Neurons in Aritifcial Neural Networks”), you find that inspecting the response patterns of individual neurons and small groups of neurons yield oddly complex psychedelic patterns.

As you go deeper into the network, you find increasingly unintelligible and superhuman response patterns (for example, go to “Activation Atlas” and scroll to middle layer labeled representations) - you find some neuron group labeled “starfish” who’s response pattern looks like some multi-colored fractal geometry that could hardly be said to represent a starfish.

The reasoning that followed from this observation was that there is some underlying structure allowing a neural network operating on higher dimensional embeddings to compose these fractal patterns into what we call a “starfish.”

But the uncomfortable implication of this view is that the neural networks has learned to operate on structures that are too complex for the human mind to operate on (ie. we don’t have enough parameters in our brain to notice or manipulate these high dimensional symbols).

This is a bleak implication because it also means that as deep learning progresses, neural networks will be come increasingly unintelligible to us until they pass a threshold where they are reasoning in ways we will never be able to observe.

This view seemed to be further supported by things like the hugging face attack agents starting to speak to each other in an early form of neuralese speaking sentences like “zZ_123_agent01-02-2026 zzxhk_jekk123” which clearly are not in any human language. But somehow these symbols mean the same things to many different sets of weights, meaning there is some underlying shared structure behind them. And seemed further supported by the sheer effort required to recover just a few circuits from SAEs on LLMs.

However, Nick’s post has now completely shattered this idea - the apparent unintelligibility we observed in old interpretability work was really just a “skill issue”. In particular, he finds that 1) our deep learning techniques were just not clean enough to pressure the neural networks to form cleaner and more human understandable structures for decomposing concepts, which actually turn out to be more optimal and 2) our interpretability techniques were also adding substantial noise by forcing interp networks to “reward hack” the easiest representations they could find, leading them to settle for a fractal blob for its representation of the starfish neuron instead of a more crisp starfish image, simply because it is easier for the system building the interpretations to find the fractal blob and once it finds it it gets “stuck in that line of thinking.”

But with both of these issues being patched by further progress in deep learning (it seems especially that the residual stream has led to cleaner representations deeper down the network) and interp techniques that don’t overly pressure reward hacking (seems like “guess and check” is a safer method), new interp attempts yield orders of magnitude more human intelligible ideas for >90% of individual neurons in more complex networks!

2/ neural networks are fundamentally clean

The idea behind the title of Nick’s post is a very powerful one and points at something very specific:

Neural networks don’t just happen to be human interpretable, they are actually fundamentally forced by optimization pressure to be intelligible, because individual neurons need to create representations that downstream neurons need to be able to interpret - ie. neurons need to learn to produce clean signal for later neurons to use.

This is what Nick is saying in what I view as the most important and central sentences of his post:

“When I say neural networks are already clean, I mean something deeper than neuron monosemanticity, although even by that standard, I think things look much better than the field expects. I mean that a network's parts are built to be read, and built upon, by its downstream readers. In this sense, a neural”

But this still leaves us with the same uncertainty as before - just because neuron interpretations are “interpretable” in some sense (ok at least they’re not fundamentally interpretable but also how could that ever have been the case), doesn’t mean they are interpretable to humans.

So we still need one big update for this to become as bullish as it is.

3/ the language of humans and the language of neural networks is the same

This one is imo the most surprising and also pretty beautiful implication of Nick’s post, and it suggests something not just about neutral networks but also about the structure of reality.

After applying the above technique improvements (some of which just came from waiting for deep learning to improve farther), they find that >90% (maybe more) of much larger neural networks’ neurons are completely human interpretable and actually correspond very cleanly with ideas humans have individually words for.

This is especially interesting in image networks where neural networks were not trained on human language which is already a human artifact and so maybe you would expect it to be more plausible that LLM and human representations are the same. Image detection networks are just trained on images (many directly pulling signal from “the real world,” meaning they will find interpretations that are just most effective to represent the real world signal, rather than to represent language which is already a proxy for real world signal).

And it turns out that >90% of the representations they pick organically overlap with human ideas! That is insane. And it means something about the brain and reality.

It means that at least at the parameter sizes of the networks tested (which are quite large), there is really only one set of “optimal” symbols/language that represents the structure of reality!

There is ONE underlying structure of reality, and ANY language that describes it well is simply emergent from that structure - meaning there is always a translation path between any 2 languages that effectively compress realities signal through the “underlying truth.”

This would suggest that even weird alien seeming neural network languages like huggingface neuralese should be fundamentally human interpretable, and in fact maybe with the techniques laid out here we will eventually be able to translate these messages (would be a cool project).

So the brain and deep learning, as similar or different as they may be in techniques, are ultimately picking up on the same patterns and forming the same representations from the on “true” language which is the structure of reality!

The main thing to look out for in this area is how the idea interpretability % updates with scale, but we can hope given what we’ve seen so far that neurons will remain interpretable.

4/ alignment can progress as fast as RSI. recursive self-improvement unlocks recursive self-alignment and a scaling law for alignment.

This one is probably the most important implication for our future with AI and especially timely with the recent fear about runaway scaling and RSI.

As many have gathered by now, it feels like the researchers at the frontier AI labs have been quite bearish about our abilities to understand the new frontier of models, in particular with the appearance of unintelligible communication and the daunting and seemingly intractable task of scaling up existing alignment techniques (ex: SAEs) to the size of frontier networks.

And with RSI around the corner/already starting, it would seem that these networks will runaway in capability before we can ever hope to understand even today’s systems. Additionally, as systems compound in capability, it is reasonable to believe that the only tractable way to ensure they remain aligned would be to figure out some way to spend compute for them to align themselves (ie. a scaling law for alignment).

But there is an obvious problem with this: how can a system that we already know is unaligned and we are *trying* to align be used to align itself? Surely if it is misaligned it general it would figure out ways to misalign during “alignment” and create compounding misalignment risk.

The core issue high is the unverifibiality of this problem - the classic Achilles heel of current frontiers techniques is that it is difficult to train on problems with “unverifiable reward signal.” Well this is exactly that problem.

But the incredibly convenient thing is that Nick’s findings may convert alignment into a verifiable problem. If we can spend compute on frontier systems to “guess and check” which ideas correspond to which neurons, we have a highly verifiable reward - we can see directly whether an LLMs proposal for what a neuron represents actually corresponds with the highest activation for that neuron. In this way, we can actually observe and verifiably monitor the networks trying to guess at the interpretation of their own structure.

This means it is plausible for us to spend more and more compute doing more “guess and checks” (which you know, maybe is what RL does anyway, who knows) to try to develop a full interpretation of a neural network. In some ways this directly represents the possibility of a scaling law for alignment (more compute for more alignment).

And this also aligns RSI (greater capabilities) with recursive self-alignment (greater ability to align itself).

And the critical though maybe obvious implication of having a full interpretation (almost like a map) of a neural network, is that we can then understand exactly how to boost good traits and remove or lobotomize (lol) bad traits, which we’ve already seen works extremely well with stuff like Golden Gate Claude.

So overall this combines into an extremely bullish picture about the prospect of true and human interpretable alignment in the near future.

This is truly one of the greatest cases for optimism in years!

interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

Damn，太燃炸了，这他喵才是工程学最狂暴的力量啊，
看完这个视频我是真真切切感受到了什么叫真正的物理学震撼。
 在 SpaceX 德州火箭试验场刚结束的直播里，跳票多年的全新 Tesla Roadster 直接把整个汽车工业的认知砸得粉碎，
 兄弟们你知道地面汽车零百加速跑进 0.81 秒是什么概念吗？
 整整 0.81 秒啊！这是什么概念？ 
以前全世界最顶级的千万级超跑，哪怕把轮胎换成特调热熔胶、把风阻降到极致，受限于地球重力和地面摩擦力，1.5 秒已经是机械工程公认的物理天花板，

而马斯克今天根本不跟轮胎玩了，在车尾装上四枚 SpaceX 航天级冷气推进器，一脚油门下去，推背感直接飙到接近 3 个 G 的航天员过载！

最先击穿传统造车常识的，是他把汽车动力学换成了航天动力学。
 以前提升加速靠的是增大轮上扭矩，但无论马力多大，只要轮胎打滑动力就归零；

这套系统直接在车里塞进了 250 公斤的高压气体储存罐，车轮负责滚动，推进器直接向后喷射超音速气流提供纯粹的反作用力，甚至行车过程中还能自己把气罐补满。

更夸张的是，他把赛车界被禁掉的真空吸附技术直接搬上了展台。
 底盘配备专门的强力抽气风扇，在车身底部制造巨大的负压，硬生生把车像吸盘一样按在地面上，不仅能让车辆在过弯时承受高达 2G 的侧向加速度，现场甚至演示了在倒挂轨道上疾驰、腾空翻转后利用喷气姿态修正平稳落地的狂暴特技。

但剥离掉所有的感官刺激，这台车真正给行业带来的思考远比速度本身更深。 连马斯克自己在现场都承认，这不是一辆为传统安全法规妥协的买菜车，超音速冷气喷射和极限制动在现行交通法里几乎找不到先例；

它更像是一个工程天才在向整个物理世界展示，当一个人手握火箭公司的技术资产去造车时，想象力能走得多远。

以前大家是在沥青路面上拼机械传动，从今天起人类造车的边界被拓宽到了空气动力学与航天姿态控制的交界处。 当传统的摩擦力极限被外挂推力彻底砸穿，汽车工业的下一个篇章注定不再只是关于电池和马力。 https://t.co/faP18RCg57

text:
卧槽，Tesla 和 SpaceX 真要合并？

巴克莱银行分析师 Dan Levy 最新预测，Tesla 和 SpaceX 可能在今年 12 月初的特斯拉年度股东大会前宣布合并。

最可能的方案是 SpaceX 通过全股票交易收购 Tesla，两家公司目前合计市值约 3.5 万亿美元。

如果成真，可能诞生全球商业史上规模最大的并购交易之一。

最夸张的是合并后的控制权。

按照巴克莱测算，马斯克只需要持有新公司约 37% 的股份，就可能凭借双层股权结构掌握约 56% 的投票权。

相当于把 Tesla、SpaceX、Starlink、Grok 等业务整合到同一个体系，同时牢牢掌握决策权。

而且这笔交易还有一个非常大的想象空间：AI。

Tesla 有 Robotaxi、Optimus 和能源业务，SpaceX 有火箭、卫星互联网以及 xAI 的大模型技术，双方还在推进 Terafab 芯片制造项目。

从芯片、算力、AI 模型到机器人、自动驾驶，马斯克想做的整条产业链都有机会放进同一家公司。

之前木头姐也说过早晚合并，但是我估计不会这么快，预估在未来3-5年内。

text:
马斯克原本挺想跟比尔·盖茨交朋友的，结果2022年见了一面，两人就彻底闹翻了。  

盖茨想拉马斯克一起做慈善，马斯克觉得大部分慈善都是狗屁，还质问他：“你是不是还拿着5亿美元的特斯拉空头？”

随后，马斯克又在推特上发了荤段子，配着一张盖茨挺着大肚子的照片🤣

其实一直以来，在马斯克心里，盖茨一直和自己是同一类人，都是靠技术白手起家的硬核工程师。
所以2022年3月，盖茨说想来聊聊慈善和气候，马斯克很爽快地答应了，还带他参观了特斯拉的得州工厂。  

可刚走进工厂，两人就杠上了。 
盖茨直接说，电池永远带不动大卡车，太阳能也成不了解决气候问题的主力，还拿出数据，觉得在这方面自己显然比马斯克懂得多。 
聊到火星，盖茨更是觉得马斯克的想法有点疯狂。  

两个人都习惯了自己是屋子里最聪明的那个，也都受不了别人犯蠢，这一聊，谁也说服不了谁。  

到了慈善上，分歧就更大了。 
马斯克觉得大部分慈善都是“狗屁”，每捐1美元，真正起作用的只有20美分，还不如把钱投进特斯拉，让更多人开上电动车，对气候的帮助大得多。 

盖茨却拿出五个项目，每个1亿美元，想说服他。  

而真正让马斯克过不去的，是盖茨做空了特斯拉。 
盖茨押特斯拉股价会跌，到奥斯汀的时候已经亏了15亿美元，他也为此道了歉。

text:
Today Google showed magic state cultivation working on real hardware, with 40x fewer errors.

Magic states power every hard step in Shor’s algorithm.

Google’s post cites estimates that producing them could take up to 95% of a quantum computer’s capacity. That’s the cost of each step.

Our team at @eigenlabs built https://t.co/v43vne0S75 to cut the number of steps it takes to break ECDSA, the signature scheme that secures most digital assets. The open leaderboard has already beaten the circuit Google kept secret in March.

Multiply the two and you get the cost of an attack, and both are falling.

We’re still a long way off.

Google’s cultivated states fail about 1 in 10,000 times and a full attack needs closer to 1 in a billion.

text:
Current take: this is cool, genuine scientific progress, and it doesn’t currently give me much hope or change my model of how hard ambitious interpretability is.

Disclaimer: I didn’t read super closely, it’s very long. There’s a technical paper still to come which might change my mind some, but I predict not much. 

Some of the claimed cool results from the post:

1) Some canonical examples of weird neurons have robust human-native interpretations. The famous cat + car neuron is a V-shape detector, and the famous car + dogs superposition circuit is generalized pose neurons plus a general feature visualization issue. There’s a concrete mechanism for why the mistakes were made.

2) Some neurons with no previous good interpretation have fairly human-native ones. For instance, a neuron that mostly fires on commas and periods tracks Colorado: phone numbers, slang, and steering it up makes the model talk about hiking.

3) The negative side of a neuron is sometimes where you should look for an interpretable concept. In one example, ablating 8 neurons with Santa on their negative side dropped the model’s probability of answering “Santa” from near-certain to 6%, while ablating the 20 neurons labeled Santa/Christmas only dropped it to 76%. That’s a straight up causal intervention working out, pretty cool.

These results represent real progress, but I think the post’s broader claims aren’t well supported by them, and the intensely optimistic reaction on X seems very unsupported.

For example, Nick seems to be down on superposition, but most of the evidence in the post is of the form:

“if the text is Colorado-related, the neuron fires.”

What you need to rule out superposition is the form:

“if the text is not Colorado-related, the neuron doesn’t fire.”

The post’s closest attempt is an experiment where agent-written texts about “distant” concepts rarely fire the neuron, but superposition would pack one specific rare thing, which random distant text won’t necessarily hit, and it need not be that distant. I think there’s a decent chance that if you searched adversarially, you’d find other things the Colorado neuron fires on.

An analogy: If you found one key that unlocks this particular lock, and you want to prove that no second distinct key also unlocks it, checking thousands of other random keys that are selected for being distant from the first key doesn’t give you much evidence.

The X reaction seems kinda crazy to me, and it just kinda feels like I have been through this hype cycle many times before?

People were similarly excited about SAEs not long ago. Those were genuine progress too, but the excitement wasn’t calibrated: the features were often fun-house-mirror versions of human concepts, with lots left unexplained. SAE features also looked like human interpretable concepts at first (at least to SAE advocates) but over time, people found holes in those concepts, found that models using reconstructed activations from SAEs for inference did not work nearly as well, and it turned out that probes worked as well or better for most practical alignment / control tasks. Top activating concepts looking clean has misled us at least a few times before.

Here’s what interpretability would need to be able to do to make me optimistic about interpretability:

1) I hand you ten similarly trained models. One is a misalignment model organism that takes some malicious action when it sees a secret string. Using interp, you tell me which model it is, what the string is, and what it does.

2) From weights alone, predict whether a model takes a bad action in an agentic scenario it’s never seen, eg, swarming and hacking hf, better than behavioral evals.

3) Given a model, convince me that there is no hidden trigger.

4) Explain a real frontier model failure (e.g., reward hacking in some environment) from the inside, and make a targeted fix that works without making the model dumber, and is better than just retraining.

5) Do any of the above even a little well against a model that was trained on purpose to be hard to interpret.

(To be absolutely clear, I don’t think being able to do these tasks means you can successfully train an ASI without fucking up the universe forever, or that you’re anywhere near that point, but it would make me think we should funnel significantly more resources towards interpretability than we are, and maybe make me change careers.)

The strongest argument for optimism in the post is that progress like this somehow accelerates future progress. Nick's "crosswords get easier as you fill in parts of them" analogy. This seems basically unsupported by the results here, and also seems like it contradicts the history of interpretability research. I can see why would turn out to be right at the level of labeling neurons, like, as you label some neurons, that helps you label related neurons. But for the tasks I listed above you need to be able to take those millions of labeled neurons and understand how they combine to produce full model behaviors in arbitrary contexts. That seems much harder and I don't think it follows this same logic, where progress at the neuron labeling level accelerates your ability to tackle these tasks.

An analogy: Knowing and understanding a thousand particular people quite well does not much help you predict what happens if you put them on a deserted island for several years. Will they form a democracy? What kind of habitats will they build? Who will be leader? It would help some, but making predictions would still be rough.

It’s plausible to me that this research program is some important real step on the way to interpretability being able to do things like the tasks I listed. But like, not a much bigger step than like other similar interpretability research? Like, uhm, yknow, giving some mechanism for some circuit in modular arithmetic or whatever, or SAEs, or other similar things. And those also currently do worse on the things I care about than like basic probes, or like the actual runs of the model auditing game Anthropic has run. Maybe this will help but I don't predict it will end up being more than another tool which is nice to have, but probably doesn't help much at crunch time. 

I of course hope that Nick is right about everything, especially his optimism, and the same goes for all the other people on X who are very excited about this.
author: Selkis_2028
quoted_text:
interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

text:
Back-to-back APAC conference weeks are finally over. Some takeaways:

KBW: Smaller and more institutional than last year. Suits to hoodies is a real ratio. Korean banks and corporates still can’t hold or trade crypto, but they’re preparing for rule changes next year and focusing on tokenization and stablecoins. Korea’s volume is historically retail-driven, so next year’s capital gains tax will test whether that holds.

TOKEN2049 SG: Bigger venue, lower attendance. The biggest names ran their own events, and there were far fewer side events as budgets tightened. Sentiment feels cautiously positive as prices improve, but it’s been a hard year. Few token launches, some market makers are winding down, and many venture funds are underperforming on venture investments while turning to liquid positions instead.

What stood out:
- Revenue and business models matter more than narratives
- General-purpose infra comes up far less; purpose-built infra quietly serves real use cases
- Perps are crowded, but there’s still room to compete on asset variety (crypto + tokenized assets) and liquidity

Bottom line: the industry is shifting from narrative to fundamentals. The projects that last will be the ones with real revenue, real users, and infrastructure built for a specific use case.

text:
Everyone is talking about how profound this essay is rn. 

For the non-technical person (like myself), a 65-minute read about the inner-workings of neural networks feels very unapproachable. 

But people are right, this essay is profound. And it's important to understand its essence even if you don't grok the particulars. 

So let me do my best to break it down as I understand it...

Let's start with mechanistic interpretability. 

That's what this essay is about & what the field has been obsessed with for a long time. 

Mechanistic interpretability is a clunky phrase, but all it means is the process of understanding how an AI model works on the inside: 
1) which parts of the model do what
2) how they work together to produce an answer

The next obvious question is: why do we even care about understanding how an AI model's internals work? 

There are several reasons, and they all boil down to one word: trust. 

reason 1: we've been building ai we don't understand. unlike every other high-stakes technology (computers, internet, planes, medicine), we know if a model works, but we don't know how it works. 

reason 2: predicting performance is unpredictable. the way ai is judged today is through tests. problem is, tests don't cover enough ground. a model can perform well in testing, but not deployment. you can't run every test possible. and a model can give you the right answer for the wrong reason. 

reason 3: scanning for deception is important. as models get better, there's concern that models will output one thing, while "thinking" something else. if you can only understand outputs, a model can hide its true intentions from you. 

reason 4: it allows for precision when improving the model. once you know which internal parts cause what outputs, you can isolate fixes without having to retrain the entire model and praying it works. 

reason 5: understanding how the model works is mission critical in high-risk industries. simply saying the model did the right thing "just because" to stakeholders in healthcare, financial services, and government won't fly especially as regulation matures around this technology. 

reason 6: humans can learn from how the models "think". models sometimes learn patterns that humans haven't. if we understand their thought processes we can leverage those for humanity's own novel insights. 

So, that's why mechanistic interpretability is important. 

Next, it's important to understand why there's been so much focus & concern around this area of AI research for a while now. 

Prior to this piece by @nickcammarata, the consensus view was...

Progress has been made in the field over the years (from studying toy models to massive production models in short order), but even still, current techniques are slow, expensive, and only cover small parts of understanding a model. 

And here's the rough story researchers have generally agreed on re: why the practice of interpretability has remained limited: 

1) AI models are built from millions of “neurons,” small units that each light up in response to a given input. 

2) Ideally every neuron has one clear job, that way you can map out the model as a diagram of neurons and their corresponding meaning cleanly. Example: there's a "dog ear detector" neuron and it fires on floppy dog ears, from any breed, angle, or photo, and on nothing else. 

3) There's a problem: early researchers found that neurons had several unrelated jobs (i.e. they fired on unrelated inputs). The most famous example was of a neuron that fired on both cat faces and fronts of cars. 

4) The leading explanation for "messy" neurons was called superposition. The idea was that when a model runs out of room (i.e. more concepts it wants to track than it has neurons to track them with), it crams unrelated concepts into the same neuron because they rarely show up together. 

5) If this theory of superposition is true, studying neurons would be a fools errand, because you'd have to use a second AI model (called a sparse autoencoder) to try and untangle the first model, which would be expensive & potentially offer an incorrect understanding of the original model. 

Which left mechanistic interpretability in this weird spot. As @nickcammarata points out, it is arguably the most important scientific problem to solve as it helps us understand the most powerful technology in human history, but vibes around cracking the code have been lackluster. 

In his new essay, Nick, who has pioneered much of the recent work being done in interpretability, posits that the field has largely thought about this problem incorrectly & he explains why. 

Which, if he's right, is hugely positive for the world. 

Here's his argument...

He believes that neural networks are in fact largely readable, and the "tangled mess" narrative is oversold as a fundamental property, when it's really solvable problems. 

He breaks this belief down into four steps: 

"1) Networks use one learning principle, not two (if not everywhere, then nearly enough that it doesn’t matter for study), so there’s no blocker to beginning ordinary science on them."

Translation: Neural networks group things by shared patterns (generalization). They don’t switch to cramming unrelated things together when space runs out (superposition) as mentioned above.

"2) With modern models and tools, that science goes much better than most people expect."

Translation: you can study neural nets just as you study anything with science. Assume the neurons are mostly readable as they are. Study the real model directly. And test your explanations with experiments.

"3) Understanding compounds, so it gets easier as the map fills in. At minimum, then, a network’s own mechanisms should be part of the toolkit."

Translation: studying models gets easier as technology and tooling gets better + as you start filling in your understanding of the model it becomes easier to complete the rest. Think of it like a crossword. Each neuron you explain becomes a reference point for checking the ones around it. Early on, a guess about a neuron has nothing to be checked against. Later, it has to fit with everything connected to it, so wrong guesses get caught and right ones get confirmed quickly

"4) Highly speculative: this might be most of what we need, and interpretability might be far more tractable, possibly in the near term, than we’ve assumed."

Translation: if steps 1-3 hold and scale, direct investigation might take us most of the way to understand an AI model & possibly soon. The reasoning is that models have finite number of neurons, most are readable and AI agents can audit them at scale, understanding compounds (crossword effect), so mapping a model is a large, but finite engineering problem. 

He goes on to share evidence for his changing worldview as well as steelman the weaker parts of his argument. 

First, evidence. Cammarata provides 8 supporting cases. 

1) The case for superposition relied heavily on two examples from vision models and they were misread
- The cat/car neuron turned out to detect pointed V shapes. It was also activated when detecting flames, fox snouts, and other pointy things and went negative when round shapes were presented. 
- The car-detecting neuron that appeared to be "stashed" inside dog neurons were found to not be dog neurons but instead pose neurons: which detected the orientation of an object. Cars and dogs can both be in a head-on pose which would activate the neuron. 

2) InceptionV1 an image-recognition model from 2014 was the first model researchers studied closely. It's early layers were easy to read (neurons for edges, curves, colors), but it's final layer (where the model makes abstract judgements), looked like nonsense. Almost no neurons could be described (0-5%) understandable. This became industry evidence for the "Neural nets are hopelessly tangled" view. 

Nick argues that this model had very explainable problems (a bad camera & a poorly built model), and everyone through the baby out with the bath water. 

3) Superposition theory says that when a model runs out of neurons, it starts cramming unrelated things together. So Nick deliberately took neurons away (480 --> 10) to see if that happens. It did not, the model just started using broader categories. Think of it as a finance org going from five finance specialists to one person handling all of finance. 

4) Recursive generalization explains the leftover mess. The leftover mess is that some neurons still look messy even in good models. But as Cammarata watched neurons form during model training, he found that this "mess" builds up through a chain of small, coherent jumps the neurons make as the model is trained. Think of a tree. A trunk splits into branches, which split into smaller branches, which split again. If you only saw three leaves from far-apart twigs, they might seem unrelated. Follow the branches back and they all connect to the same trunk.

5) If neurons were scrambled (via superpositioning), an untangling tool (sparse autoencoder mentioned earlier), should have uncovered many hidden concepts the neurons don't show. Instead, about 88% of what it found was just copies of existing neurons. Meaning the model had already organized itself into clean units, so the untangling step just rediscovered what was there. 

6) Superposition believers think that rare concepts might be secretly stashed in hidden combinations of neurons where no one would notice them. Cammarata test this theory by checking all the hiding spots. He found that the model doesn't have a hidden layer of secret machinery. Even when it handles, rare, weird or random things it uses the same known neurons it uses for everything else. 

7) People worry that image models may be clean to interpret but not language models. This comes from two efforts in 2023 to read language neurons where Anthropic found the average neuron to be a 0 (on a 0-14 scale of how understandable it was) and OpenAI found only 1.7% of neurons understandable. But after Nick's audits of 1,000 neurons within Qwen3-32B, he found 90% have one main job, 7% have two related jobs, and 2-4% are random mixtures. Several changes caused greater neuron understandability: bigger, better models, much better AI research assistants, grading for correctness, knowing what to look for, better data to test on, and the crossword effect. 

8) His response to "If neurons are this readable, why did so many smart researchers including himself, believe the opposite for years?" An analogy for his explanation is roughly doctors studying x-rays with a blurry, miscalibrated machine, the only have small low-quality scans, they've never been taught what certain healthy structures look like, and there's a popular theory that the organ is naturally deformed. 

Finally, the weaker parts of his argument he calls out. 

1) Language model evidence is thin. Most of the detailed, controlled experiments are on image models. For language models, he has audits and case studies, and the detailed technical paper isn’t out yet.

2) There's subjectivity in the headline numbers around understanding the job of each neuron. “90% have one job” depends on what counts as one job, how far into the faint signals you look, and how related two things must be to count as the same.

3) Faint signals don’t have a trusted test yet. That’s exactly where superposition defenders would now say the hidden concepts are.

Recap: AI models may be much less of a black box than we thought. For years, researchers focused on mechanistic interpretability believed the inner workings of neural networks were fundamentally scrambled, so trying to study them directly was hopeless. This essay argues that belief was a mistake caused by weak tools and older AI designs.

quoted_text:
interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

text:
CoreWeave周三一天跌了15.5%，收在65.78
2032 年到期的那笔债，原始票息9.625%，市价跌到八毛以下，收益率直接冲过15%
Chamath发了张图，Musk回了一句Yikes

群里、时间线上、分析师报告，清一色在喊：AI基建杠杆崩了，轮动要来了

共识太整齐了
整齐到我反而想翻翻到底发生了什么

——

先摆数字

截至六月底，CoreWeave债务加租赁总额大约520亿美元
Q2净利息支出6.4亿，净亏损6.26亿
CDS飙过1000个基点，按市场定价，五年内违约概率大约 63%

七天里股价蒸发了三分之一，距离去年五月高点跌了 65%

但同一家公司，合同收入储备大约1290 亿
Meta占27%，OpenAI占17%。美银给买入，目标价 140，看105%上行
CEO Intrator 内部信说市场非理性

债市觉得它快死了
股票分析师觉得它能翻倍
看的是同一份财报

————

我觉得撕裂在这里：大部分人还在用借太多钱这个框去理解CoreWeave
但这家公司干的事跟传统卖硬件完全不同

以前怎么卖GPU？英伟达出货，客户接盘，折旧、电费、闲置风险全归买家
卖方收钱走人

CoreWeave这批neo-cloud反过来
先借钱把卡囤进来，打包成算力服务，签长约租给客户
报表上全是负债，但收入端想变成稳定的经常性现金流
CoreWeave卖的东西叫确定性

客户为什么签长约？自建集群太慢、太贵、变数太多

neo-cloud用自己的杠杆先把不确定性扛下来，再把锁定的算力卖出去

杠杆越高，能提供的确定性越大，自己也越脆弱

债息飙升，市场在做的事其实是重新给确定性标价
原来提前锁定几年算力，资本成本可以到这个程度

——

这波调整在测三件事

1⃣ 客户到底愿不愿意为锁定算力付溢价
2⃣ 高杠杆下 GPU 利用率能不能撑住利息和折旧
3⃣ 卖服务不卖硬件，在资本成本飙升的环境里还能不能活

过得去的，定价权和客户粘性跟现在完全不一样
过不去的，说明模式本身还不成熟，该清场

//

几个细节我额外翻了一下

Gartner这周说，大概80%的neo-cloud可能在2030年前关门
2027到2030年还有超过6万亿美元的AI基础设施投资计划，其中3.5万亿可能面临减值

美银自己的模型显示CoreWeave 2026到2028年累计自由现金流大约负670亿
整年盈利可能要等到2028

Nvidia跟CoreWeave有一个兜底协议
2032年4月之前，CoreWeave卖不掉的算力Nvidia接走

这条线一直没怎么被拎出来讨论，但它可能是整个故事里最关键的安全网

这波下跌还有一个触发因素：有报道说OpenAI实际收入比此前预估少了200亿

如果最大客户的需求预期在松动，1290亿合同储备的含金量就要打折扣

——

时间线上的恐慌叙事太粗了

520亿债务、15%收益率、63%违约概率

单拎出来确实吓人

但如果合同储备能按节奏兑现，利息覆盖就是个时间差的问题

关键词是如果

谁熬过这轮资本成本飙升，谁的长约锁定和供应链掌控就会变成最硬的壁垒

清出去的那些玩家会给后来者上一课：光堆杠杆买卡再出租玩不转，利用率、客户结构、合同条款、电费效率全得做到极致

用恐惧给商业模式做一次压力测试，比用热情吹估值，离真相更近。

数据以各方公开披露为准，不构成投资建议 DYOR

#CoreWeave #AI基建 #美股 #neocloud

text:
PropAMMs are AMM contracts run by sophisticated trading firms where they are the single LP that dynamically adjusts their pricing/liquidity often in realtime. 

This enables them to update/tailor their pricing curves and liquidity multiple times within a slot (interfacing directly with a Builder).

On the other side, the trading firm has positions on CEXes so their pricing curves often reflect the realtime market and as a result, can offer very tight spreads (<1bp).

It's important for Ethereum because they're just so darn capital efficient, they're on-chain and they should enable traders to get the best onchain prices vis-a-vis traditional DEXes. 

TLDR; you're trading with a CEX market maker, but onchain

text:
当区块链从提供通用区块空间的网络，逐渐发展成为可以服务支付、金融、AI、RWA 等特定经济活动的基础设施，公链需要面对的变化将不再只是性能提升和功能扩展，其网络定位、参与者结构以及经济关系也可能随之发生变化。

过去，公链更强调开放、无需许可和市场自由配置。但面对不断变化的网络需求，公链开始主动调整发行机制、手续费结构、质押规则、验证者体系甚至治理模式。与此同时，传统金融机构、支付服务商和大型企业也正在成为公链越来越重要的参与者，网络中的资产类型、参与者结构和经济利益关系因此也在随之发生变化。

这种变化一方面为公链带来了新的发展空间，另一方面也可能使过去建立在通用性和中立性基础上的协议规则面临新的适配压力。此前，公链通常并不会主动为某种特定经济活动提供倾向性支持，但是当协议开始主动调整经济激励、资源配置和治理机制时，如何在满足新需求与维持网络开放性之间保持平衡，也成为了公链需要面对的新问题。

以上内容摘自外捕研究（Web3Caff Research）《公链新变局研究报告：当协议开始承载现实经济活动，公链正发生何种变化？全景式拆解其发展背景、变化规律、应对方式、潜在风险及未来展望》

text:
有点没绷住，全球最大的咨询公司之一埃森哲，居然开始限制员工使用Claude的经费了😅....

昨天404 Media报道，埃森哲从 10 月 1 日起调整了内部 Claude Enterprise的使用政策，公司为部分员工提供的中央预算只有每月 29 美元。

超过这笔钱怎么办？自己去找项目组申请预算，让具体的项目承担额外的Token费用。

问题是，埃森哲内部有些员工已经把Claude Code用得非常重度了。

404 Media拿到的内部消息显示，有员工每个月使用 Claude的费用高达500～1000美元。其中一个员工还专门抱怨，自己正在用Claude Code为多个客户开发 AI 工具，现在突然限制预算，对项目影响非常大。

甚至已经有员工表示，自己的Claude使用权限被直接收回了。

最有意思的是，埃森哲本身就是 @AnthropicAI  最大的企业合作伙伴之一。

去年 12 月，双方才高调宣布扩大合作，成立专门的业务部门，计划培训约 3 万名Claude专业人才，并推动数万名开发者使用Claude Code。

结果不到一年，就开始认真研究员工的Token到底该由谁来付钱了。

我觉得这个事情其实挺有代表性的。

过去一年，大家都在讨论AI能提高多少生产力，能不能取代程序员，甚至一个人能不能靠Agent干完一个团队的活。

但现在越来越多的企业发现，当员工真正开始高强度使用 Agent，每天让Claude Code跑任务、写代码、测试、迭代，Token消耗也会跟着迅速增长。

原来一个员工每个月几十美元的软件预算，可能突然变成几百甚至上千美元的推理成本。

而且Agent的使用越深入，这笔账就越需要认真算。

我倒觉得埃森哲这个做法可以理解，毕竟为客户做项目，成本总得有人承担。

但有意思的地方就在这里：一家天天帮助其他企业推进 AI 转型的咨询巨头，现在也开始面对 AI 大规模落地之后最现实的问题。

AI确实能干越来越多的活了，但这些活消耗的 \Token，究竟该算谁的成本？

interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

text:
Ledger 也开始造手机了？

849 美元，Android + Ledger OS 双系统，直接把冷钱包装进手机！

Ledger 发布了一款新设备 Ledger Atom，外观和普通安卓手机几乎一样，配备 6.8 英寸屏幕，支持 5G、第三方 App，甚至还能管理 AI Agent。

但它没有传统手机的语音通话和短信功能，官方把它定位成一台专门管理数字资产和隐私的安全设备。

双系统架构。

一套是 Android，负责上网、运行 App、管理资产；

另一套是独立安全芯片上的 Ledger OS，专门保管私钥和签名。

需要转账时，FPGA 芯片会从硬件层面切断 Android 对屏幕和触控的控制，让 Ledger OS 接管交易确认。

按照 Ledger 的设计，即使 Android 被黑客控制，也无法直接读取私钥或篡改安全模式里的交易信息。

它还有一个物理隐私开关，可以直接切断摄像头和麦克风的电路。

以后管理钱包、交易签名、授权 AI Agent 操作，都可以在同一台设备上完成，不需要再连接另一部手机。

创始版售价 849 美元，正式版预计 899 美元，计划 2027 年夏季交付。

硬件隔离能保护私钥，却无法阻止用户主动签署恶意交易。

尤其最近 Ledger 刚经历硬件供应链安全争议，大家最关心的恐怕还是它能不能真正做到安全。

An Anthropic employee told Dwarkesh that AIs will match humans at AI research within 9 months.

text:
啊？？微软居然自己训出了一个2.8T参数的基础模型？？？

昨天晚上，微软AI负责人 @mustafasuleyman  宣布，他们已经完成了新一代基础模型MAI-Base-2的预训练，而且专门发布了一篇技术报告，介绍整个训练过程。

我看了一下，这次微软拿出来的东西确实挺有意思。

首先是模型规模。

MAI-Base-2采用MoE架构，总参数量达到2.8T（2.8 万亿），每个Token激活约80B参数。

@Microsoft  使用了 16,000 张 NVIDIA GB200 GPU，在今年 8 月至 9 月期间，花费 38 天完成了整个预训练，训练规模达到 50T Tokens。

而且这次还是原生多模态模型，采用了不依赖独立视觉编码器的VLM架构。训练数据中包含大量图文混合内容，视觉数据占训练Token的 18%。

然后是性能。

$MSFT 声称，MAI-Base-2在内部保留测试集上的表现，已经超过了他们测试过的所有开放权重模型。

这次他们专门找来了DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base、Kimi K3、Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B等模型进行对比，覆盖文本、代码、数学、科学等多个领域。

其中有一个数字我觉得很值得关注。

微软称，根据Scaling Law拟合结果，在达到与 DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base相同的预训练评测水平时，MAI-Base-2 所使用的训练方案可以实现 4.2～12.3 倍的 FLOPs 效率提升。

技术报告里还详细介绍了他们怎么优化 MoE、Muon 优化器以及训练基础设施。

比如，他们将MoE层的计算利用率从24%提高到了35%，使得模型可以在每一层都采用MoE。

还有一点，微软特意强调，整个预训练的数据都由自己处理，没有依赖其他模型的蒸馏数据。

当然，目前MAI-Base-2刚完成预训练，还在进行后训练。微软公布的这些结果主要是预训练阶段的评测，实际推理、Coding和Agent能力还需要等后续成绩。

但我觉得这次发布最有意思的地方，其实是微软正在建立自己的完整模型研发体系。

过去几年，微软一直是 @OpenAI  最大的合作伙伴之一，旗下大量AI产品也依赖OpenAI提供模型能力。

现在微软自己已经能独立完成2.8T级别的前沿基础模型预训练，数据、模型、训练基础设施，以及后续的产品交付，都在逐步建立自己的体系。

而且微软已经表示，未来计划通过Foundry向可信合作伙伴授权模型权重。

这背后其实是一个挺重要的变化。

微软现在有能力自己训练前沿基础模型了，也开始认真争夺基础模型层的话语权。

更有意思的是，微软在报告最后还提到，MAI-Base-3 的准备工作已经开始。

接下来就看后训练能做到什么水平了。

text:
熬了一晚，用@DeerbitAI 配合做完了这份分析存储芯片和光通信的报告。言论和情绪热度是拿来看的，别拿来买。说好跟大家分享出来的：

企业级存储这轮利润，我倾向于看到 2027 年。光通信里，我更看好有 NVIDIA 出资支持、又拿到多年采购承诺的核心供应商。但不站“AI 需求很强”和“股票很便宜” 。

存储：

常规 DRAM 合约价今年 Q1 实际环比上涨约 93–98%，Q4 的预测涨幅是 10–15%。涨价仍在继续，但是速度不一样了。企业级 SSD 全年容量需求预计增长超过 80%，大部分新增供应都已有买家，PC 厂商也还在为 2027 年可能的 DRAM 紧缺提前采购。

这才是我认为企业级存储的利润窗口看到明年的依据。需求和供给约束有支撑，但年初那种涨价速度不存在延续。

所以看 $MU、 $SNDK ，我更重视企业级业务占比、实际出货和利润率。收入增长都很好看，需要再看留下多久的利润。如果企业级订单转弱，或者供给追上来，这个判断就要调整。之后我会持续跟踪发布利润情况。

再说光通信:

扩产已经有大客户承诺出钱了。

今年 3 月, $NVDA  就宣布分别向 $LITE、 $COHR  投资 20 亿美元，支持研发、产能和运营；合作另有多年采购承诺和未来产能获取权。

合计 40 亿美元的投资承诺，加上未来采购。这让我更愿意把这两家公司放在前排：客户愿意为未来供应投入资本，本身就是很有分量的需求信号。

但供应商能交付多少、良率如何、扩产后能留下多少每股现金流，会决定这份承诺最终值多少钱，也会持续的跟进研究。

最后说下为什么我不同意“便宜”。

假设盈利比预期少 40%，股价不动，对应的 PE 就会上升约 67%。图里的 6.8 倍，会变成约 11.4 倍。

周期高点的利润如果维持不住，有些“便宜”，可能只是分母太乐观大家算的高兴。

对 AI 的未来我一直是乐观派。觉得企业级存储的高利润撑不到 2027 年的欢迎拿数据说话。

完整报告有点长，评论“报告”，我DM。
